text:
Following the Democratic gains in Congress on November 3, questions have arisen about whether the administration’s immigration policies are likely to change.

We do not anticipate significant changes to U.S. immigration policy affecting the business community or the issuance of nonimmigrant and immigrant visas. The executive branch that oversees and directs the Department of Homeland Security and its policy directives are likely to remain largely unchanged.

Key Takeaways from Our Immigration Team

The current climate should serve as the planning baseline for employers or foreign national employees for the remainder of this term. Organizations that build procedures for timelines, documentation, and contingency planning around today's stricter standards will be better positioned than those waiting for a policy shift.

Changes to Immigration Policy Under Trump Administration

Since President Trump’s inauguration in January 2025, the administration’s guidance has resulted in increased denial rates across visa, immigration, and adjustment of status cases. A substantial shift in policy interpretation appears unlikely. Major changes during this administration have included travel bans, pauses in immigrant visa processing, wage-weighted H-1B lottery regulations, four-year limits on student visas, the termination of many longstanding TPS programs, and stricter public charge rules.

USCIS has also issued policy memoranda establishing shorter response periods for requests for additional evidence and asserting its authority to deny cases without first seeking further clarification of the submissions.

In January, when Congress reconvenes with a majority of democrats in the House and Senate, we may see bills put forward for comprehensive legalization on the immigration agenda. It would remain to be seen if these bills might pass both houses and actually materialize.

title: Jewish groups divided over Stephen Miller's appointment as White House chief of staff
description:
Right-leaning pro-Israel groups hailed US President Donald Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as the next White House chief of staff, welcoming the Jewish aide’s appointment as a safeguard against antisemitism in an era marked by an increase in attacks on Jews and Israel.
Liberal Jewish groups expressed alarm, saying his hardline politics endangered the community.

text:
Right-leaning pro-Israel groups hailed US President Donald Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as the next White House chief of staff, welcoming the Jewish aide’s appointment as a safeguard against antisemitism in an era marked by an increase in attacks on Jews and Israel. Liberal Jewish groups expressed alarm, saying his hardline politics endangered the community.

In a letter congratulating Miller, groups including the Combat Antisemitism Movement, the Louis D. Brandeis Center for Human Rights Under Law, and the Zionist Organization of America expressed an interest in working with Miller to “hold institutions accountable when they fail to protect Jewish Americans from discrimination and harassment.”

The writers, who also included the American Association of Jewish Lawyers and Jurists, the Coalition for Jewish Values and the Israeli-American Civic Action Network, described Miller’s appointment as “a meaningful reflection of the longstanding contributions of Jewish Americans to public service.”

Just days after the Republican Party incurred massive losses in the midterm elections, Trump announced that he was replacing former chief of staff Susie Wiles with Miller, who had previously served as her deputy. In a Truth Social post, he described Miller as one of his “most trusted advisors.”

The chief of staff holds one of the most powerful White House positions, acting as a gatekeeper to the president and helping to shape his daily agenda.

Liberal Jewish voices warned that Trump’s promotion of Stephen Miller to the role of White House chief of staff could make Jewish communities more vulnerable.

“We expect this appointment to only reinforce some of the most dangerous ways the administration has normalized antisemitism and broader extremism,” Amy Spitalnick, CEO of the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, noting Miller’s embrace of anti-immigrant rhetoric popular on the far right.

Spitalnick said there is a throughline between the hard-line immigration policies Miller has shaped as a longtime confidant to Trump and the flourishing of antisemitism in recent years.

“At the core of the anti-immigrant agenda Miller has spearheaded are deeply antisemitic conspiracy theories about ‘replacement’ and ‘invasion’ that have already fueled a cycle of deadly violence targeting Jews and others,” she said.

Jewish community divided over best means of combating antisemitism

The dueling sentiments from across the Jewish political spectrum were a signal of how divided the community has become during the second Trump term over the best means of combating antisemitism: Through aggressive policing of elite institutions, which Trump favors, or through opposition to what liberal groups say is the president’s systematic corrosion of civil rights protections.

The groups on the right that welcomed Miller’s appointment have generally been pleased by the steps Trump has taken to counter antisemitism on the left. In January 2025, Trump issued an executive order requiring new measures for combating antisemitism.

The Justice Department then launched a multi-agency Task Force to Combat Antisemitism. This past May, the department announced the formation of an Advisory Committee on Antisemitism, while emphasizing a “commitment to protecting Americans from unlawful discrimination and antisemitic threats.” Much of the focus has been on allegations of antisemitic harassment on university campuses.

While it’s unclear what Miller will do on these specific issues, his supporters see his key role as likely to strengthen such efforts.

Miller has longstanding links to Trump, including on a personal level. Miller’s wedding officiant at the Trump DC hotel was Rabbi Aryeh Lightstone, who was involved with the administration’s Abraham Accords to establish peaceful relations between Israel and several Arab neighbors.

But Miller’s critics have pointed out that he, along with Trump and other top Republicans have embraced troubling conspiracy theories that can be linked to Jews. Namely, that Democrats want to flood America with immigrants who are likely to vote against Republicans. At Trump’s October 2024 campaign rally at Madison Square Garden, Miller declared, “America is for Americans and Americans only.”

A more extreme version of the conspiracy theory, which blames Jews for organizing an “invasion” of people of color to replace whites, fueled a number of deadly attacks over the past decade, including the massacre at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh in 2018.

The White House press office, which fields media communications for the chief of staff, did not respond to requests for comment.

Spitalnick also slammed the current administration for failing to “protect the civil rights of Jewish – and all – people,” by rolling back programs aimed at countering hate, including at the Office for Civil Rights in the Department of Education and extremism prevention programs at the Department of Homeland Security.

Spitalnick also referred to a 2019 letter sent by Jewish Democratic members of Congress urging Trump to dismiss Miller, who was his senior adviser at the time. The lawmakers argued that his “support for white nationalist and virulently anti-immigrant tropes is wholly unacceptable and disqualifying for a government employee.”

Regarding the current appointment, Spitalnick warned that Miller’s role could “make Jewish and so many other vulnerable communities less safe, instead of advancing the civil rights and pro-democracy policies we know are inherent to our security.”

“As the president and vice president are now seemingly pinning the US election results on Israel, we should be concerned about further scapegoating of the Jewish and Israeli American communities,” she added.

The liberal pro-Israel lobby J Street, meanwhile, posted a Haaretz analysis that likened Miller to Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right minister in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition known for his extreme nationalistic rhetoric.

“Stephen Miller and Itamar Ben-Gvir both owe their prominence and access to power to their enablers – Trump and Netanyahu – and both traffic in racism and nativism to attempt to build power and incite fear,” the J Street post stated.

Robert Reich, US secretary of labor in the Clinton administration, wrote in a Facebook post that Miller’s appointment was “not a positive development for anyone interested in mending our government or healing our nation.” Reich, who is Jewish and also served in the Ford and Carter administrations, expressed concern that Miller would have outsized influence on the president’s decisions.

“Miller is bigoted, xenophobic, and vicious — the architect and chief advocate of Trump’s loathsome immigration policy,” Reich stated, accusing him of conducting a “brutal Kristallnacht against undocumented immigrants.” Kristallnacht refers to the wave of deadly anti-Jewish violence in parts of Nazi-occupied Europe in 1938.

Katie Miller, who is also Jewish and married to Stephen Miller, defended her husband this weekend, after Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed called him a “broken man” on ABC’s This Week with George Stephanopoulos.

text:
Driving to the doctor

Aliya Rahman

Aliya Rahman, who is autistic and disabled, was driving to a doctor’s appointment in January when she reached an intersection where protesters were confronting immigration officers. She said several agents swarmed her car and yelled at her to move out of the way. They broke her window and pulled her from the car.

“Nobody ever asked me for ID, my name or my citizenship,” Rahman said.

DHS said agents detained Rahman because she ignored their instructions. She denied that, saying that she was confused and saw no way to move without hitting someone.

She said agents then shackled her feet and held her in a detention cell at the federal building. She passed out and awoke in a hospital room. She was released without charges later that day.

Sleeping in her bedroom

Jeyli Salguero

In January, Jeyli Salguero awoke when she heard someone banging on her door and then the sound of the door breaking open. Federal agents, their guns drawn, rushed inside and told her family they were looking for her brother.

“We told them yes he lived here, but he doesn’t live here anymore,” Salguero said she told the agents. “They started getting a bit more angry and were like, ‘Since you’re not collaborating, we’re gonna start checking your status.’” An agent grabbed Salguero’s phone and ordered Salguero to face a wall. In an ongoing lawsuit, Salguero has said that the agents entered the home without a valid warrant. DHS said that agents were searching for a fugitive, and that it has suspended the policy of entering homes without a judicial warrant.

Her father has temporary protected status but had not received paperwork showing that his status had been renewed. He was handcuffed and then detained for a month. Salguero’s older sister, who was undocumented, was handcuffed and deported to El Salvador. The rest of her family is now planning to sell their home and move to El Salvador. “It’s been a mental toll — a very big mental toll on all of us.”

Protesting the Broadview ICE Detention Center

Juan Muñoz

Juan Muñoz, an elected member of the Board of Trustees that governs Oak Park Township outside of Chicago, was participating in an October protest outside the Broadview ICE Detention Center when he said that he was knocked to the ground by the commander of the Border Patrol. “When I looked up,” Muñoz recalled, “it was Commander Greg Bovino who was standing over me.” In depositions, Bovino denied tackling Muñoz, saying videos of the arrests showed no “reportable uses of force.”

Muñoz said agents knocked away his phone and zip-tied his hands. “Every agent that I encountered, I told the same thing, ‘I’m an elected official.’ No response.”

Muñoz was held inside of the detention center for eight hours before agents dropped him off at a gas station, without explaining why he’d been held. “They were over capacity, keeping people for way longer than that facility was intended for,” he recalled about the detention center. “It was filthy. They don’t have proper hygiene products or are able to feed people properly,” Muñoz said. DHS did not comment on his specific detention. But, referring to Muñoz and other protesters detained with him, it posted a comment on social media, saying, “We will NOT allow violent activists to lay hands on our law enforcement.”

Responding to ICE in a hospital

Jessie Fuentes

In October 2025, Chicago Alderperson Jessie Fuentes said she rushed to a local emergency room because she’d been told that ICE agents had been spotted inside. She identified herself to the agents as an elected official and began asking them whether they’d obtained a warrant. Video taken of the incident shows that agents grabbed and handcuffed her. Fuentes was held for 15 minutes, during which time members of her staff posted the video online and her supporters gathered outside the hospital to demand her release. DHS, in a written statement, told ProPublica that Fuentes was put in “handcuffs but NEVER placed under arrest.”

“These individuals are operating above the law,” Fuentes said. “They’re operating with impunity.”

Monitoring ICE operations

Caitlin Arwen

Caitlin Arwen was scrolling through a Facebook group for moms in October when she noticed a shared post that said immigration agents were detaining people in her town, which is about an hour’s drive outside of Chicago. Later that day she saw some of the vehicles that had been posted on Facebook and began following them, honking her horn to alert residents of their presence. One of the vehicles slammed on its brakes. U.S. marshals who were working with ICE surrounded her car, broke her window and pulled her out.

“They threw me on the broken glass, and they were all on top of me. I couldn’t breathe,” she recalled. Arwen estimates she was kept handcuffed face down on broken glass for roughly 35 minutes. “They taunted me, took photos of me, called me names, berated me and acted like I was somehow deserving of this.” DHS referred questions about Arwen’s arrest to the U.S. Marshals Service. A spokesperson for the service said Arwen’s arrest was a “task force arrest” and declined further comment.

Arwen was taken to a hospital, where marshals handcuffed her to the bed. After she was discharged, agents shackled her and moved her to a DHS detention facility, where she was not allowed to contact a lawyer or anyone else for help. “I didn’t have access to water or food the whole time,” said Arwen, adding that she was held for several hours. “Nobody showed me their badge all day. No one identified themselves. No one once read me my Miranda rights.”

Though federal officials declined to prosecute Arwen, state authorities charged her with traffic violations and obstruction of law enforcement. She has pleaded not guilty.

title: ICE deportations and arrests hit record high as Trump faces reckoning over immigration crackdown
description:
ICE also reported more than 491,000 immigration arrests during the fiscal year ending Sept. 30, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests — another record, according to DHS.
But they also arrive at a politically complicated moment for Mr. Trump.
"Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE's history.
It is also something Mr. Trump made a central focus of his campaign in his successful 2024 presidential run.
But the sharp decline in illegal border crossings and the surge in ICE enforcement come as the political landscape has shifted, too.
text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported a record 483,200 people in fiscal year 2026, according to new Department of Homeland Security figures obtained by CBS News, marking a historic escalation in President Trump's signature immigration crackdown, even as voters grapple with the increase in interior enforcement.

The total number of individuals deported represents the highest annual figure in ICE's reported history, surpassing the law enforcement agency's previous record of 442,640 in fiscal year 2025. ICE also reported more than 491,000 immigration arrests during the fiscal year ending Sept. 30, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests — another record, according to DHS. Administrative arrests are those in which alleged undocumented immigrants are arrested for civil violations rather than criminal charges.

The records underscore a defining feature of Mr. Trump's second presidency — a sweeping enforcement campaign reshaped by dramatic immigration policy and the operational expansion of the federal law enforcement footprint in communities far from the border. But they also arrive at a politically complicated moment for Mr. Trump.

Following sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections, the president has publicly acknowledged that parts of his deportation campaign may have gone too far. Yet that admission was coupled with a decision to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of many of his most restrictive immigration policies, to White House chief of staff.

These new figures underscore a tension further reflected within American public opinion. CBS News polls have shown widespread support for border security alongside increasing discomfort with how immigration laws are enforced in communities nationwide.

Behind the record-breaking numbers

According to DHS, the new deportation total is approximately 18% higher than the 409,849 removals ICE recorded in fiscal year 2012, during the Obama administration, a longstanding agency benchmark. The new record is also nearly 78% higher than the 271,484 deportations recorded in fiscal year 2024, the last full fiscal year under President Biden.

ICE reported a total of 50,925 arrests in the month of August alone, eclipsing the previous monthly high set in July. By September, the agency was still carrying out more than 48,000 arrests a month, according to DHS, reflecting a sustained rapid pace of enforcement.

Still, a record number of reported deportations does not necessarily mean a record number of formal removal orders carried out. ICE's deportation figures do not include governmentwide statistics, which include actions by U.S. Customs and Border Protection and distinguish between formal removals, voluntary returns and voluntary departures. Using broader measures, nationwide deportations reached higher thresholds during portions of the early 2000s.

A new analysis published Wednesday by Syracuse University's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, or TRAC, raised additional questions about how DHS counts deportations. Based on case-by-case federal immigration records, researchers found that formal removals accounted for just 63% of deportations in July and August 2026, with the remainder consisting of voluntary departures and returns.

"I couldn't be prouder of the brave men and women of ICE, who just broke more historic records," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement Thursday that accompanied the new numbers. "Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE's history. September 2026 was the best September in ICE's history in terms of arrests. The total number of ICE arrests in Fiscal Year 2026 was more than all three full fiscal years under Biden combined, as the patriots of ICE work around the clock to make America safe again. Thanks to President Trump's leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives."

The "worst of the worst" — and a broader reality

The Trump administration has consistently defended its campaign as a public safety mission, boasting arrests and deportations of people accused or convicted of serious crimes, those DHS has repeatedly described as the "worst of the worst." It is also something Mr. Trump made a central focus of his campaign in his successful 2024 presidential run.

In its accounting of the 2026 fiscal year's deportations, DHS has highlighted several such cases: Raul Genesis Ortiz Moran, a Mexican national charged with second-degree murder and aggravated sexual assault in connection with the death of a 2-year-old girl in Virginia. The Louisa County Sheriff's Office independently confirmed the charges.

The department also cited Soili Xiomara Aparicio-Santos, a Honduran national deported in April who, according to DHS, was convicted of attempting to murder her newborn son in New York.

The cases illustrate the serious public safety threats immigration officers can encounter, but are not representative of hundreds of thousands in arrests.

DHS has repeatedly argued that immigrants without U.S. criminal records can still have criminal histories overseas or pose security risks to the public. The department also often notes that immigration law alone justifies civil arrest and deportation. Still, federal authorities have not publicly provided comprehensive evidence showing how many arrested immigrants without U.S. criminal records have committed crimes abroad.

An August CBS News analysis found that in July 2026, for the first time during Mr. Trump's second term, more than half of ICE arrests involved immigrants who had neither criminal convictions nor pending criminal charges. That analysis also found that approximately 6% of people booked into ICE detention during Mr. Trump's second administration had convictions for violent crimes.

Separately, the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute found that only about 20% of approximately 980,000 deportations carried out collectively by ICE and CBP between January 2025 and July 2026 involved someone with a criminal conviction. Among deported immigrants who had lived in the U.S. for at least two years, 71% had no criminal conviction.

Many Americans believe immigration enforcement has gone too far

According to CBS News national exit polling from the 2026 midterm elections, 58% of voters said the Trump administration's immigration enforcement had gone too far. Another 22% said it had been about right, while 20% believed it had not gone far enough.

While support for border security remains high, it does not necessarily translate into support for tactics and operations used to enforce immigration law in American cities and towns nationwide.

In a "60 Minutes interview," the president acknowledged that his immigration crackdown had taken a political toll.

"I think it was too tough," Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes" correspondent Ross Douthat.

Trump added that his administration received high marks for securing the border and removing dangerous criminals, but faced criticism for deporting longtime immigrants who held jobs, worked in industries such as landscaping and hospitality, and in some cases paid taxes.

Mr. Trump also expressed interest in working with congressional Democrats in the new Congress to create and pass immigration legislation, a shocking acknowledgment from a president who built much of his political identity around the promise of mass deportations.

A new White House chief of staff

As Stephen Miller — a longtime aide of President Trump who has historically pushed for higher arrest targets — takes the helm as chief of staff, multiple administration officials tell CBS News that they do not expect the crackdown to slow down following the election.

In recent weeks, ICE officials have been instructed to aim for approximately 19,000 arrests per week, according to sources familiar with the agency's planning — a target established before the midterms and substantially above its historical pace.

The targets come as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, with some voicing support for more scrutiny of the administration's immigration operations, spending and enforcement tactics. But their ability to force changes could be constrained by the billions already appropriated to ICE, in addition to presidential veto power.

A sweeping tax and spending law signed by Mr. Trump in July 2025 allocated roughly $170 billion for immigration enforcement and border security, including $75 billion in additional funding for ICE. Of that, $45 billion was designated to expand immigrant detention capacity, while nearly $30 billion was allocated for arrests, transportation, deportation operations and additional personnel.

For years, Mr. Trump's immigration message rested on a premise that resonated with millions of voters: the U.S. needed to regain control of its border and enforce its immigration laws.

But the sharp decline in illegal border crossings and the surge in ICE enforcement come as the political landscape has shifted, too.

The question facing Mr. Trump in the final two years of his presidency is whether an enforcement campaign that has achieved unprecedented scale by ICE's own accounting can harness the confidence of an American public increasingly divided over how the presidential mandate to crack down on immigration is being carried out.

title: Democratic representatives elected in the midterms demand immigration reform at the Capitol | U.S.
description:
But there were also new faces, freshly elected on November 3, who have come to Washington hoping to shake up a Congress that for decades has been unable to pass immigration reform.
This is an opportunity to address the issue of immigration reform.
And, in part, that requires us to push hard for immigration reform.
“To the Republicans: understand that we’ve lost the party; you lost Texas, you lost the Latino vote, you lost the House of Representatives and the Senate.
It’s time for President Trump to step aside so we can get real results.
text:
November 11 is Veterans Day in the United States, but stetsons proliferated Wednesday in front of the Capitol. Politicians and business leaders from Texas and Arizona joined forces to demand immigration reform outside the landmark complex that houses both chambers of Congress, which will be under Democratic control starting in January. Familiar faces from the Senate, such as Arizona Senator Rubén Gallego, and from the House of Representatives, including Texas representatives Henry Cuellar, Vicente González, Joaquín Castro, Verónica Escobar, and Sylvia García, were present.

But there were also new faces, freshly elected on November 3, who have come to Washington hoping to shake up a Congress that for decades has been unable to pass immigration reform. JoAnna Mendoza, from Arizona, and Bobby Pulido, the former Tejano singer who was elected to represent Texas’s 15th district, were among them. “In the last election, on November 3, we sent a clear message: we are tired of cruelty and we are tired of corruption,” he said.

Pulido was one of the protagonists of the midterms that helped turn an emblematic Republican state blue — Texas became a key example of the Democrats’ sweeping success in the elections. In his region, arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have wreaked havoc on families and the economy. “I am married to a Mexican. My son is from a mixed-status family. We need to fix this. And I want to tell you that I have taken note of the members who are here right now. Count on my commitment to work on this tirelessly. This is extremely important,” he added.

Pulido introduced his colleague Leticia Gutiérrez, a previously unknown face in Washington who will be sworn in as a congresswoman in January after defeating the Republican candidate despite her campaign’s limited resources. Her 9th district is where Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado was killed in July by gunfire from an ICE agent. At the altar where he was honored, residents placed their stickers on election day to show they had voted with immigration policy in mind.

“We should not be spending money on these racist policies that keep targeting our working communities, like Lorenzo Salgado’s, who was killed in my Magnolia Park community. That is my neighborhood, and my family lives there. He was not just a father; he was everyone’s father. Enough. We need to move forward,” Gutiérrez said.

Rejection of the Trump administration’s immigration policy was decisive in the Republican defeat in the midterms, and Democrats want to use the majorities they will enjoy in both chambers to push for a reform that would make it easier to legalize undocumented immigrants who have lived in the country for years.

Joaquín Castro, the representative from San Antonio, Texas, said “change is on the way.” In January, “we will have a Republican president — President Trump — and a Congress with a strong Democratic presence. This is an opportunity to address the issue of immigration reform. It is an opportunity to be true to the history of this country. History tells us that our nation became the most powerful and prosperous on Earth not in spite of immigrants, but because of them. I want us to legislate along those lines,” he said.

Deal with Trump

Rubén Gallego, for his part, recalled how the Latino vote was crucial in delivering victory to the Democrats, largely because of the harassment they face due to the racial profiling used in the deportation campaign.

“Latinos are giving Democrats the chance to win their vote back. And, in part, that requires us to push hard for immigration reform. That includes the possibility of reaching an agreement with Donald Trump,” the senator said.

Latinos voted en masse against the Republicans after a portion of their electorate switched parties in 2024 to support Trump’s return to the White House.

In an interview on CBS’s 60 Minutes on Sunday, the president acknowledged that his immigration policy had been too harsh, resulting in the deportation of many migrants who had worked and paid taxes in the U.S. for years. However, the appointment of Stephen Miller — an advocate of the hardest line — as chief of staff sent contradictory signals about his intentions.

Among the business leaders demonstrating in front of the Capitol was Mario Guerrero, president of the South Texas Builders Association. His sector is one of the most-affected by the labor shortage caused by ICE arrests.

Guerrero is one of the Republicans who, after voting for Trump three times, chose to cast his vote for the Democrats. “To the Republicans: understand that we’ve lost the party; you lost Texas, you lost the Latino vote, you lost the House of Representatives and the Senate. It’s time for President Trump to step aside so we can get real results. Every election is important, but these were historic. Texas has gone Democratic,” he said. And he issued a warning: “A friendly reminder to my friends in the Democratic Party: don’t mess with us. And don’t squander this opportunity, like Biden and Obama did.”

text:
A St. Peter, Minnesota, nurse is suing the federal government, alleging Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents pointed guns at her, pulled her from her car and knelt on her back as she recorded them during Operation Metro Surge, court documents say.

Jamie Martens, 47, filed the lawsuit Monday seeking $550,000 in damages for alleged assault, battery, false arrest, negligence and infliction of emotional distress.

The documents say Martens was observing and recording ICE from her vehicle in the St. Peter area on Jan. 29 when four agents pointed their guns at her and "forcefully tore her out of her car." The suit says they dragged her across the pavement and knelt on her lower back.

Martens was "terrified that the agents were going to murder her," the documents say. The suit says the agents' actions aggravated injuries from hip surgery she had just had.

The agents began driving Martens to the Whipple Federal Building, the epicenter of the immigration crackdown in Minnesota, but returned her to St. Peter after the city's police chief contacted ICE and told them to bring her back.

The suit calls the arrest "a complete failure of training and supervision" and says the agents "acted irrationally and conducted themselves unprofessionally."

Video of Martens' arrest went viral on social media. The Department of Homeland Security responded in a post on X, calling her an "agitator" and claiming she tried to ram the agents with her car.

title: At least 23 states considered laws governing ICE and schools this year - NPR
description:
Texas state law prohibits local entities, including campus police, from obstructing federal immigration enforcement.
"The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement, and instead trusts them to use common sense."
An NPR analysis found that, so far this year, at least 23 states have considered new legislative proposals — in some cases multiple proposals — governing federal immigration officers and K-12 public schools.
At least eight states already had laws governing immigration enforcement and K-12 schools at the start of 2026.
But after the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year, lawmakers considered at least five different proposals around ICE and schools.
text:
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

Andrea Garza says it's not unusual or alarming when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are spotted near a school in Laredo, Texas, a border town.

In other parts of the country, "seeing the presence of border patrol would be, you know, different, maybe shocking. Just something from another world, right?" she said. "It's something very normal here."

Garza is a school leader with the United Independent School District , which serves Laredo. Federal data shows 94% of her district's community is Hispanic. Garza said some families have been in Laredo for generations, while others came more recently, and the federal government is one of her area's largest employers.

She said she knows what she would do if ICE comes knocking: If they don't have a warrant or subpoena, they don't get in.

"We serve 'in loco parentis' for students," she said, meaning "in place of a parent" when the students' rights are challenged.

"It's not interpreted, in the way we see it, as interfering with the law," Garza explained. "It is more just verifying that we are all following the law."

Texas state law prohibits local entities, including campus police, from obstructing federal immigration enforcement. But NPR found no state laws that directly address how much access these officers should have in K-12 public schools.

And it's not just Texas. Many states lack clear policies governing what these interactions should look like. Recent federal changes haven't helped.

At the beginning of President Trump's second term, the administration rescinded a policy that protected schools, among other "sensitive" places, from immigration enforcement.

"Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America's schools and churches to avoid arrest," a statement from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said at the time. "The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement, and instead trusts them to use common sense."

In some places, school leaders and researchers say Trump's immigration policies have led to enrollment drops.

DHS, which houses ICE, has said that ICE does not raid or target schools.

But reporting from K-12 Dive shows the last academic year still saw several incidents of ICE agents on school grounds. When that happens, education leaders often rely on a patchwork of state and district policies to know what to do.

This year, many state legislatures tried to update those policies.

An NPR analysis found that, so far this year, at least 23 states have considered new legislative proposals — in some cases multiple proposals — governing federal immigration officers and K-12 public schools.

The vast majority of the state proposals NPR reviewed — 35 out of 40 — sought to limit federal officers' access to K-12 campuses and students; only one proposal — in Mississippi — sought to ensure that schools cooperate with ICE. The rest didn't explicitly limit or increase access or cooperation.

Thomas Saenz is president and general counsel of the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, an organization that advocates for Latinos living in the U.S. He said the elimination of the federal sensitive locations policy is likely driving many states to establish their own protections, "belts and suspenders, as they say."

But while lawmakers seem to agree there's a need for clearer policies, in many places, they've struggled to find consensus over what those policies should be. Of the 40 proposals NPR reviewed, only 11 became laws by the beginning of this school year.

From requiring a warrant to requiring cooperation

Minnesota, Arizona, Delaware, Georgia, Maine and Nebraska are among the state legislatures that considered restricting ICE access to schools.

Several of these proposals specified the need for a warrant. Others aimed to restrict what school police and school resource officers, or SROs, can and can't do, including when it comes to immigration-related arrests.

On the other side of the spectrum, Mississippi considered and passed a law requiring government entities, including school districts, to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement.

And a few states considered requiring school boards to adopt policies outlining how they would respond to immigration authorities on school property.

At least eight states already had laws governing immigration enforcement and K-12 schools at the start of 2026. A few of those states — including Connecticut, Maryland and Oregon — considered additional legislation this year.

Recent state proposals have also aimed to allow public schools to charge tuition for students who aren't U.S. citizens or legal immigrants. Such proposals would challenge the decades-old landmark Supreme Court ruling Plyler v. Doe, which established that all children, regardless of immigration status, have the right to a free K-12 public education.

NPR did not include these proposals in its analysis. According to reporting from Education Week, as of July, at least two states were considering proposals challenging Plyler. Similar efforts failed in at least five other states.

Proposals target sensitive locations and student enrollment

Following the Trump administration's decision to rescind the policy protecting "sensitive" places, some states have been trying to set their own rules around where immigration enforcement can and can't go.

A few states — including West Virginia, Hawaii and Kansas — made a push this year to restrict ICE access by designating school campuses as sensitive locations. None of those three states' proposals passed.

Some states already have laws that explicitly ban or restrict these types of sanctuary policies. That didn't stop Missouri from considering a proposal this spring to limit school cooperation with immigration enforcement. An existing state law prohibiting municipalities from adopting sanctuary policies and requiring cooperation calls into question how far such a proposal could go.

Lawmakers in Tennessee considered multiple proposals this year from across the political spectrum, including one to track K-12 students' legal status, which opponents argued was part of an effort to challenge Plyler, and another that would require schools to immediately notify all students, parents and employees if immigration officers were on school grounds.

"As legislators, we cannot make informed decisions without data, and right now we simply do not know what the attendance is in our school systems across the state, regarding children who are here illegally," Tennessee Rep. Jason Zachary (R-Knoxville) said in a March hearing, where he spoke in favor of the measure that would have required schools to report students who are undocumented.

The bill did not make it to a final vote.

Meanwhile, another Tennessee proposal this year would have prohibited certain sensitive areas, including schools, from being used as staging areas, processing locations or operational bases for immigration enforcement.

"Everybody deserves to have a great learning environment, and it's hard to teach when you are worried that one of your students is going to be taken," Tennessee Rep. Gabby Salinas (D-Memphis), who sponsored that bill, told NPR. The proposal ultimately failed.

Minnesota principals await legislation

NPR was not able to find a pre-existing state law in Minnesota. But after the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year, lawmakers considered at least five different proposals around ICE and schools.

They ranged from stricter warrant requirements to mandating that schools develop procedures for handling requests from law enforcement. None of the five proposals made it to a final vote.

That means school leaders like Principal Kenny Newby are left waiting.

Newby leads Justice Alan Page Elementary School in Maplewood, Minn., just outside the Twin Cities. He said if ICE ever comes to his school, his goal is to be kind, stay calm and be firm.

In the absence of state laws, he said he has his own district's policies to lean on: Staff members are supposed to welcome the ICE officers, start a conversation, ask for required paperwork and notify school-level administrators. Those administrators then reach out to district leaders.

If the officers have a warrant, they would be directed to the district office for next steps. Newby stressed: "We would not allow them to have direct contact with students."

Rob Reetz is the principal of Mounds View High School in nearby Arden Hills. He said it would be helpful to have a state law governing how schools are supposed to interact with federal immigration officers; if nothing else, a law like that could simplify interactions between districts.

Right now, Reetz said, if a sports team from his school travels to play against a team from another district and ICE shows up at the game, it's unclear which district's protocols adults should follow.

Still, if ICE does come knocking at his school, Reetz worries they won't necessarily follow rules set by the state or any other entity.

He said he remembers learning in January that federal agents had been spotted at Roosevelt High School in Minneapolis. At the time, MPR News reported that armed U.S. Border Patrol officers came onto school property during dismissal and "began tackling people, handcuffed two staff members and released chemical weapons on bystanders."

"It contributed to this uncertainty about how would our interactions go with immigration enforcement if they were to be on our campus," Reetz said.

Newby echoed these concerns. He said he and his staff would feel more supported if there were "clear expectations on keeping schools a safe place."

text:
President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I’m certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

Kaine is not alone.

“We’re gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We’ll have to see if he’s serious, but I don’t trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election’s lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they’ve been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it’s a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn’t chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

‘Beating the other side’

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

“I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He’s also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It’s not even a result. It’s almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn’t on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan’s election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia’s two-word statement on Election Day: “Lawyer up.”

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?” she said. “They’re going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

text:
An illegal immigrant with a prior criminal history was arrested Wednesday after allegedly dragging a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer with his car while fleeing an arrest attempt outside Chicago, federal officials said.

Jose Garnica-Naranjo, 32, a Mexican citizen, was taken into custody a day after violently resisting a targeted immigration enforcement operation, according to the Department of Homeland Security.

“This illegal alien used his vehicle to assault one of our ICE officers, hospitalizing the officer,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

“Thankfully, the officer has since been released from the hospital. This is just the latest example of the staggering rise in anti-ICE violence, with our officers facing a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them.”

ICE officers spotted Garnica-Naranjo leaving a home in Chicago Heights on Tuesday morning. Officers followed his car at a distance before attempting to initiate a traffic stop, DHS said.

When officers approached the vehicle, they instructed Garnica-Naranjo to turn off the engine, but he allegedly refused to comply.

“When officers attempted to remove him from the vehicle, Garnica accelerated and fled while an ERO Chicago officer was partially inside the vehicle through the driver-side window,” DHS said in a statement.

Garnica-Naranjo then drove over a raised center median planted with trees, causing the officer to be thrown from the vehicle, according to authorities.

As Garnica-Naranjo fled, his car struck the injured officer, who was subsequently taken to a local hospital.

The officer suffered contusions, cuts and scrapes to his legs, though tests confirmed no broken bones.

ICE noted that Garnica-Naranjo’s criminal record includes prior convictions for domestic violence and assault.

Mullin blamed violence against immigration officers on rhetoric from Democratic elected officials who have accused ICE of terrorizing neighborhoods during law enforcement operations.

“This is the result of anti-ICE rhetoric from sanctuary politicians like Illinois Governor JB Pritzker,” he said.

“DHS is calling on Governor Pritzker and all other sanctuary politicians to knock off this violent rhetoric and start cooperating with ICE before any more officers are injured in the line of duty.”

text:
The American publisher Crucial Comix has released a collection of political comics documenting the impact of immigration enforcement in the United States. Among the 25 contributions is a two-page comic about Minneapolis, written by Italian journalist Laura Cappon and illustrated by Gianluca Costantini.

In January 2026, Minneapolis became the center of a national confrontation over immigration enforcement, civil liberties, and the use of federal power. As immigration agents carried out raids across Minnesota, residents organized protests, documented arrests, and mobilized networks of solidarity. Journalists followed events on the streets, while artists began searching for another way to record what was happening.

Among them were three Minneapolis-based cartoonists, K. Woodman-Maynard, Jason Walz, and Trung Le Nguyen, who launched an artistic initiative called Cartoonists Against ICE. Their idea was to invite cartoonists to document the human consequences of the operations conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and other federal immigration authorities.

What began as an online call for solidarity grew into an international artistic response. In autumn 2026, the independent American publisher Crucial Comix transformed part of that collective effort into a printed anthology, bringing together 25 cartoonists whose work explores fear, resistance, solidarity, and the lives of communities affected by immigration enforcement.

Among the contributions is a two-page comic about Minneapolis, written by Italian journalist Laura Cappon and drawn by Gianluca Costantini, the artist and founder of ChannelDraw.

The collaboration brings together two forms of storytelling: journalism, which investigates and documents events, and comics, which can give those events a visual narrative. Their contribution connects the experiences of Minneapolis to a wider international discussion about immigration, state power, and the responsibilities of those who witness injustice.

The context in which the comic was created was especially dramatic.

On January 7, 2026, Renée Nicole Good, a 37-year-old Minneapolis resident and mother of three, was fatally shot by an ICE officer. Her death provoked widespread protests and intensified scrutiny of federal immigration operations in the city.

Seventeen days later, on January 24, another Minneapolis resident, 37-year-old intensive care nurse Alex Jeffrey Pretti, was shot and killed by a U.S. Border Patrol officer during a federal immigration enforcement operation. Pretti worked at a hospital serving military veterans. His death further escalated the confrontation between federal authorities, local communities, and demonstrators.

The two killings became defining moments in a broader crisis that raised serious questions about the use of force, the monitoring of federal agents, and the right of residents to document government operations.

For Laura Cappon, Minneapolis was not simply a distant news story.

As a journalist working for the Italian public broadcaster Rai, she traveled to Minnesota to report on the immigration crackdown for the television program In Mezz’ora. Together with her colleague Daniele Babbo, she accompanied local volunteers who monitored the movements of federal immigration officers and alerted communities to their presence.

On January 25, 2026, while the journalists were traveling in a vehicle with one of these volunteers, federal agents intercepted their car.

In footage broadcast by Rai, officers can be heard threatening to break the vehicle’s window and forcibly remove its occupants if they continued following and recording them. The journalists identified themselves as members of the press.

The incident attracted attention in Italy, where journalists’ organizations expressed concern about the treatment of reporters covering the operations.

It also revealed something about the atmosphere in Minneapolis: journalists documenting public events could themselves become targets of intimidation.

Cappon’s experience gives particular significance to her collaboration with Costantini. The two-page comic belongs to a form of visual journalism in which written accounts and drawings work together to preserve events that might otherwise be reduced to fleeting images in the news cycle.

For Costantini, whose work has long explored political repression, migration, freedom of expression, and human rights, the collaboration continues a sustained investigation into the relationship between drawing and contemporary history.

His approach is rooted in the belief that comics can do more than illustrate information. They can connect political events to individual experiences, make distant situations more immediate, and encourage readers to examine what lies behind the headlines.

The artistic collaboration with Laura Cappon also has an earlier history. In a 2024 interview published on ChannelDraw, Costantini discussed the importance of working with journalists and writers and mentioned a children’s publishing project he was developing with Cappon. The Minneapolis comic represents another expression of that dialogue between reporting and drawing, this time within an international collective publication.

The origins of Cartoonists Against ICE are closely connected to the experiences of artists living in Minnesota.

In January, Woodman-Maynard, Walz, and Nguyen created a recognizable visual template dominated by icy blue tones. They encouraged artists to produce short, personal comics about immigration enforcement in their communities and share them on social media using the hashtag #ICEOUTCOMICS.

The initiative was deliberately accessible. Artists did not need to produce long graphic narratives or follow an established editorial structure. A few panels could be enough to describe an encounter, document a frightening incident, express solidarity, or explain how a community was responding.

The project also emphasized the importance of individual testimony. Rather than attempting to construct a single comprehensive account of the immigration crackdown, it invited hundreds of artists to contribute their own observations and perspectives.

The result was a growing visual archive of experiences from Minneapolis and other American cities.

Cartoonists Against ICE Zine

Published by Crucial Comix, this anthology brings together work by 25 cartoonists across the United States documenting how the 2026 ICE raids affected people and their communities.

Buy from Crucial Comix

In an interview published by Crucial Comix in January 2026, Trung Le Nguyen described the fear that had entered his daily life, even though he was an American citizen. Living near George Floyd Square, he explained how the increased federal presence had changed something as ordinary as taking his dog outside.

His contribution illustrated how immigration enforcement could affect not only people facing deportation but also the wider communities around them.

The campaign soon attracted artists from across the United States and beyond. Among the cartoonists associated with the project and its publication are Lucy Knisley, Aubrey Hirsch, Rosemary Mosco, Jason Walz, K. Woodman-Maynard, and Trung Le Nguyen.

Their works move between personal testimony, documentary observation, political criticism, and reflections on solidarity.

The printed anthology published by Crucial Comix brings together 25 contributions in a 50-page zine measuring 5.5 by 8.5 inches. Priced at $12, the publication is designed to remain accessible while helping sustain independent comics and the communities represented in its pages.

The publisher has announced that all profits from the zine will be donated to the Minnesota Immigrant Rights Action Committee (MIRAC), an organization involved in defending immigrant rights and supporting community mobilization.

The publication therefore serves a dual purpose: it documents the events of 2026 while also raising money for people organizing in response to immigration enforcement.

Crucial Comix is an independent, cartoonist-run publisher founded in 2024, specializing in nonfiction comics and zines. Its editorial approach emphasizes collaboration, personal narratives, and the ability of comics to address subjects often overlooked by mainstream publishing.

The choice of a small printed zine is itself significant. In an age when political images circulate rapidly through social media before disappearing into constantly changing feeds, a physical publication offers another form of preservation.

The drawings become pages that can be kept, shared, circulated through bookstores, and revisited years after the events that inspired them.

That is particularly important for stories about immigration enforcement, where public attention frequently focuses on spectacular confrontations while neglecting the everyday experiences of people living under uncertainty.

Cartoonists Against ICE brings these experiences into a shared visual space. Its value lies not in offering a single interpretation, but in gathering different perspectives through the language of comics.

The contribution by Laura Cappon and Gianluca Costantini is part of that broader effort.

Two pages cannot tell the entire story of Minneapolis. But they can connect the work of a journalist who documented events in the city with the visual language of an artist who has spent decades portraying political struggles and defending human rights.

The project also connects with Costantini’s wider artistic research, including ICE: Faces Against Erasure, a ChannelDraw initiative exploring how portraits and drawings can confront the human consequences of immigration enforcement.

The Minneapolis story demonstrates that graphic journalism does not need to be monumental to be meaningful. Sometimes a short narrative is enough to preserve a testimony, draw attention to an injustice, or connect people separated by geography.

In Cartoonists Against ICE, the individual voices of journalists and artists become part of a collective record.

What began in Minneapolis as an urgent response to events on the streets has become a publication that carries those stories beyond the city, beyond the United States, and beyond the immediacy of the news.

And among its pages, the words of Laura Cappon and the drawings of Gianluca Costantini contribute to that memory.

Cartoonists Against ICE is published by Crucial Comix and is available through the publisher’s official website.

text:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of fatally shooting a Colombian national in July made what his sister considers anti-immigrant statements more than five years earlier, a copy of the emails shared with ABC News shows.

Relatives have previously identified David Brouillette as the ICE officer who fatally shot Johan Sebastián Duran Guerrero during an immigration enforcement operation in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13.

In an email dated Jan. 5, 2021, Elizabeth Emen, Brouillette's sister, invited him to record a video wishing her child a happy birthday.

Two days later, Brouillette responded, "you said that '[REDACTED] doesn't need a racist uncle in his life.'"

"Now you would like me to send your son a video for his birthday to be a part of that memory. YOUR choices affects YOUR kids," Brouillette added, according to one of the emails shared with ABC News.

Emen said Brouillette was referring to previous comments he had allegedly made about her former partner, a Colombian national, who was living in the country legally and with whom she has two children. The partner was a graduate student pursuing a Ph.D and at the time and had been dating Emen for five years, Emen said.

Emen shared the emails with ABC News. Names are redacted and they contain several typos. The emails were first reported by the New York Times.

According to one email, Emen responded that Brouillette had made "racist/xenophobic" comments about her partner "not being a citizen."

In a response dated Jan. 11, 2021, Brouillette said that the partner "can takes his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries."

"He does not emulate what it means to be an American..rather he emulates what it's like to be entitled and think he has a seat at a table that has no room for his (or your ignorance)," Brouillette wrote, according to the email.

Brouillette added that the partner's "bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers. He sure doesn't have a problem with freeloading off of our country, not claiming to be part of it..and then criticizing it," according to the email provided by Emen.

A friend of Emen's told ABC News they recalled speaking to her about her brother's comments soon after the exchange.

ABC News has been unable to reach David Brouillette for comment. A number belonging to him appears to have been disconnected. He did not respond to a request for comment sent to his last known email address.

Emen said that exchange ended her relationship with her brother.

"That was a very overt and excessive expression of his beliefs," she told ABC News in an interview. "When I saw his actions on July 13, I just couldn't believe that it had been allowed to get to that point. I can't believe that he was onboarded into a federal agency and provided a weapon."

At the time of the shooting, an ICE spokesperson said the agency was in Biddeford "conducting targeted surveillance on the last known address of an illegal alien with a final order of removal," and when an "illegal alien departed the residence in a vehicle," ICE agents "attempted to conduct a vehicle stop."

"The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and fearing for public safety an officer discharged his weapon," ICE said.

Maine Sen. Angus King told reporters Duran Guerrero was not the target of the operation.

Emen, a licensed therapist, said she grew up with her brother until she moved away to college. Most of their adult relationship was long distance through phone and video calls up until 2021, she said.

She first learned her brother was an ICE agent when she recognized him from a photo in an article about the shooting, she said. She's now calling the agency's hiring practices into question.

"If it was rigorous, I imagine they might have talked to the people close to him about his behavior, about his motivation to join, and whether or not he could do what was asked of him and use the least amount of force possible in his role," she said.

The Maine Attorney General's Office is investigating the shooting. Brouillette has not been charged with a crime.

In a social media post earlier Wednesday, Democratic lawmakers on the House Homeland Security said they will investigate the emails.

"Democrats will investigate who approved this hire and why ICE ignored the serious red flags," the lawmakers said.

DHS has not identified the officer. A spokesperson said the agency "will never confirm or deny attempts to dox our law enforcement officers."

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson did not identify the officer and defended the agency's hiring practices.

"Incoming ICE officers, many already with years of law enforcement experience, are onboarded in accordance with applicable policies and standards. Any claims of substandard training or vetting are FALSE. This administration is preserving ICE's reputation as one of the most elite law enforcement agencies not only in the U.S., but the entire world," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson did not comment on Brouillette's alleged remarks.

In a statement, an attorney representing Duran Guerrero's family said his death was the result of the "government's failure to properly screen" ICE agents.

"David Brouillette is the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training," attorney Sean P. Murphy said.

Emen says she's now coming forward about her brother in an attempt to seek justice and support for Duran Guerrero's family.

"I've watched their speaking out after learning about my brother's actions and repeatedly my thoughts and prayers have been with them and I'll do what I can to support an investigation," she said.
