The federal government claims a legal dispute over the H-2A agricultural guestworker program could have far-reaching implications for its regulatory enforcement capabilities.

The U.S. Supreme Court recently heard oral arguments in the case, which centers on the Department of Labor’s ability to impose civil penalties on farms employing H-2A workers.

The nation’s highest court is expected to decide whether DOL can enforce such fines through its in-house administrative process, or if such actions must instead be directly adjudicated by a federal court.

The DOL argues that the Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals wrongly ruled last year that farms are entitled to have such cases decided in federal court, rather than through the administrative process.

If the Third Circuit’s ruling is upheld, the federal government argues it would be left with a “mess,” as agencies would have “no predictability for what we’re supposed to do” in enforcement proceedings involving H-2A as well as other government programs.

“We need to be able to structure our operations on this stuff because it affects so many cases, so many resources, the power of the executive branch, and our relationship with the courts and how courts’ resources are impacted,” said Sarah Harris, the federal government’s attorney, during oral arguments Nov. 10.

The underlying lawsuit pertains to a New Jersey vegetable farm, Sun Valley Orchards, which was fined more than $550,000 for alleged H-2A violations, such as providing workers with inadequate access to restrooms, kitchen facilities and transportation.

The legal question before the Supreme Court doesn’t center on the substance of those allegations, but rather on whether the dispute relates to “public rights” or “private rights.”

The DOL argues that H-2A regulations fundamentally pertain to immigration, which implicates “public rights” that are subject to in-house administrative enforcement processes.

However, the Third Circuit agreed with Sun Valley Orchards that the matter actually concerns employment contracts, which are within the sphere of “private rights” that must be adjudicated directly in federal court.

Organizations such as the National Council of Agricultural Employers thinks the Third Circuit correctly ruled in the case, as it believes the administrative process amounts to the DOL serving as “judge, jury and executioner.”

During oral arguments before the nation’s highest court, the federal government claimed the Third Circuit’s interpretation is incorrect, since the DOL isn’t actually trying to enforce contracts between the farm and its workers.

“The agency is adjudicating the employer’s violations of its regulatory promises to the government,” said Harris, the government’s attorney.

The conditions of H-2A employment entail the “public policy” of immigration, since DOL’s conditional permission is required to import workers, she said.

“That classic public rights dispute doesn’t convert to private rights just because the government requires employers to embed those federal regulations in their contracts as a further enforcement mechanism,” Harris said.

While the permission to import workers does involve immigration, and thus “public policy,” the dispute in this case concerns working conditions that are within the realm of “private rights,” said Robert Johnson, attorney for Sun Valley Orchards.

“If you have the inspection that finds these violations, it doesn’t result in deporting the workers,” he said. “The workers can stay. They can continue to work.”

In deciding whether a government action involves “public rights” or “private rights,” it’s necessary to “look closely at what’s the nature of the claim, what’s the nature of the remedy,” which in this case doesn’t actually pertain to immigration, Johnson said.

However, the federal government warned that such an interpretation could result in a “hodgepodge,” in which enforcement agencies would have trouble drawing the line between what involves “public rights” or private rights,” countered Harris.

Such problems would extend to enforcement actions involving Medicare, Medicaid and student loans, among other programs, as the government could be left with “no clarity as to what the scope of public rights looks like,” she said.

“The government cannot live like that. We have too many schemes involving civil penalties, involving things that historically have analogized to public rights, to live under uncertainty,” Harris said. “Because we have an accumulating number of cases that could be subject years from now to complete wipeout if we don’t have additional certainty.”

text:
Alameda County is calling on ICE to stop conducting operations outside a Dublin jail amid a recent uptick in immigration enforcement across the Bay Area.

Members of the county-backed immigration-related rapid response network ACILEP said they believe that, starting around Oct. 25, rotating groups of up to six ICE agents began using the parking lot outside Santa Rita Jail as a hub for detaining people exiting and entering the facility.

“They’ve been, like, bum-rushing people upon release,” said Tash Nguyen of Restore Oakland, one of dozens of community and nonprofit advocates who have been keeping vigil outside the jail in rotation. Nguyen described agents “racially profiling people, detaining and then releasing them, if they’re not who they’re looking for.”

Nguyen added that she’s also seen ICE officers entering the lobby and asking the sheriff’s office staff about specific individuals in their custody.

Alameda County Interim Counsel Andrea Weddle penned a cease-and-desist letter to ICE on Monday, detailing several occasions where the sheriff’s office instructed agents “to leave and to refrain from conducting civil immigration enforcement activities in and around the jail and its parking lot.” The letter added that “ICE personnel have repeatedly ignored those instructions.”

Alameda County Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas issued her own statement on Monday as well, noting that the county’s ICE-free zones policy prohibits ICE from entering county property without a judicial warrant, or from using county property, including the jail’s parking lot and lobby, as staging grounds for its activities.

The sheriff’s office is also prohibited by its own departmental policy from having any contact or communication with ICE, except in cases of a criminal warrant.

“ICE pursued someone from the parking lot into the lobby and detained them. … I would say a lot of them are rogue, incredibly untrained and unprofessional,” Fortunato Bas said, stressing that the approach is putting the public at risk — restricting “people’s ability to do the normal things that they would do,” like running errands or going to school and work.

“That is not keeping our community safe,” Fortunato Bas said.

Advocates said that as of Friday night, the sheriff’s office had locked the jail lobby, ostensibly with the goal of keeping ICE at bay. The sheriff’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Folks like Nguyen said they would prefer to see sheriff’s deputies preventing ICE from entering the parking lot altogether, barring proof of a warrant, while allowing visitors and others to continue to use the space to arrange for safe passage.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment about the cease-and-desist letter, and it’s unclear exactly what steps Alameda County will take if its warnings are further ignored, but Fortunato Bas said her body would continue to push back. The number of local arrests across the Bay Area as of Tuesday totals at least 19.

“Our board will have to meet and make some decisions about what the next step will be, and it would likely be legal action,” she said.

Meanwhile, Fortunato Bas said the county aims to discuss ways to improve the training and protocols concerning ICE at area hospitals, after federal immigration agents last month entered Wilma Chan Highland Hospital without showing a warrant and maintained custody of a patient.

In 2025, the county supervisors created Alameda County Together for All, or ACT for All, a committee to support those impacted by federal policy and benefit changes. Fortunato Bas said that ACT for All will hold a hearing Dec. 7 on the county’s immigration enforcement response plan. It also aims to discuss a report by the Alameda Health System, which the committee requested after the ICE incident at Wilma Chan Highland Hospital.

text:
A Colorado Immigration and Customs Enforcement official testified Monday that he directed agents to immediately re-arrest immigrants freed by federal judges after hearing his “colleagues” in Minnesota were doing the same.

Acting Denver Field Office Director Nathan Rasper told U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney he heard courts in Minnesota “allowed the immediate re-arrest of an alien released.” Two federal judges in Minnesota have found instant re-arrests did not violate their orders, but two others strongly disagreed. An appellate court has yet to weigh in.

Monday’s hearing was the second Sweeney has held to question ICE officials’ actions after learning a man she ordered released was immediately re-detained on Oct. 27. Rasper testified he stopped the re-arrests after the first hearing on Nov. 4.

“Releasing somebody momentarily is not releasing somebody at all,” Sweeney said at the Nov. 4 hearing.

The re-arrest tactic had become common in Colorado.

At the first hearing, assistant U.S. attorney Andrew Soler, representing the government, said the man re-detained Oct. 27 was “at least the 10th in a week.”

After that hearing, Sweeney required the government to list every Colorado case since Oct. 27 in which ICE re-arrested someone within 12 hours of a court-ordered release — a window of about nine days.

MPR News has not been able to review the full list submitted by the government, but a court order shows it included 14 people who had since been released again. The ACLU of Colorado told the court Monday the list was likely an undercount.

MPR News has confirmed at least eight men in Minnesota have been instantly re-arrested by ICE agents after federal judges ordered their release.

The men were brought to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building for processing, signed release paperwork and handed their belongings. Agents re-arrested them before they could leave federal property. One man was instantly re-arrested twice.

ICE’s St. Paul field office did not answer whether it advised agents in other states on re-arrests of people released by federal judges.

Instead, an unnamed spokesperson for ICE’s Midwest office defended the practice of re-arrests Tuesday, writing, in part: “When appropriate, ICE will address the issues identified by the court and take further action consistent with applicable law and court orders, which can include rearresting an offender.”

A different unnamed spokesperson for ICE previously wrote on Oct. 27 that ICE “may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision” and saying ICE cannot do that is “nothing short of sabotage.”

Sweeney’s written order on whether she will hold the government in contempt is pending.

The incoming Democratic chair of the powerful congressional oversight committee said it appears Donald Trump has “something to hide” after the White House threatened criminal investigations over the party’s planned scrutiny of the administration.

Robert Garcia, ranking member of the oversight committee in the House of Representatives, vowed to press on in the face of what he

called “baseless threats” after receiving a letter from White House counsel William Scharf which warned that Democratic pledges to use to investigate the president “may cross the line into blatant criminality”.

Scharf argued that congressional inquiries need a legitimate legislative purpose and cannot be used to punish targets or lay the ground for prosecutions.

Garcia said in a statement that Congress’s authority comes from article I of the constitution, “not from the permission of the White House”. He described that power as inherent in the job of writing laws.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse,” Garcia said on Wednesday, accusing the administration of continuing to weaponize the government with “threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress”.

Corruption became a key issue in last week’s midterm elections. While the economy was the issue voters named most often as the country’s top problem in the NBC News exit poll, 90% of voters said corruption was a crucial or major factor in their votes.

Having promised during the campaign to tackle those issues, Democrats won back control of both chambers of Congress, and will arrive in January with their largest House majority since 2008. Trump wrote on social media that he was not responsible for the Republican losses, and later posted an image of a cap embroidered with the word “veto”.

Scharf’s letter also pointed to public remarks by incoming Democratic lawmakers. It said the Representative-elect Richard Ojeda of North Carolina wants to see defense secretary Pete Hegseth “squirm”, that Texas representative-elect Katy Padilla Stout told witnesses to “put makeup on for the cameras” and that Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona described accountability as eventually ending in jail. It also took aim at Garcia’s “Lawyer Up” campaign, saying his intent was “not to legislate, but to intimidate”.

Garcia was unmoved. “We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DoJ or from the president’s lawyers,” he said.

text:
As we approach the midway point of the second Trump administration and the start of a new Congress, we are at a critical moment for refugee protection in the United States. The U.S. Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) has been fundamentally dismantled, leaving thousands of people without the safety and stability they were promised.

Here’s where things stand, and what comes next.

How has the Trump administration targeted refugees?

On January 20, 2025, the administration sent an unequivocal message about their plan to undermine USRAP. Within hours of President Trump’s inauguration, he signed an executive order that indefinitely suspended refugee processing and admissions. Effective immediately, refugee arrivals stopped, and more than 100,000 people who were already vetted for admission to the U.S. were left stranded overseas.

Although the executive order allows for the possibility of exceptions to the ban on refugee arrivals, so far, nearly all of these have gone to white South Africans. Last year’s refugee admissions goal was ultimately set at 17,500 people, a historic low. The same is true for the current fiscal year.

To make matters worse, in a shocking turn of events, the Trump administration has systematically expanded its targeting of refugees to include weakening protections for those who are already here. In more than four decades since the formalization of USRAP with the passage of the 1980 Refugee Act, we have never seen anything like this before.

Give today

As the world's oldest refugee agency, HIAS will always stand for refugees — no matter who is president. And we will do all we can to support our clients, every day, as we have for more than 120 years. Give with confidence to HIAS.

Why is the U.S. government re-vetting resettled refugees?

The first strike came at the end of 2025 when United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) announced that they would begin to re-vet and, in some cases, reinterview resettled refugees who were admitted into the U.S. during the Biden administration.

Then, the situation intensified in January 2026, with the launch of Operation PARRIS (Post-Admission Refugee Reverification and Integrity Strengthening). The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claimed that this targeted refugee re-vetting program would help to address alleged fraud in USRAP but provided no public evidence to back up these claims. They focused their efforts on resettled refugees in Minnesota who did not yet have their lawful permanent resident status, resulting in people being arrested in their homes and then flown out of state to detention facilities.

Eventually, a District Court judge stopped the arrests and detention of refugees from Minnesota. Later, a federal judge ensured that the refugee detention policy could not be implemented anywhere in the country. However, the re-vetting and reinterview process continues, causing immense stress and instability in the lives of people who followed every rule and did everything asked of them before they were legally admitted into the U.S.

What is happening to refugees’ green card applications?

At the same time the administration announced its re-vetting plans, they also officially announced that they would no longer process or adjudicate green card applications for refugees who were admitted during the Biden administration. Keep in mind that according to U.S. law, refugees are required to apply for their green cards after one year. The policy places refugees in an impossible position: federal law requires them to apply for permanent residency, while the administration is refusing to decide their applications, yet reinterviewing and re-vetting them if they do not yet have their green cards.

In addition, last summer, Congress passed H.R.1, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB) Act, which cuts essential food and medical benefits to refugees if they do not have their green cards. Yet, of course, refugees who arrived during the Biden administration cannot avoid these massive obstacles because their green card applications are on hold. It is a twisted catch-22 that leaves refugees at risk for hunger, lack of access to medical care, and uncertainty about their futures in the very country that promised them permanent safety.

Related News

On the Offense: HIAS Files Multiple Legal Challenges to the Trump Administration’s Attacks

Read More

Can the U.S. government take away someone’s refugee status?

On October 14, 2026, DHS issued a new rule that will make it dramatically easier for the Trump administration to terminate the refugee status of people who were resettled through USRAP and do not yet have their green cards, even though green card adjudications are on indefinite hold. The new policy is intended to reduce the number of days that someone has to challenge the administration’s effort to terminate their refugee status from 30 days to 10 days, making it essentially impossible for them to defend their status and why they should not quickly be removed from the U.S., and potentially sent back into harm’s way.

A federal court has put a temporary block on implementation following the filing of litigation by a group of individual refugees and several organizations, including HIAS. However, this pause is just effective through early December 2026, and we continue to look to the courts for a permanent termination of the rule.

How is HIAS fighting back against these anti-refugee policies?

HIAS immediately took our fight to the courts. We are a co-lead plaintiff in the Pacito v. Rubio case, challenging the ban on refugee arrivals. We are also a co-lead plaintiff in the recently filed PANA v. Edlow case which challenges the re-vetting, green card holds, and refugee status termination policies. In addition, we continue to educate lawmakers about what this administration has done to USRAP and the changes that must be made.

The U.S. made a promise of safety to refugees who followed every rule required of them. HIAS is fighting to ensure that promise is kept. Join us in urging lawmakers to restore a fair refugee admissions system and protect refugees who are already rebuilding their lives in the U.S. Learn more about how to take action with HIAS here.

text:
Congresswoman Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) released the following statement in response to a New York Times investigation revealing that ICE armed and deployed David Brouillette before reviewing his background check findings:

ICE handed David Brouillette a gun and sent him into Maine communities before anyone at the agency had reviewed his background check. The agency restricted his access to certain computer systems because he had not been fully cleared, yet apparently saw no problem trusting him with the power to take someone’s life. That is an unconscionable betrayal of the public’s trust.

Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero should be alive today. He was a young father, building a life for his family in Maine. He was following a lawful immigration process. His family will live with his loss forever. They deserve to know every decision that put Brouillette on the streets with a badge and a gun and deserve accountability for their tragic loss.

Journalists had already uncovered deeply disturbing allegations of violence and abuse against Brouillette. The Times now reveals further warning signs, including vile, racist comments about his own sister’s longtime Colombian partner. His own mother told the Times her son was dangerous and shouldn't have weapons. A thorough review could have brought these serious warning signs to light before ICE sent him out to carry out Stephen Miller’s aggressive immigration crackdown. The danger was foreseeable. Johan Sebastián’s death was preventable.

Who authorized his deployment? What would a thorough review have revealed? An agency whistleblower has already warned the DHS Inspector General of an "unprecedented lowering of standards.” How many other agents are carrying guns in our communities without completed vetting?

I have demanded answers from DHS about training and background checks in the days following Johan Sebastián’s death. This reporting makes a full, independent investigation even more urgent. DHS must release Brouillette’s hiring, vetting, training, and deployment records and cooperate fully with independent investigators.

ICE must be abolished and that is what I will continue to fight for. But perfect can’t get in the way of better. Until we can abolish ICE, this agency needs serious, immediate reforms. I am working on legislation to ensure federal agents are never armed and deployed into our streets without being fully vetted. Our communities’ safety cannot depend on whether this administration finds basic safeguards convenient.

Responsibility reaches beyond the officer who pulled the trigger. It extends to the leadership that armed and deployed him, and to an administration that put its deportation agenda ahead of human life. Every official responsible must be held accountable. Johan Sebastián’s family deserves justice, and I will keep fighting until they get it.

text:
At the Supreme Court, the justices seemed divided on Tuesday in a case that could undermine the ability of many federal regulatory agencies to fine businesses that violate federal laws.

For decades, farmers have relied on a federal immigration program that allows them to temporarily employ migrant workers to pick crops.

In addition to wages, farm owners must provide basic necessities, such as housing, access to meals and water. The whole system is essentially policed by the Department of Labor to ensure that foreign workers don't undercut domestic laborers.

In that role, the department fined Sun Valley Orchards, based in New Jersey, a half-million dollars for unsanitary conditions, including providing unsafe drinking water, housing people in 20-bunk rooms, broken sinks and other violations, including failure to pay promised wages.

Sun Valley is disputing the charges and contends that the Department of Labor imposing monetary fines based on its administrative proceedings is unconstitutional. Sun Valley also says the process denies them the right to a jury trial when and if they appeal to a federal court.

At the high court Tuesday, Chief Justice John Roberts strongly suggested that the Trump administration, and many administrations before it, have exceeded the power of the executive branch. In this case, potentially wading into the judicial branch's territory.

Addressing Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who represented the Labor Department, Roberts said, "It seems to me you're just trying to leverage … the broad authority [of the executive branch] beyond the justification for its application."

Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked how disruptive it would be for the federal courts to enforce the law instead of the designated agency (in this case the Department of Labor).

Harris responded succinctly, "If the court were to say civil penalties always have to be in Article III courts, that's kind of the nuclear option."

Harris added that such a ruling would disrupt programs as diverse as Medicare, Medicaid, the federal student loan program and more.

That prompted this question from Justice Elena Kagan: "Why not just go to court always?" Harris quickly responded, "I think it would be catastrophic." She went on to explain that a system like that would inevitably result in massive under-enforcement of the law, given limited resources.

Lawyer Robert Johnson represented Sun Valley Orchards. "To be sure," he said, "the statute contemplates penalties, but it says nothing about where those penalties should be adjudicated."

Johnson further contended that penalties should be imposed by the federal courts, not the administrative agencies that do most of that work under current law.

To that Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson replied, "It seems like you're just sort of fighting the reality of … what Congress was trying to do … in ensuring that we don't have farm workers coming in and undercutting domestic workers."

A more skeptical observation came from Justice Brett Kavanaugh: "What you're proposing is really at war with clarity," he said, adding, "I think that's not great systematically going forward."

Justice Samuel Alito pointedly added, "What you're outlining is sort of a hodge-podge opinion, and maybe sometimes courts write that sort of thing," to which Justice Kagan quickly chimed in with a chuckling crowd in the court, "Not ever us!"

In rebuttal, Deputy Solicitor General Harris was unusually candid. "It would be a big deal for the government to lose, but an even bigger deal would be to have a mess," she said. She later added, "A lot of other statutory regimes also would be on the cutting-room floor."

And if that's the case, she said, the administration will have to go to Congress. Her voice rising, she added, "Please tell us now ... if we need to get Legislative Affairs on it right now, because this will snowball."

text:
WASHINGTON — The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress -- may amount to "blatant criminality."

White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

Garcia most likely would chair the powerful panel in the new Democratic-controlled Congress that is seated in January. Garcia warned Trump officials to "lawyer up" after his party's stunning victories in last week's midterm elections.

In response, Scharf wrote in Monday's letter that "threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality." The letter's existence was first reported by Punchbowl News.

Garcia said in response to the letter that "it appears Donald Trump has something to hide" and stressed that Congress's investigative powers do not need the "permission of the White House."

"Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate," Garcia said. "The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse."

Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.

Garcia also wants to look at the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Other targets include Trump's White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family's role in mineral deals and Trump's crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that "there could be" a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying "Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it's through subpoenas or letters — so we're not going to stop working with Congress."

"Nothing I've said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise," he added.

text:
Hack unmasks ICE and other federal agents

Nearly 500 agents work in the Buffalo area. Advocates for migrants say the release provides a degree of necessary transparency.

Share on

Vehicles on the Peace Bridge, one site of Customs and Border Patrol employment in Western New York.

A total of 485 ICE, Border Patrol and other immigration and customs related agents work at some 20 offices, bridges and detention sites for migrants across Western New York.

That’s according to a recent hack of Department of Homeland Security employee data which was posted online October 28. The data provides a first-ever detailed look at the workforce of the federal government’s immigration and customs operations in the region.

As Investigative Post has previously reported, immigration arrests across Western New York have skyrocketed since Donald Trump’s return to office, and the ICE detention center in Batavia is routinely overcrowded. In response, community activists have documented arrests, recording photos and videos of masked agents and the unmarked cars they drive.

The hacked employment data lists employee names, job titles, supervisors, email addresses, phone numbers, and the office to which they’re assigned to work. Most are agents, but the list also includes back-office employees, as well. The hacked data appears to be current through August and shows that:

Customs and Border Protection, the largest regional agency, employs 325 between Buffalo, Cheektowaga, Niagara Falls, Grand Island, Town of Tonawanda and Lewiston. That includes agents working at the four bridges to Canada and those on the streets.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) employs 81 between Buffalo and Batavia.

U.S. Customs and Immigration Services employs 43 in Buffalo.

Homeland Security Investigations, a specialized unit that works alongside ICE, employs 35 in Buffalo.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which coordinates the nation’s cybersecurity defense systems, has one employee working in Buffalo.

Investigative Post is not publishing the names of individual employees at this time, save for a handful of supervisors.

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson acknowledged the authenticity of the data saying the agency was “aware of a potential breach” but declined to answer additional questions. The spokesperson called the hack a “security threat” and said the agency was working “to ensure all [employees] are properly protected.”

The hack was done by a group calling itself the Department of Peace, which said it took the action after a July statement by DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. It released information for 41,000 employees nationally.

“On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ‘turning up the heat’,” the statement said. “This is what happens to ICE when you do that.”

The Department of Peace hackers gave that statement to Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit that collects, analyzes and publishes hacked data. Journalists and researchers with the organization have published a searchable database of the DHS data online.

Local immigration advocates said the hack is a needed dose of transparency for agencies that have been operating with a heavy hand for years.

“I don’t think many know how significant the DHS footprint is in our community, both in terms of the facilities they control, but also just in terms of the number of agents who are operating on our streets,” said Melissa Hubbard, who’s involved with the Evict ICE from 250 Delaware campaign. “Just having that information, I think, is critical for the public.”

Local leadership with ICE and Customs and Border Protection, the two largest agencies operating in Western New York, did not return requests for comment. Neither did the labor union representing Border Patrol agents. Jack Delaney, a spokesperson for the National Treasury Employees Union, which represents CBP employees, declined to comment.

What the data shows

In Western New York, the bulk of the workforce is Customs and Border Protection, the parent agency of the U.S. Border Patrol. That agency employs two-thirds of those listed in the database — 325 in total. Around 100 carry the title CBP Officer while 19 are classified as Border Patrol Agents. The rest of the workforce is made up of various supervisors and specialists.

CBP also boasts the greatest number of office locations, at 13. That includes the Peace, Rainbow and Lewiston-Queenston bridges and Border Patrol stations in Niagara Falls, Grand Island and the Town of Tonawanda. Its homebase is the 8th floor of the Larkin at Exchange Building, where 160 employees are assigned.

A separate federal database shows CBP rents nearly 55,000 square feet of the Larkin at Exchange Building, at a cost of $1.9 million annually. Its lease expires in 2040.

The hacked data lists Rose Brophy as director of field operations for CBP and Sharon Swiatek as assistant director for field operations. Both are based at CBP’s office at the Buffalo Niagara International Airport in Cheektowaga, according to the data.

ICE, meanwhile, counts 25 agents in Buffalo and another 56 employees at the Batavia detention center. The bulk of its workforce are deportation or detention officers. The rest of the Batavia workforce — guards, food service workers, etc. — is employed by the facility management firm Akima.

ICE’s homebase is the 7th floor of 250 Delaware Ave. in downtown Buffalo. Activists in recent months have staged numerous protests, aiming to pressure building owner Uniland Development to not renew its lease with the agency. That lease expires in March. ICE currently pays Uniland $2 million annually for 53,000 square feet.

Philip Rhoney is listed as acting field office director while James Bausch and Stephen Kurzdorfer are listed as deputy field office directors. Recent federal lawsuits list Peter Sukmanowski as acting deputy field office director. All are based out of the offices at 250 Delaware Ave.

At U.S. Customs and Immigration Services, Edward Newman is listed as the district director. Leadership of Homeland Security Investigations and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency weren’t included in the data.

The data additionally confirms several office locations for immigration agents.

One of them is the Electric Tower on Washington Street. Eight Homeland Security Investigation agents and one from CBP work on the sixth floor, the database shows. Details of the lease were not available. David Chiazza, executive vice president for building owner Iskalo Development, did not return a request for comment.

Another location is 130 Delaware Ave., which houses the Buffalo immigration court. Numerous immigration arrests have occurred there as migrants leave their court hearings. The database confirms that five ICE agents and two Homeland Security Investigations agents are based there. Multiple federal agencies rent 92,000 square feet of the building and pay $2.6 million in annual rent.

The database also lists one CBP agent as working at 270 Michigan St., an office building occupied primarily by the federal Drug Enforcement Agency. The database lists the employee as a security guard. The DEA rents about 22,000 square feet from Ellicott Development at a cost of $618,000 annually.

Limitations of the data

The data, according to the researchers and journalists who helped publish it, comes from a hack of a login service called Okta that DHS employees use to access agency software. Included is a field that lists the date the employee’s login profile was created.

It’s not clear, however, if that date corresponds to the date an employee was hired. The data, a snapshot in time, also does not indicate how much the workforce has grown since Trump’s return to office. In 2025 and 2026, Congressional Republicans passed billions in new spending for immigration agencies, which has led to a spate of hiring nationally.

The hacked data also does not include salary information.

A Buffalo ICE agent spotted in Minneapolis in January. Photo by Raven Geary | Unraveled.

Another limitation: The data provides no information on agents’ movements throughout the country. In January, for example, journalist Raven Geary of the outlet Unraveled shared with Investigative Post a photo they captured of a Buffalo ICE agent working in Minneapolis during the agency’s surge in that city. The hacked data does not indicate how many Buffalo agents have been temporarily assigned elsewhere, or how many agents from other regions have been sent to work in Western New York.

Finally, the data lists relatively few agents as assigned to the four bridges to Canada. Twenty-nine are listed as working at the Peace Bridge, 12 at the Rainbow Bridge and nine at the Lewiston-Queenston Bridge.

A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson declined to answer a question about the workforce assigned to the bridges, but said the agency’s staff nationally has grown from 65,000 to 70,000 in the past two years.

A boon for advocates

In May, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the Bivens Act as part of the state budget, which, in part, allows New Yorkers to sue federal agents in state court for alleged violations of the U.S. Constitution.

Advocates said the transparency provided by the data breach makes those lawsuits possible. Before, they said, victims may have had video evidence of a violent arrest but didn’t know the agents’ names. That’s now changed, said Lauren Harper, an expert on government secrecy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation.

“I think if you get into scenarios where you have enforcement actions gone wrong … I don’t think it’s hard to draw a line between [the data, and] how you get accountability for abuse of force,” Harper said.

She added that the employee data provides fodder for the Democrats who are about to take control of the House Oversight Committee.

“We know that ICE activities are going to be the subject of congressional investigation,” she said. “Information like this could be useful there.”

It’s also possible, Harper and others said, that the data aids in the filing of Freedom of Information Act requests. Harper cautioned that ICE maintains a status as a “security agency” meaning that it’s exempt from releasing broad swaths of information.

But knowing agents’ names could nonetheless help local advocates.

“It gives us a lot more tools,” said Aaron Krupp, regional coordinator for Justice for Migrant Families.

Added Hubbard: “We deserve to know what our public servants are doing, who they are, because it’s our money being used to pay them.”

Six Democratic lawmakers are asking the Trump administration to confirm where an 8-year-old Haitian boy is being held and what steps officials are taking to reunite him with his family after he was transferred to federal care following an immigration check-in in San Diego.

“Video footage appears to show the use of restraints on a child who seemed to pose no threat to those around him, raising serious questions about the handling of this incident,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. They said they were concerned about the basis for the action and the potential harm to a child who appeared for a required hearing.

The boy, a third grader at Fay Elementary School, was taken into federal care on Nov. 5 after attending an ICE appointment with his uncle, according to lawmakers. He had been living with his uncle and cousins after his father was deported to Mexico last year, advocates and school officials told ABC News.

The boy also lost Temporary Protected Status earlier this year after the United States ended it for more than 350,000 Haitians in August.

Lawmakers said San Diego Unified School District sent crisis counselors to Fay Elementary to support classmates who were distressed by his absence.

“They did not give the father the opportunity or chance to actually put in place legal guardianship for the kid,” said Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance.

text:
New reports highlight how the Trump administration has used “third country” deportations to remove LGBTQ+ refugees from the United States — including those previously granted safe harbor after fleeing countries where anti-LGBTQ+ laws and sentiments put their lives at risk.

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is supposed to deport ICE detainees to countries immigrants self-designate. This usually means sending them back to a country of origin or to a country where they have connections. The practice of sending undocumented immigrants to “third countries” — countries they are not from and are not connected to — is typically permitted only when sending them to their designated countries is “impractical, inadvisable, or impossible.”

However, even that permission comes with a caveat. The law states that people should not be sent to countries where their lives or freedom would be threatened — especially when they have expressed fear of being sent to that location.

DHS has not released information about the number of people it has sent to “third countries” under President Donald Trump administration, but recent reporting by Reuters found preliminary data pointing to at least 40,000 cases — including dozens of instances where LGBTQ+ people who could not be sent to their designated countries were sent to countries that are not safe for the LGBTQ+ community.

Reuters tracked 40 people from African nations, Iraq, Jamaica and Russia who were deported to countries with anti-LGBTQ+ laws and sentiment, including criminalization of same-sex sexual acts and abuses against LGBTQ+ people — such as “corrective rape” and conversion practices.

A nonpartisan research brief published Oct. 23 by the Congressional Research Service outlines the risks of “third country” deportations. The agency, a division of the Library of Congress, provides policy and legal analysis to members of Congress and their staff. The brief documents cases in which deportees faced human rights abuses, were denied due process, encountered life-threatening civil conflict or were forcibly returned to the countries they had fled.

Human Rights Watch published a report on Oct. 8 documenting at least 500 of these cases, where detainees were sent to African nations without a “meaningful chance to contest their removals or to articulate their fears of being removed to these countries.” This report highlights the plight of refugees who were previously granted protection in the United States based on persecution they’ve experienced or feared in their home countries because of their sexual orientation or gender identity.

Although DHS did not send them back to the countries from which they fled, these LGBTQ+ refugees were not assessed for risks or fears before they were sent to alternative locations.

One person interviewed as part of the report did not learn where they were being sent until they were on a plane. They tried to protest the placement based on fears about LGBTQ+ mistreatment but were threatened.

“The judge’s order prevented the United States from deporting the person to their home country, but they said that US immigration officers gave them no chance to challenge their removal to the third country — a country that has a law that criminalizes same-sex relations and where LGBT people have been known to experience discrimination and violence — on the basis that they would likely be persecuted there for the same reason they could not be sent to their home country,” the report states.

One trans interviewee was sent to an African nation that has no path for trans people to receive identity documents that match their self-expression — creating heightened risks due to a mismatch between their presentation and documents.

“Some countries arbitrarily detained people they had accepted, and some have sent people onward to the risk of persecution or torture in their home countries, violating the international law principle of nonrefoulement,” the report states.

Some undocumented immigrants who were sent to unsafe countries were previously awarded special protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT) rule — which is intended to prevent the United States from deporting people to a country where they are more likely than not to face violence or torture.

This should be true for Ms. D.B., a Jamaican trans woman described by the National Immigration Law Center as someone who won CAT protection many years ago. She fled Jamaica as a youth after experiencing anti-LGBTQ+ harassment and violence and spent two decades in New York City before Trump’s immigration policy changed. Since October 2025, she has been held in an all-male detention and has faced attempts to send her to at least six different countries — including two that pose significant threats.

Although Ms. D.B. has not been removed from the United States, she still faces significant hardships living in detention. And there doesn’t seem to be meaningful progress toward change.

During a interview on “60 Minutes” about the massive loss for Republicans across the country during this year’s midterm elections, Trump said his administration’s aggressive deportation policies may have played a role in the “bluenami.” He also noted that deportations may have gone too far — acknowledging that his policies have been “too tough” on undocumented immigrants and admitting that many of them had meaningful jobs, paid taxes, were longtime residents, and had not committed crimes.

“I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs that created one violation or breaking of the law and that was that they came into the country illegally,” he said. “Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out and there’s a large part of the country that thinks they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel or doing something, right? And in some cases paying taxes.”

When asked if his deportation policy “went too far,” Trump agreed: “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”

He went on to explain that although there are many people who want all undocumented immigrants removed from the country, there are also many people who have “modified” views on the subject:

“In other words, get the killers out. Get all the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out. But let the people that are here — and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” he said.

text:
President Donald Trump's deportation offensive is continuing unabated, despite the widespread Republican defeats in the midterm elections.

Video above: Surveillance video shows ICE agents arrest Wisconsin state trooper at airport

In Los Angeles, masked immigration officers in body armor blocked a hospital emergency room driveway in a heavily Latino neighborhood early Saturday. In central Alabama, twin 19-year-old brothers from Venezuela were arrested while driving back to college a day after the election.

Advocates reported arrests from California to Michigan to Massachusetts. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has not released numbers.

After Democrats trounced the GOP and won control of the next Congress, Trump said his immigration crackdown may have been “too tough” and suggested it was time to sit down with the rival party.

“I’d love to do something on immigration,” he said in an interview with CBS' “60 Minutes” recorded Friday.

Hours later, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, said his orders had not changed.

“Deportations will continue,” Mullin wrote in an online post the day after the election, warning that ICE takes no days off and that “this includes on Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Election Day.”

María Bilbao, a campaign coordinator for the American Friends Service Committee in Miami, said she has received at least one call a day from someone detained in South Florida since the election.

“Everything remains exactly the same. The arrests have not ceased at all,” Bilbao said.

Florida Highway Patrol officers and ICE agents have detained people in their cars, as well as places including supermarkets, pharmacies and gas stations. Immigrants under supervision have also been arrested when they showed up at ICE's Miami office for their appointments.

Officers assembled outside a Los Angeles hospital

Erick Gasca, 31, got home Friday night after an evening playing board games with friends. He lives near Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Los Angeles.

An “unprecedented” number of vehicles with tinted windows and no license plates were parked near the hospital's emergency room entrance, he said.

“I thought they were going to raid the hospital or something,” he recalled.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to explain the officers’ presence there, though Bill Essayli, the top Justice Department prosecutor in Los Angeles, said they were bringing a detainee for medical treatment. Essayli said two people were arrested for assaulting federal agents.

“ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches,” DHS said in a statement.

The agents' presence attracted some 30 residents and passersby. Footage shot by Gasca’s cousin, Michelle Rivera, shows protesters shouting and officers pinning someone down.

The hospital said it wasn't involved.

“White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement,” hospital president Daniel Fontoura said in a statement, adding it would not let such activities “compromise our commitment to patient care and safety.”

A couple is arrested at the Phoenix airport

A married couple from Orlando, Florida, was arrested Saturday at the airport in Phoenix while traveling to a funeral.

Gustavo Romanello and Agustin Baccega, both from Argentina, have work permits while they seek asylum after entering the United States about six years ago, according to Jonathan Batchelor, a family friend.

Batchelor was on the phone with them at the time. A mutual friend died Friday and the couple was visiting for the funeral Saturday. As the couple left the airport, two casually dressed officers asked if one was Agustin Baccega. Batchelor heard the officer say, “Asylum seekers are not in the United States legally.”

Batchelor said he could hear Romanello walking alongside his husband during the arrest and asking the officers how to collect his things. Batchelor said they then asked what his name was, “and then the guard said, ‘Oh, do you have another set of handcuffs? This is another one.’”

The voices grew distant, and the call then ended.

Both men remain in detention centers. They worked as acrobats in Florida and had no criminal record, Batchelor said.

“This is just taking good people who have been following the rules out of their lives and out of the lives of those who rely upon them and care about them,” Batchelor said.

DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the arrests.

Twin brothers seized while driving back to college

The brothers were headed back to college after visiting their parents when they were stopped in a small city in central Alabama.

Luis and Carlos Orta-Santoro, 19-year-olds born in Venezuela and living in the U.S. for four years, are soccer players at Wallace State Community College in Hanceville, Alabama.

Relatives say they have pending asylum applications, valid work permits, and no criminal records. Both are now in an immigration detention facility.

“Our family is devastated,” said their aunt, Carolina Orta.

DHS said that while they had entered the country legally, they had “overstayed in defiance of our laws,” and their case would be heard by an immigration judge. It said pending asylum applications do not confer legal status in the U.S.

The school said in a statement, “Both young men are valued members of the Wallace State community, and our thoughts are with them during this difficult time. We sincerely hope for a positive resolution to their situation.”

A Haitian boy is taken into custody, drawing protests in San Diego

An 8-year-old Haitian boy had been living with his uncle in San Diego since his father was deported last year. The uncle, who is not a legal guardian, took him to an ICE office when the boy was summoned Nov. 4 and taken into custody.

That left the boy “without the support of their family, community and their school,” according to a letter to top administration officials from San Diego Unified School District Superintendent Fabi Bagula and school board members.

“Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” they wrote.

ICE has defended its actions.

Johny Oxeda, pastor of the Fairmount Haitian Community Church, which helped get legal representation for the boy, said he’ll ultimately benefit by going through legal channels.

Activists, though, were furious.

“This is not child protection,” said Guerline Jozef of Haitian Bridge Alliance, adding, “this is state-inflicted trauma.”

text:
Greg Bovino has been waiting nine months for this.

The former Border Patrol commander became the swaggering face of President Donald Trump’s street-level immigration sweeps, leading agents through Los Angeles, Chicago and, finally, Minneapolis, where the killing of two U.S. citizens by federal officers in January sparked national outcry, set off a political storm and ended his time in the field. He retired in March, convinced that the administration had lost its nerve.

So when Trump announced Nov. 6 that Stephen Miller, then the White House's deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, would become his new chief of staff, Bovino saw a correction – and vindication.

"I think President Trump finally realizes he got duped, and he brought in the individual who was actually telling him the truth the whole time," Bovino said in an interview with USA TODAY.

Not all politicians in Washington share that view. Miller’s promotion came three days after an election in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, and in which nearly 6 in 10 voters told exit pollsters the administration’s immigration enforcement had gone too far. Some Republican lawmakers have blamed Miller, who designed and directed much of that enforcement, for turning what had been one of the party’s strongest issues into a liability.

"Horrible decision," Rep. Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, one of several Republicans who had called for Miller’s firing in the days after the vote, told USA TODAY.

To Democrats, business leaders and immigrant advocates, the pick was proof that Trump intended to double down.

Sen. Alex Padilla of California, who in a statement called Miller the architect of "the cruelest immigration policies this country has seen in modern times," promised Democrats would answer with subpoenas and investigations once they take power in January.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to USA TODAY's request for comment. In a statement, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers defended the choice, crediting Miller with helping to deliver "the most secure border in history," as well as a record drop in fentanyl overdoses and crime and a new Homeland Security Task Force that she said has "decimated dangerous cartels."

"Stephen Miller’s dedication to making our country safer and wealthier will be even better suited to his new role as Chief of Staff," Rogers added.

Miller’s elevation has sharpened a dispute over immigration that has divided Republicans for much of the year. On one side are those who believe the administration’s aggressive mass deportation campaign, which has swept up tens of thousands of people with no criminal record, immigrants with pending cases and U.S. citizens, cost them the votes of Latinos and independents who had backed Trump in 2024. On the other are hard-liners like Bovino, who argue the party lost because it retreated after Minneapolis, trading highly visible raids for a quieter approach that left its most committed voters feeling betrayed.

"This was not a mandate for the Democrats," Bovino said. "This was a mandate for the feckless Republicans in the Republican Party. When you hear a politician or some special interest saying that immigration went too far, actually, it’s the opposite of what they’re saying. It’s the surrender in Minnesota, which Stephen Miller and many of us did not want."

How that argument is settled will shape the final two years of Trump’s presidency, and the lives of millions of immigrants living in the country.

For now, the president appears to be standing in both camps. In an interview with "60 Minutes" that aired Nov. 8, Trump said his deportations "might be too tough" and suggested he could reach a deal with Democrats for immigrants who have lived in the country for years. The next day, following a torrent of criticism from conservative influencers, the House Freedom Caucus and the Heritage Foundation, he told reporters there would be no amnesty.

Miller, 41, has given no sign that he intends to change course. Appearing alongside Trump on the day of the announcement, he praised the president for having "saved our border from annihilation" and pledging "absolute loyalty" to him.

He has spent much of his career working to defeat precisely the kind of compromise the president described, according to interviews with lawmakers and current and former administration officials. In 2018, the last time Trump appeared ready to strike an immigration deal with Democrats, the talks collapsed after a White House meeting that lawmakers in both parties blamed on Miller. Now he decides who gets in the room.

The architect

Allies and critics alike describe Miller as the most influential force behind Trump’s immigration policy for the better part of a decade. His views, they say, have barely moved.

"The one thing about Stephen is that it’s a constant," Mick Mulvaney, who supervised Miller as Trump’s acting chief of staff during the first term, said in an interview with Bill O’Reilly earlier this year. "Stephen was just as adamant and militant about this in the first term."

As a teenager in liberal Santa Monica, California, Miller railed against Spanish-language announcements at his high school. Jean Guerrero, whose 2020 biography "Hatemonger" traces Miller's rise, describes a young man drawn early to provocation and conservative talk radio. As an aide to Sen. Jeff Sessions of Alabama, he helped defeat the 2013 bipartisan bill that would have offered millions of undocumented immigrants a path to citizenship. In Trump’s first term, he drove the travel ban on several predominantly Muslim countries and the "zero tolerance" policy that separated thousands of migrant children from their parents.

What changed in the second term was his reach. As deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, Miller drafted the executive orders Trump signed on his first day back in office, including one to end birthright citizenship. The administration suspended refugee admissions and later capped them at the lowest level in the program’s history, deported Venezuelan men to a prison in El Salvador under a rarely used wartime law and sent troops into American cities.

Miller, who was described as "obsessively hands-on" by a former Department of Homeland Security official, also reached directly into the machinery of enforcement. Miller set a goal of 3,000 immigration arrests a day and stayed in close contact with the commanders charged with meeting it, Bovino said.

"He wants results," Bovino said. "He doesn’t want rhetoric."

Miller had long argued that arrests alone could never achieve the scale of deportations Trump promised, Bovino said. The answer was what Bovino called "total spectrum immigration enforcement," a campaign to make life so hard for immigrants that they would leave on their own.

"That’s where Stephen Miller and the U.S. Border Patrol saw eye to eye," Bovino said. The idea was to squeeze every part of daily life, he said, until it became "too hard for them to work, live, play, procreate, or do anything else here in our country."

The operations that swept through American cities under then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem beginning in the summer of 2025 were the first test, Bovino said. Border Patrol agents moved through Los Angeles, Chicago, Charlotte and New Orleans in convoys, making arrests in parking lots and on sidewalks as cameras recorded them. The spectacle was intentional, Bovino said. The raids were meant to be seen – and to be feared.

"That visibility encourages self-deportations. That’s where we win this thing," Bovino said.

But not everyone in the Trump administration shared that vision, he said. A faction of senior officials, including former chief of staff Susie Wiles, the border czar Tom Homan and Rodney Scott, the commissioner of Customs and Border Protection, came to see the raids as a political liability and worked to rein them in, according to Bovino, who referred to them as "the gatekeepers."

The killings in Minneapolis gave that faction the upper hand, Bovino said. In January, federal agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during an immigration surge in the city. Miller’s description of Pretti as a would-be assassin and "domestic terrorist" drew condemnation from Democrats and Republicans alike. Trump told advisers he was uncomfortable with how far Miller had pushed "on some fronts," The Wall Street Journal reported, and Bovino believes the officials who had long opposed the operations seized on the deaths to end them.

"They used those casualties for their own machinations," he said.

Within weeks, the most visible figures of the crackdown had been pushed aside. Bovino was reassigned to California and retired in March – a removal engineered by "the gatekeepers," he said. Trump fired Noem that same month and replaced her with Sen. Markwayne Mullin of Oklahoma, while Miller, who for more than a year had been the crackdown’s most combative public defender, largely receded from view.

Enforcement continued under Mullin and Homan. But the convoys gave way to arrests carried out with far less fanfare, many of them by a growing number of local police officers deputized through what are known as 287(g) agreements. Still, DHS has touted record numbers of arrests over the last months.

For Bovino, the absence of spectacle is itself the failure.

"That’s what you call the softer approach, the cowardice approach," he said.

Rogers, the White House spokeswoman, said Miller had worked alongside Homan and Mullin to carry out "President Trump's America First immigration policies," calling him "an instrumental player." Her statement did not address Bovino’s account of his removal or his criticism of how enforcement has changed since Minneapolis.

What comes next

For a brief moment after the election, it seemed that compromise on immigration, which has eluded Washington for decades, might finally be within reach.

On "60 Minutes," Trump said immigrants who had lived in the country for a decade or more deserved a chance to "work a deal." The next morning, Mullin said he would be open to permanent legal status for young immigrants protected under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, and that the president had encouraged him to talk with Democrats, POLITICO reported. Rep. María Elvira Salazar of Florida, a Republican who has spent years pushing a bill to legalize longtime undocumented immigrants, said Trump had described its very core.

The backlash from the right was swift. "NO AMNESTY GARBAGE UNDER ANY OTHER NAME," the House Freedom Caucus posted on social media. More outcry followed from the online right wing. By the afternoon of Nov. 9, both Mullin and Trump were promising there would be no amnesty.

Miller had already signaled where he stood. On a call with national security officials the day after the election, he pressed ahead with the enforcement agenda and made no mention of the party’s losses, according to an official familiar with the call, which The New York Times first reported.

For Mullin, the retreat was a familiar one. He had been overruled by the president over the summer, after suspending most ICE vehicle stops following two fatal shootings. In September, guidance directing some ICE officers to focus on immigrants with criminal records was rescinded within hours, after an outcry from hawks and a phone call from Trump to Fox News insisting the agency would continue arresting anyone in the country illegally.

A former DHS official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters, said Mullin and Miller had clashed over enforcement.

In public, Mullin called Miller’s promotion "an excellent choice," and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth praised him as a fighter who "never backs down."

The pressure from the other direction has been just as strong. About 58% of voters said enforcement had gone too far, according to NBC News exit polling, though Republicans kept a narrow edge as the party voters trusted on immigration.

One of the sharpest breaks came among Latino voters. Republican House candidates won about a third of their votes this year, down from the 46% who backed Trump in 2024, according to NBC News exit polls. In Texas, where Democrats swept every statewide race, Stephanie Valencia, a co-founder of the Latino research firm Equis, attributed the swing in part to "immigration overreach and a set of broken promises from Republicans."

Those promises, she said, centered on deporting dangerous criminals. Yet about 70% of the people now held in ICE detention have no criminal conviction, according to Syracuse University’s Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse data.

Employers who depend on immigrant labor, many of them once Trump supporters, have joined immigrant advocates in denouncing the pick.

"Stephen Miller lost the Hispanic vote. He lost Texas," said Rebecca Shi, CEO of the American Business Immigration Coalition. "Trump is a businessman and fires people who underperform so this is senseless. Time will tell if Stephen Miller continues to wreck the economy, destroy families, tarnish the Republican political coalition and obliterate Trump’s legacy."

Kica Matos, president of the National Immigration Law Center, said voters had made clear the administration’s agenda "is exactly the opposite of what they want."

Democrats, who take control of both chambers in January, have shown little appetite for negotiating with Miller. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker, said Nov. 9 that he had "zero interest" in working with him, and others have promised investigations and subpoenas. Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former Georgia congresswoman and onetime Trump ally turned critic, predicted the scrutiny would only drive Miller harder.

Miller "was kind of already running the White House in so many ways, so you can expect more of the same from the White House that you were probably already pissed off and frustrated about," Greene said in a video posted to X. "Only this time he’s going to go into a hyper, hyper mode because they’re about to get investigated in every way possible by the Democrats who are going to control the all powerful House and Senate committees."

Bovino is counting on it. Immigration enforcement is federal law, he said, and no Democratic Congress can stop it. Nor does he expect Miller to be deterred by subpoenas. He said he would return to the Border Patrol in a heartbeat if asked, and that he would not come back to a gentler version of the job.

"If you thought it was hard last time," he said, "what you saw before was child’s play."

description:

text:
By Andrew Rice

The Center Square

U.S. Supreme Court justices appeared divided on Tuesday over whether administrative agencies or federal courts should adjudicate migrant farm worker disputes.

The high court heard arguments in U.S. Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case challenging a more than $550,000 fee against a New Jersey farm for allegedly not providing required amenities to migrant farm workers as part of the H-2A visa program.

The H-2A visa program allows employers to recruit seasonal migrant farmworkers to address worker shortages. The businesses must provide adequate housing, fair pay, transportation and job protections to recruit workers. The requirements are designed to prevent depriving U.S. citizens of a job.

An administrative judge within the Labor Department assessed the fine over improper living conditions and unfair wages for the migrant workers against Sun Valley Orchards. The New Jersey farm later went out of business following the fine.

Sarah Harris, a principal Deputy Solicitor General, argued for the Labor Department. She said the dispute was primarily over the public rights issue of immigration, although private rights over housing and pay were involved in the case.

“That classic public rights dispute doesn’t convert to private rights just because the government requires those programs to be embedded,” Harris told justices on the court.

Several justices on the high court appeared to push back on Harris’ arguments. Justice Clarence Thomas said the case cannot solely rely on the immigration authority granted to the federal government.

“You can’t rely on immigration as a basis for this,” Thomas said. “[There are] plenty of civil penalties in the immigration process.”

Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Amy Coney Barrett appeared cautious about allowing the executive branch to have broad, sweeping powers in its adjudication of farm worker programs.

“It seems to me you’re trying to extend broad authority beyond the justification of its application,” Roberts told Harris.

Harris said Congress authorized the administrative state to handle a wide range of adjudications because federal judges do not have the resources to handle the array of issues present. She pointed to the thousands of welfare claims adjudicated by executive branch agencies on a regular basis.

“If you’re outsourcing and transferring everything that has been in agencies to federal courts [there] is resource constraints,” Harris said.

Harris said Congress gave authority to the secretary of labor to “impose” fines against businesses that employ migrant workers.

Robert Johnson, a lawyer for Sun Valley Orchards, argued that the dispute rests on differences in a contract and should be adjudicated by a federal court.

“The government invokes the idea of immigration but does not issue a judgment imposing breaches of contract at a labor issue here,” Johnson told justices on the high court.

However, justices on the high court appeared to sharply disagree with Johnson. Justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson said immigration was a central issue in the case regardless of the contractual disagreement.

“You’re trying to get us to say the H-2A program is not an immigration program, but it is an immigration program,” Kagan told Johnson. “It's about the admission of foreign workers.”

Kagan said businesses that do not provide adequate pay, living conditions and other necessary resources to the government are committing visa fraud. She said the contracts are required to ensure fairness to American workers when migrants are recruited.

“We allowed these people to be brought in on a certain set of conditions,” Kagan said. “It's a condition of admission, the condition has been violated.”

Sotomayor posed a hypothetical situation where a business broke its contract by placing a farmworker in a factory. She said, under Johnson’s proposal, the government executive branch would not be able to adjudicate it.

“You’re seriously suggesting that that could not be administratively adjudicated?”

Johnson pushed back. He said the specifics in this case do not pose that question.

"What you’re suggesting is a hypothetical where the statements would be made under false pretenses," Johnson retorted. "Look at the nature of the allegation to see why that is not the case [here]."

Harris urged justices on the high court to issue a narrow ruling in the case. She cautioned against a ruling that would allow any issue regarding civil penalties to immediately be handled by the federal judiciary.

“It would be a big deal for the government to lose, a bigger deal to have no clarity on what public rights look like,” Harris said. “The government cannot live like that.”

text:
Aliya Rahman, the Minneapolis woman pulled from her car and arrested by federal immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge, is suing the federal government, alleging excessive force, false arrest and negligence.

Rahman, a U.S. citizen, filed the lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Minnesota, nearly 10 months after her Jan. 13 arrest. The moment was captured on video and drew national attention.

Rahman hopes her lawsuit leads to systemic change.

"I feel that if some are using my case as a lens to now see this problem more clearly, it is not my place to cover that lens, but to widen the aperture," Rahman said.

She was driving to a medical appointment when she encountered federal agents near Park Avenue and East 34th Street in south Minneapolis. Multiple videos show agents smash her car window, drag her out and carry her face down by her arms and legs through the street while handcuffed.

Rahman lives with autism and other disabilities related to a traumatic brain injury. The lawsuit alleges she repeatedly told officers about her disabilities and asked for accommodations and medical assistance.

Her attorneys say officers ignored those requests while she was held at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building at Fort Snelling. Rahman eventually lost consciousness.

The lawsuit claims federal agents didn't call 911 for 30 minutes while her cellmate begged for help, saying Rahman woke up and opened her eyes in the hospital's emergency room.

At a news conference Tuesday, Rahman said the incident continues to affect her.

"This didn't change my worldview, but it definitely changed everything about how I move around the world," Rahman said. "I am still dealing with lasting injuries."

She said she expects those injuries to be lifelong. Rahman's attorneys say they filed an administrative claim with federal agencies in April, outlining what happened and seeking compensation. They said the government did not respond within the required six-month period, allowing them to move forward with the lawsuit.

"It is the job of the attorneys and I to win this case so we can thicken the line around what people that call themselves law enforcement are permitted to do to another human being," she said.

In June, Rahman and her attorneys filed a civil rights complaint with the Department of Homeland Security's Civil Rights Division, requesting an investigation into her arrest and treatment in custody.

Rahman and her legal team stood alongside local leaders from COPAL and the Minnesota Freedom Fund during Tuesday's news conference. They hope their joint effort amplifies their bigger picture mission.

"We stand together because we recognize that while this lawsuit and the many lawsuits that are coming and have already been filed are important, but lawsuits without movements cannot change the tide," said Jessica Gingold, senior counsel with the MacArthur Justice Center.

Rahman said she hopes her case will also help others who experienced alleged misconduct during Operation Metro Surge pursue accountability.

WCCO reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

"We are aware of the lawsuit and look forward to vigorously defending ourselves in court," the statement says.

DHS previously said claims that Rahman was denied medical care were false. The agency said she was arrested for obstructing federal officers. However, Rahman was never criminally charged.

The federal government has 60 days to respond to the lawsuit.

Some have drawn parallels with the US, where arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement have soared under Donald Trump’s administration.
“It’s a law of fear,” said Carine Thibaut, the director of Amnesty International’s French-speaking Belgian section, citing the impact the raids could have on children and on people who had opened their homes to migrants.
