text:
Belgium could see ICE-style home raids that echo the US crackdown on immigration, rights campaigners have warned, after MPs approved a law that allows police to forcibly enter properties to remove undocumented people.

For months, intense debate has swirled across Belgium over measures introduced by the ruling right-leaning coalition to ramp up expulsions of people who have been denied the right to stay in the country.

In the run-up to the parliamentary vote last Friday, more than 60 protests were held across the country, adding to criticism voiced by NGOs, judges and lawyers’ associations over the measures. Some have drawn parallels with the US, where arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement have soared under Donald Trump’s administration.

The law, which is set to take effect next spring, gives the Belgian immigration office the power to ask an investigating judge to authorise entry into residences that may be housing anyone without papers, including homes where migrants are being hosted by friends or family.

Once this warrant has been obtained, police will be able to enter people’s homes without consent between 5am and 9pm, potentially in the presence of children. Once inside, they can detain people and carry out searches for identity documents.

“It’s a law of fear,” said Carine Thibaut, the director of Amnesty International’s French-speaking Belgian section, citing the impact the raids could have on children and on people who had opened their homes to migrants. “It really disseminates fear.”

Officials have said the measures will be targeted at people who have been denied asylum in Belgium, who have ignored orders to leave and who are seen as a threat to public order or national security.

A broad range of critics have said that the law is vague on what constitutes a public threat, citing cases where these terms were used for people who had carried out undeclared work, run a red light or shoplifted, meaning it will be up to individual judges to determine whether private homes can be turned into sites of immigration enforcement.

According to Amnesty International, the judges would not have full investigative powers but instead would be limited on who they could ask for additional information, while the legislation fails to provide a means for people to appeal or challenge any decisions that are made.

“They always say it’s for criminals,” Thibaut said. “We always answer that they already have all the tools to address this problem, because they can do that through the normal justice system.”

Her organisation is among the 20 rights groups that have warned that the law perpetuates the conflation of lack of legal status with delinquency. “The home is inviolable. This constitutional principle should never depend on the administrative status of those who live there,” they said.

The view was echoed at the Brussels-based Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants, known as Picum. “This really has nothing to do with people who have committed crimes,” said Chiara Catelli, an advocacy officer. “It’s really about wanting to return people, deporting people, which is an administrative procedure.”

She added: “We’ve all seen the devastating consequences of home raids in the US, where they fuel fear and violence and tear families apart. It’s deeply alarming that an EU member state is now moving in the same direction.”

Catelli noted that similar, hardline measures were already in place in countries such as the Netherlands and Germany. The EU’s recently approved returns regulation, aimed at ramping up deportations across the bloc, includes similar provisions, meaning other member states could soon adopt comparable measures, she said. “We’re really afraid that this is the beginning of something that will become more widespread.”

Thibaut said that measures such as those in Belgium would gradually chip away at the rights of everyone. “It’s the beginning of reducing the state of law and the respect for human rights,” she said.

“This time it is for people without papers; after that, it might be people who are using drugs. That’s the way you slowly, slowly dismantle a society based on human rights, on respect for justice and on separation of powers.”

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Reps. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) and Debbie Dingell (MI-06) introduced the Lebanon TPS Act, a bill to secure and extend temporary protected status for Lebanon, which is currently set to expire later this month. Those who qualify for TPS are allowed to remain in the U.S. temporarily while conditions in their country of origin remain too dangerous for a safe return.

“We must stand up for our Lebanese neighbors,” said Rep. Tlaib. “The Israeli government continues to illegally occupy and ethnically cleanse entire towns in Lebanon, bulldozing homes that have housed our constituents’ families for generations. Israeli airstrikes continue to kill Lebanese civilians, armed and funded with our tax dollars. To tear Lebanese TPS holders from our communities and send them back to suffer from these war crimes is unacceptable. Our neighbors deserve safety and stability. They belong here, and I will always fight for them.”

“Michigan is home to tens of thousands of Lebanese Americans who have lived here for generations. Today, they live in fear for their families as conditions in Lebanon are too dangerous for them to return. We have a responsibility to provide refuge to those seeking shelter from catastrophe and conflict, and I have long fought for temporary protected status to provide safety and security to those who need it most,” said Rep. Dingell. “We must extend temporary protected status until we can ensure that families can safely return home.”

Conditions in Lebanon have drastically deteriorated since the country was first designated for TPS in November 2024. Over the past 25 months, Israeli military assaults have killed nearly 9,000 Lebanese and injured over 30,000 others. Since March of this year, the people of Lebanon have endured a large-scale Israeli ground invasion and bombing campaign that has killed over 4,380 people and forcibly displaced 1.2 million—over 20% of the entire Lebanese population—from their homes. Those displaced have faced acute shortages of shelter, food, water, healthcare, and education.

Hundreds of thousands remain displaced, significant Lebanese territory remains under illegal military occupation, and entire towns and villages have been systematically demolished, leaving countless Lebanese with no homes to return to at all.

Rather than leave the safety of Lebanese TPS holders up to the whims of the Trump administration, Reps. Tlaib and Dingell’s bill would designate TPS for Lebanon until April 2029.

The Lebanon TPS Act is cosponsored by 18 additional Members of Congress: U.S. Reps. Dwight Evans (PA-03), Maxwell Frost (FL-10), Sylvia R. Garcia (TX-29), Jesús “Chuy” García (IL-04), Jonathan L. text:
HOUSTON, Texas (KTRK) -- Three Houston City Council members are pushing to turn Mayor John Whitmire's executive order limiting the Houston Police Department's cooperation with ICE into a city ordinance.

PREVIOUS REPORT: Houston mayor signs order to limit cooperation with ICE, says 'elections matter' after Democrats win

Whitmire announced Friday that he had signed an executive order directing HPD to contact ICE only if a suspect has an active criminal warrant or has been arrested for a new criminal offense that could result in jail time.

In the days since, council members Alejandra Salinas, Edward Pollard and Tiffany Thomas have come together to say they want that executive order to become a city ordinance.

Pollard said making it such would ensure the policy remains the same moving forward.

“This is the exact same language (as the executive order)," said Pollard. "Putting it in ordinance form means that no other administration in the future would be able to change it."

Salinas said their proposed amendment would require additional transparency related to public reporting of HPD's interactions with ICE.

"This should be a no-brainer for this administration and every council member that voted the right time, the first time, to limit our cooperation with ICE," Salinas said.

In a statement to ABC13, the Mayor's Office said in part: "Mayor Whitmire stands by his executive order as the City's approach to addressing these challenges. He believes that amending the ordinance to include additional provisions would put the City of Houston at even greater risk of violating state law."

At Tuesday's press conference, the council members said if the executive order does not violate state law, their proposed ordinance should not either.

The council members said their proposal must undergo legal review before it can go up for a vote in council, which Salinas said could happen in a matter of weeks.

name: Litigation
title: Eleven new relists in search of four votes | SCOTUSblog
description:
The district court certified a class of people subject to the proclamation who are or will be present in the United States.
A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C.
A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit affirmed the denial of turnover.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C.
Returning Relists Khatibi v. Yip, 25-1240 Issue: Whether private instruction in courses required for state licensure constitutes a government speech.
text:
The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

First, some old business. The justices disposed of two repeat visitors last week, producing one winner and one loser. After three relists, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown finally got the nod. The court will decide when bankruptcy courts can refuse to enforce arbitration agreements in suits alleging violations of the automatic stay. But two-time relist Clemente Properties, Inc. v. Pierluisi-Urrutia struck out: The court denied without comment the petition brought by Roberto Clemente’s family over Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image, which raised questions about takings of intangible property and Puerto Rico’s sovereign immunity.

After a quiet week, the relist pipeline is suddenly gushing: The justices have served up 11 new relists for Friday’s conference, up from four last week. Several come in pairs or trios, and the federal government – the court’s most successful repeat litigant – advocates review in three of them.

The government seeks asylum – from the D.C. Circuit

The most consequential new relist this week may be Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services. On his first day back in office, President Donald Trump issued Proclamation 10888, which suspended the entry of aliens “engaged in the invasion across the southern border” and barred those who violate the suspension from invoking provisions of the immigration laws that would let them stay, including asylum.

Three nonprofits and 13 individuals sued. The district court certified a class of people subject to the proclamation who are or will be present in the United States. It held unlawful the proclamation’s restrictions on asylum and other statutory protections, as well as its authorization of removal procedures outside those established by Congress, and issued a classwide injunction. A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit narrowed the class definition, but affirmed. It reasoned that although asylum is discretionary, the executive cannot categorically deny covered migrants access to asylum by proclamation and informal guidance rather than through the procedures Congress prescribed. Judge Justin Walker dissented in relevant part.

The solicitor general’s petition argues that asylum is discretionary and that the president may categorically deny it to those covered by the proclamation. Requiring the government to accept applications it has already decided to reject, the government contends, serves no purpose. It also challenges the classwide injunction and the breadth of the certified class. The government argues that the ruling threatens to revive chaos at the border. Iowa and 21 other states support the petition, arguing that the decision undermines the federal duty to protect the states against invasion.

The respondents’ brief in opposition argues that Congress expressly gave noncitizens physically present in the United States the right to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered, and that the president cannot eliminate that right by proclamation. They emphasize the absence of a circuit split and dispute the government’s claims that the policy was responsible for reducing border crossings. They call the remedial issues fact-bound and say the government overstates the border crisis, noting that apprehensions had already fallen more than 90% from their peak before the proclamation.

The D.C. Circuit’s mandate is stayed, leaving the asylum restrictions in place for now. The absence of a split weighs against review, but the invalidation of a major administration policy could well persuade the justices to take another trip to the border. Will the court resolve this case quickly or let it sit for a while as it decides what to do, as it has in other high-profile cases?

GEO-political disputes

Our first group of cases asks whether Washington may regulate private companies that run federal immigration detention centers. In GEO Group, Inc. v. Nwauzor, a class of detainees and the state sued GEO, which operates the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma under a federal contract, for not paying Washington’s minimum wage to detainees in a voluntary work program for which ICE reimburses $1 a day. GEO argues it’s not a conventional labor relationship, but just an effort to prevent the detainees from becoming restless from idleness. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit certified the question to the Washington Supreme Court, which held that the state minimum-wage law applied to the detained workers. A divided panel of the 9th Circuit then rejected GEO’s supremacy clause defenses, leaving GEO with a judgment it puts at about $37 million. Seven judges voted to rehear the case en banc, and six joined dissents, arguing that (among other things) the state law “interferes with federal immigration-detention policy” and thus directly regulates the federal government.

GEO argues that Washington cannot regulate a federal detention program through a contractor while exempting its own detainees from the wage law. Washington and the detainees respond that the law applies equally to every private detention contractor, whether it works for a city, the state or the federal government, and that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit applies the same test as the 9th. The detainees also note that ICE has since revised its detention standards, which they say limits the decision’s future impact.

In a court-invited amicus brief, the U.S. solicitor general recommends granting review. The government argues that the law discriminates against the federal government, because Washington exempts its own facilities while barring itself from contracting with private ones, and that federal statutes leave detainee pay to the Secretary of Homeland Security. It also says the decision conflicts with a decision of the 3rd Circuit ruling on a New Jersey law targeting private detention contractors.

GEO Group, Inc. v. Ferguson challenges a 2023 Washington statute regulating private civil detention facilities, which GEO says reaches its Tacoma facility alone. The district court preliminarily enjoined it, but the 9th Circuit vacated that ruling, rejecting GEO’s direct regulation and preemption claims and remanding on its discrimination claim against private contractors. GEO says Washington is micromanaging federal detention by regulating a contractor; the state says its requirements resemble those governing other civil facilities. It also points to further proceedings on remand as a reason not to intervene yet.

A grant in Nwauzor seems likely; Ferguson presents a closer question, but at minimum it seems likely to be held if Nwauzor is granted.

Initial public … omissions?

Two companies that went public while business was booming present a question of required disclosures in federal securities filings: How much bad news must a company reveal? Two related relists ask the justices to clarify when withholding information makes an IPO registration statement misleading under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933.

In Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, the online brokerage rode the GameStop meme-stock frenzy and Dogecoin boom into its July 2021 IPO. Robinhood warned that trading might decline and provided an estimate of second-quarter revenue, but investors say it withheld information showing that trading and other business metrics were already declining. A district court dismissed their claims, but a divided panel of the 9th Circuit revived them. Robinhood’s petition argues that merely omitting material information cannot create liability unless the omission makes an affirmative statement misleading or violates a specific disclosure requirement. The investors respond that the company’s disclosures presented a misleading picture of its performance. The U.S. solicitor general, invited to weigh in, recommends granting review on the Section 11 misleading-omissions question, but not on a separate question concerning disclosures of known trends under Item 303 of Regulation S-K (which the agency is reviewing).

In ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, a webinar-platform provider prospered as businesses moved online during the pandemic. Investors allege that the company knew before the IPO that many pandemic-era customers did not intend to renew. An unpublished 9th Circuit memorandum revived the suit. ON24 asks whether describing an unmaterialized risk as hypothetical is misleading, alleging a split with the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd and 10th Circuits, and raises two questions that overlap with Robinhood’s. ON24 argues that the court improperly required it to predict future customer cancellations; the investors respond that “the warned-of risk was already materializing.” ON24 also asks the justices either to grant its petition or hold it for Robinhood. Leadersel Innotech answers that the 9th Circuit decision is non-precedential and that the panel found the risk had already begun to materialize.

With the solicitor general supporting review in Robinhood, a grant there looks plausible. Whether ON24 gets invited along is less certain. It seems a likelier hold.

Afghanistan’s frozen billions

It’s not every week that the Taliban is a respondent in the Supreme Court. That said, it has not responded, leaving an Afghan diplomat filing an amicus brief to oppose review – not on the Taliban’s behalf, but on behalf of the Afghan people.

When the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, the Treasury Department blocked billions of dollars that Da Afghanistan Bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Victims holding judgments against the Taliban sought to execute on the funds under Section 201(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which makes the blocked assets of a terrorist party and its “agency or instrumentality” subject to execution.

A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit affirmed the denial of turnover. It held that an entity’s status as a terrorist organization’s instrumentality must be determined when its assets were blocked, before the Taliban installed its officials at the bank. Separately, the panel rejected other plaintiffs’ attempt at prejudgment attachment, holding that Da Afghanistan Bank enjoys sovereign immunity as the central bank of Afghanistan, which the executive continues to recognize as a foreign state. Judge Richard Sullivan dissented.

In Havlish v. The Taliban, judgment holders challenge the blocking-date rule, alleging a conflict between the 2nd Circuit and the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 9th and 11th Circuits. They are backed by Iowa and 30 other states.

In Owens v. The Taliban, plaintiffs who lacked judgments when the district court ruled say the 2nd Circuit is the first court of appeals to require courts to defer to the executive on “foreign state” status, and thus “breaks with th[e] consensus” positions of the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd, and 6th Circuits. Ashton v. The Taliban joins Owens in arguing that courts should not defer to the executive branch in determining whether an entity is a “foreign state” entitled to sovereign immunity, and seeks a GVR in light of this year’s decision in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Corporación CIMEX, S.A.

As noted, no respondent has appeared. The only opposition is an amicus brief jointly filed in the three cases by Naseer Faiq, chargé d’affaires of Afghanistan’s mission to the United Nations, who says no one is currently authorized to appear for Afghanistan in U.S. courts. He argues that the facts are unlikely to recur, that there is no circuit split, and that the immunity issue affects only the petitioners’ priority among creditors. The Havlish petitioners have sought leave to respond, arguing that the legal question is likely to recur in terrorism litigation and does indeed implicate a circuit split.

At the very least, the court will need more time to figure out what to do when the respondent seems unwilling to appear to defend the cases.

Location, location, regulation

How many places can a state declare off-limits to firearms before the Second Amendment right to carry in public becomes largely theoretical? That’s the question in Novotny v. Moore, a challenge to Maryland’s extensive restrictions on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”

Maryland prohibits licensed gun owners from carrying firearms in numerous locations, including public transportation, parks and forests, healthcare facilities, museums, stadiums, casinos, public demonstrations, and establishments serving alcohol. I thought this was America! A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld those restrictions, finding historical support for them under the Supreme Court’s decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Judge G. Steven Agee dissented as to many of the restrictions, warning that the majority had stretched the sensitive-places exception too far. The panel separately struck down Maryland’s presumptive ban on carrying firearms on private property open to the public.(After this year’s decision in Wolford v. Lopez, which struck down Hawaii’s similar private-property rule, Maryland dropped its own cert petition seeking review of that ruling.)

The gun owners’ petition argues that historical restrictions on carrying firearms in sensitive places were generally limited to locations where the government provides security, not ordinary places where people gather. Maryland responds that historical regulations support restrictions at crowded places and locations serving vulnerable populations, and contends that review is unnecessary because the lower courts largely agree on the governing principles.

Invoking Wolford, the petitioners ask the justices to grant review or at least send the case back for reconsideration. Whether the court is ready to take on the sensitive-places doctrine so soon after Wolford remains to be seen. But reconsideration under Wolford seems like a real possibility.

A fine line on phone locations

In Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, the Commission fined Sprint $12.2 million and T-Mobile $80.1 million for failing to adequately safeguard customers’ location information shared with third-party aggregators, including by continuing to disclose the information after learning of significant security vulnerabilities. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the penalties, concluding that information about a cellphone’s location – even when no call is underway – qualifies as confidential “customer proprietary network information” under the Communications Act.

The carriers’ petition argues that the statute protects only call-location information, not all device-location data. They also contend that the FCC circumvented a statutory penalty cap by treating separate relationships with third-party companies as multiple “continuing violations,” and that the D.C. Circuit improperly deferred to the agency’s interpretation despite Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. But the carriers’ principal request is narrower: They ask the justices to send the case back in light of this year’s decision in FCC v. AT&T, which held that an FCC forfeiture order does not itself compel payment. That opinion, the carriers say, rested on a key government concession: A company can refuse to pay and contest the penalty in a subsequent enforcement proceeding with a jury. Sprint and T-Mobile say they paid under protest because the FCC’s orders demanded payment and existing precedent left them little choice. The government responds that the carriers always had the option not to pay, that they failed to preserve their claim of being misled, and that AT&T provides no reason for reconsideration. The carriers disagree.

A remand remains possible, although the government notes that the court rejected a comparable request from Verizon. For now, Sprint and T-Mobile are hoping the justices will take their call.

When hot pursuit goes cold

How long can a “hot pursuit” stay hot after police lose sight of the suspect? That’s the question in City of North Las Vegas v. Jones, a case arising from a search for a suspected domestic abuser that ended with police entering a stranger’s backyard and shooting two dogs. The suspect was never found.

After officers saw a man flee over a backyard wall, the officers stated that they established a neighborhood perimeter rather than pursuing him on foot. A K-9 officer arrived about 18 minutes later, and during the ensuing search, his police dog alerted them toward a walled backyard. An officer climbed in without a warrant. Three pit bulls emerged, two of which attacked the police dog and were shot. The dogs’ owners, Genoa Jones and Cornell Tinsley, sued. The district court granted the officers qualified immunity, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed on the warrantless-entry claim, holding that the officers had not been in immediate and continuous pursuit and that circuit precedent clearly established the search’s illegality. It left intact qualified immunity for shooting the dogs. Eight judges dissented from the denial of rehearing en banc.

The city’s petition argues that the officers never abandoned the pursuit: They say they established a perimeter and used a police dog to locate a potentially dangerous suspect. Even if the search was unlawful, the city argues, no sufficiently specific precedent clearly established that fact. It also asks the justices to hold that only Supreme Court decisions – not lower-court precedent – can clearly establish law for qualified-immunity purposes. The homeowners respond that the officers never actually established a perimeter or chased the suspect and instead just conducted a neighborhood-wide search without knowing his whereabouts.

The eight dissenting judges may help keep the petition warm. But the court closely reviews many petitions in cases where police are denied qualified immunity, and unless the error was clear enough to warrant summary reversal, the justices may let this pursuit go cold – perhaps with a dissent from denial of cert.

The court has enough to chew on that it seems likely to take a while to finish processing this week’s new offerings. As for me, I’ll be watching Monday’s orders to find out how much of this I get to reuse.

New Relists

GEO Group, Inc. v. Nwauzor, 25-828

Issue: Whether the supremacy clause allows a state to reclassify federal immigration detainees participating in a federal work program as employees and thereby impose its state minimum-wage law just because a private contractor provides detention services at the federal facility where the detainees are housed.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, 25-944

Issues: (1) Whether an issuer violates Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933’s misleading-omissions prong by failing to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider material, without an inquiry into whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading; and (2) whether an issuer violates Item 303 – and thus Section 11(a)’s required-statements prong – by failing to disclose and quantify interim financial data before quarterly reporting deadlines.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

Novotny v. Moore, 25-1324

Issue: Whether Maryland’s numerous prohibitions on carrying firearms in many places frequented by the general public violate the Second and 14th Amendments.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

City of North Las Vegas, Nevada v. Jones, 25-1355

Issues: (1) Whether officers’ warrantless search of a backyard in close proximity to the domestic violence victim’s residence was a lawful “hot pursuit” when the suspect’s trail was temporarily lost within the perimeter for approximately 18 minutes but recovered through immediate and continuous police efforts; (2) whether, even if the search did not qualify as a “hot pursuit,” the officers were entitled to qualified immunity because no “clearly established law” was violated; and (3) whether, in the interest of avoiding the perpetual flood of federal court qualified immunity litigation, the court should decide that clearly established law means only the decisions of the Supreme Court, and not lower court decisions, which fail to provide police departments with meaningful guidance because they are highly fact-determinative and subject to numerous differing and often contradictory judicial interpretations.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, 25-1376

Issues: (1) Whether an issuer violates Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933’s misleading-omissions prong by describing unmaterialized risks as hypothetical; (2) whether an issuer violates Section 11(a)’s misleading-omissions prong whenever it omits information related to a disclosed fact regardless of whether the omission renders an affirmative statement misleading; and (3) whether an issuer violates Item 303 of Regulation S-K – and thus the prong of Section 11(a) prohibiting the omission of required statements – by failing to disclose immaterial facts as “known trends or uncertainties” that are reasonably likely to have a material impact on financial results.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, 25-1422

Issues: (1) Whether this court should grant, vacate, and remand in light of FCC v. AT&T, Inc. and the government’s concessions in that case; (2) whether “location” customer proprietary network information under 47 U.S.C. § 222 refers only to call-location information, not other formation about the location of a mobile device; and (3) whether the number of “continuing violations” arising from a single failure to act under 47 U.S.C. § 503(b) is a legal question for courts to decide, without deferring to the Federal Communications Commission’s conclusion.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

GEO Group, Inc. v. Ferguson, 26-71

Issue: Whether the supremacy clause permits a state to enact a law micromanaging the details of how a federal contractor must provide services at a federal detention facility, while exempting the state’s own detention facilities from all those requirements.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, 26-239

Issues: (1) Whether Presidential Proclamation No. 10888 and its implementing guidance – which suspended the entry of certain aliens and precluded their access to statutory provisions that would enable their continued presence in the country, including asylum – are lawful; (2) whether 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1) bars the classwide relief entered by the district court; and (3) whether the class definition comports with Article III and Rule 23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

Havlish v. The Taliban, 26-292

Issue: Whether, under the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, a plaintiff’s right to execute on blocked assets depends on whether the assets’ owner was a terrorist party or its agency or instrumentality at the time the assets were blocked.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

Ashton v. The Taliban, 26-293

Issue: Whether, in light of the court’s intervening decision in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Corporación CIMEX, S.A., which confirms that a court – not the Executive Branch – must resolve through ordinary statutory construction whether an entity is a “foreign state” entitled to sovereign immunity, the judgment below should be vacated and remanded so that the Second Circuit must reconsider, under the correct framework, whether the Taliban and its instrumentalities are entitled to immunity under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

Owens v. The Taliban, 26-294

Issue: Whether the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act requires courts to independently interpret its provisions, or whether a court must defer to State Department websites and Department of Justice litigation filings in determining whether an entity is entitled to sovereign immunity under the FSIA.

(Relisted after the Nov. 6 conference.)

Returning Relists

Khatibi v. Yip, 25-1240

Issue: Whether private instruction in courses required for state licensure constitutes a government speech.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Moore v. Romero, 25-1295

Issues: (1) Whether, in a use-of-force case which involves multiple instances of force, Barnes v. Felix requires that each use-of-force be analyzed progressively from before the first instance of force used through the last instance of force used, considering the information known to the officer, the suspect’s prior actions (including any compliance, non-compliance, resistance, and reaching or grabbing for a weapon), and the suspect’s reactions to those prior use(s)-of-force; and (2) whether, when analyzing a defendant law enforcement officer’s motion brought under Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c), in a use-of-force case where body camera video clearly depicts the entire lead-up to and application of force by a law enforcement officer, whether the lower courts may analyze the clearly established prong of qualified immunity at a more general, plaintiff-friendly, level than at the motion for summary judgment stage of litigation.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

City of Bossier City v. Hershey, 25-1323

Issues: (1) Whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a violation of a clearly established constitutional right; and (2) whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a complete lack of training on the constitutional right in question.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Hershey v. City of Bossier City, 25-1389

Issue: Whether the principles of Hope v. Pelzer are limited to Eighth Amendment claims or extend to free speech and free exercise clause claims such that petitioner’s constitutional claims should not be barred by qualified immunity.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

StandWithUs Center for Legal Justice v. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 25-1404

Issues: (1) Whether the harassers’ subjective discriminatory intent is an element of a hostile environment claim under Title VI; and (2) whether the First Amendment bars a plaintiff from pleading a Title VI hostile environment claim based on “protected speech.”

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Bauer v. Marks, 25-1413

Issue: Whether the law clearly established that the officer’s use of a less-lethal projectile, under the totality of the circumstances, constituted an unreasonable use of force in violation of the Fourth Amendment.

(Relisted after the Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Brown v. United States, 25-1342

Issue: Whether an automobile is per se an instrumentality of interstate commerce, which would make a federal offense of every kidnapping involving an automobile under 18 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1).

(Relisted after the Oct. 16 and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Allen v. Caster, 26-116

Issues:(1) Whether the district court erred by not requiring plaintiffs to offer an alternative map that performed just as well as the state’s map with respect to the state’s districting criteria; (2) whether the district court erred by finding racial-bloc voting without accounting for politics; (3) whether the district court erred by finding that the totality of circumstances suggests an objective likelihood of discrimination; and (4) whether the state violated the 14th Amendment by declining to draw a race-based plan.

text:
The Trump administration said the facility, once a private prison, opened to immigrant detainees this week. Critics of the new detention center are planning a vigil and rally for Saturday.

By Christopher Magan

The Minnesota Star Tribune

November 10, 2026 at 4:58PM

Advertisement

The long-empty prison in the western Minnesota town of Appleton began accepting detainees just months after the federal government purchased the prison to hold immigrants facing deportation.

“DHS opened the Appleton Detention Facility on Nov. 9 to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations,” a spokesperson for Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a prepared statement.

On Monday evening, one of the six white prison buses that had been making test runs to the facility dropped off several detainees, according to several local residents. The federal government’s online detainee locator also lists at least one immigrant in custody at what’s now called the Appleton Detention Facility.

Expanded image view

ICE purchased the prison in August for $496 million from CoreCivic, more than six times the $75 million the private prison company offered to sell the facility to the Minnesota Department of Corrections a year ago.

Advertisement

An ICE spokesperson said a previous “nonbinding” offer to the state did not include a formal appraisal or take into account the cost of building a new facility. The spokesperson noted that estimates to replace the similarly sized Stillwater prison were around $1.3 billion.

“The site gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction,” the statement said.

ICE hired CoreCivic to operate the Appleton detention center and the company expects to earn $75 million over five years from the deal. The prison will need 500 employees when the 1,600-bed prison is operating at full capacity next year. So far, CoreCivic officials say they have hired about 125 people.

To fill the gap, CoreCivic brought in a startup team and workers have filled the city’s lone hotel in the small prairie town of 1,400, along with the few other places to stay in surrounding communities.

Access concerns

Appleton is roughly a three-hour drive from the Twin Cities, and immigration attorneys are concerned the detention center remoteness will make it hard to provide legal help.

A review of American Immigration Lawyers Association membership data by the Binger Center for New Americans at the University of Minnesota Law School found just three immigration attorneys within 100 miles of Appleton. The review also noted there is an office in Willmar for the non-profit Mid-Minnesota Legal Aid, which is one of the state’s largest providers of free attorneys for immigrants.

“We are going to make sure people in Appleton are served,” said Luke Grundman, Legal Aid’s litigation director, who added that three full-time attorneys work in the Willmar office. “The logistics are up in the air until we know what our access will look like.”

Minnesota has about 60 immigration attorneys statewide, and they have been overwhelmed since President Donald Trump returned to office with a push for mass deportations.

Having an attorney can make or break an immigrant’s chances of winning their case, especially when they are in detention. Detained immigrants with legal representation were more likely to avoid deportation and be released on bond, a recent analysis by the Midwest Immigrant Defenders Alliance found.

Advertisement

“You have a large number of people who feel access to a lawyer is the difference between being deported and being able to stay with their families,” said Linus Chan, one of the report’s authors who is also an attorney, law professor and director of the U’s Detainee Rights Clinic. “The more difficult these facilities are to reach, the bigger the challenge.”

Advertisement

Advertisement

In a statement, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said all detainees are given “a court-approved list of free or low-cost attorneys” and have “access to phones they can use to contact their lawyers.”

CoreCivic said private legal visitations, in-person and virtual, are available to detainees seven days a week.

Most immigration cases are treated as civil matters in special courts overseen by the Executive Office for Immigration Review, an arm of the Justice Department. Immigrants are not guaranteed a government-funded attorney so they have to find and pay for their own lawyers.

The Trump administration’s push to detain everyone who entered the country illegally, no matter how long they have been living in the U.S., means a growing number are forced to fight their cases from detention.

Advertisement

“We’ve constantly been working underwater,” Chan said. “We were at the bottom of a pool. I feel like we are about to be at the bottom of an ocean.”

Expanded image view

CoreCivic makes up lost tax revenue, for now

Before CoreCivic sold the prison to ICE in August it was one of the largest property taxpayers in Appleton. The prison was valued at roughly $14 million, according to Swift County records. The city, county and school districts received about $800,000 in annual property taxes.

text:
The West Bloomfield Police Department says U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are conducting an "enforcement operation" in one of the township's neighborhoods on Tuesday.

Agents are at a private residence in the Lakeridge of Wabeek neighborhood, according to police. Police say three people were completing work at the residence when ICE arrived. As of 3:25 p.m., the scene was active, according to police.

CBS News Detroit spoke with Democratic state Rep. Noah Arbit (West Bloomfield), who said that a law enforcement official told him that a crew member called federal agents on three other crew members.

"It's sickening how they are so proud of what they did," said activist Katy Alvarato, who was at the scene. "They had caution tape all around, like if someone is being murdered. They were hardworking guys."

Police did not immediately say whether the individuals were detained.

"The West Bloomfield Police Department was not involved in planning, initiating, or conducting this operation. The department received minimal notification and no details with regards to the actions of federal authorities," police said.

"Federal law enforcement agencies have independent authority to conduct enforcement operations within their jurisdiction. The West Bloomfield Police Department's responsibility remains the safety and security of everyone who lives, works, or visits our community."

This is the second time in a week that ICE conducted enforcement in Metro Detroit. On Saturday, Nov. 7, federal agents arrested three people in Dearborn.

In a statement to CBS News Detroit, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that Gustavo Adolfo Osorio Hernandez, Luis Fernando Monge-Vides, and Andoni Leonel Vasquez Martinez, all from Honduras, were arrested during a vehicle stop in Dearborn. DHS said the three people will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

text:
Loved ones are rallying in support of a University of Maryland (UMD) student and her mother, who were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) last week.

Maria Flores Garcia and her mother were taken into custody last week at ICE's Baltimore field office, according to Flores Garcia's boyfriend, Cesar Saavedra. The mother and daughter were originally at the office for a routine check-in for Flores Garcia's mother.

In a statement to WJZ, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed that Flores Garcia was arrested on November 5.

A promising student

Before becoming a UMD student, Flores Garcia was Parkdale High School's Class of 2026 valedictorian.

In her speech at graduation, she talked about the struggles she and her family faced coming to Maryland from El Salvador when she was nine-years-old.

She also talked about how she overcame all of that to become valedictorian -- reminding her classmates that anything is possible.

Flores Garcia got a full ride scholarship to UMD.

"Through our lives, we'll continue to face challenges, struggles...moments of doubt, and obstacles that seem impossible to overcome," she said in her speech. "But it is crucial you never underestimate the power of determination."

Saavedra said Flores Garcia and her mother were taken into custody last week, and are now being detained in Louisiana. Flores Garcia was accompanying her mother for the check-in, but chose to stay with her when ICE chose to bring her into custody, according to Saavedra.

The DHS spokesperson said Garcia came to the U.S. illegally and was arrested in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas in 2016.

Despite being placed into removal proceedings, she was released into the country. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal on Feb. 23, 2021, according to DHS.

"She will remain in ICE custody pending her removal from the United States. This administration will not ignore the rule of law," the DHS spokesperson said.

Support for Garcia

Saavedra started an online fundraiser over the weekend and he said it has already surpassed its goal of $25,000. The money will be going toward legal fees and other urgent costs.

"It's obviously very hard for the moment for the family. I've been trying to just stay as the most composed one, most calmed one," Saavedra said. "[I've] just been trying to help out the family that's detained and the family that is here outside as well."

In a statement, UMD told WJZ it's aware of Garcia's detainment.

"Our thoughts are with our student and their family and friends," a UMD spokesperson said. "We are working to provide resources when possible and appropriate."

Prince George's County Executive Aisha Braveboy also put out a statement on the situation, assuring Garcia and her family that they are not alone. Braveboy said in part, "We are calling for Maria's immediate release and safe return now."

Maryland U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen also reacted to the arrest. "Donald Trump's reckless and out-of-control ICE operations continue to wreak havoc on our communities, Van Hollen said.

"Detaining Maria Flores Garcia – a former high school valedictorian and current student at the University of Maryland – puts a clear lie to ICE's claim that they are going after 'the worst of the worst.' They are not. They are going after whoever they please, and it's clear they're not making our communities any safer," he added.

text:
By VALERIE GONZALEZ and TIM SULLIVAN

It’s business as usual for President Donald Trump’s deportation offensive despite the Republican wipeout in the midterm elections.

In Los Angeles, masked immigration officers in body armor blocked a hospital emergency room driveway in a heavily Latino neighborhood early Saturday. In central Alabama, twin 19-year-old brothers from Venezuela were arrested while driving back to college a day after the election.

Advocates reported arrests from California to Michigan to Massachusetts. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has not released numbers.

After Democrats trounced the GOP and won control of the next Congress, Trump said his immigration crackdown may have been “too tough” and suggested it was time to sit down with the rival party.

“I’d love to do something on immigration,” he said in an interview with CBS “60 Minutes” recorded Friday.

Hours later, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, said his orders had not changed.

“Deportations will continue,” Mullin wrote in an online post the day after the election, warning that ICE takes no days off and that “this includes on Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Election Day.”

María Bilbao, a campaign coordinator for the American Friends Service Committee in Miami, said she has received at least one call a day from someone detained in South Florida since the election.

“Everything remains exactly the same. The arrests have not ceased at all,” Bilbao said.

Florida Highway Patrol officers and ICE agents have detained people in their cars, as well as places including supermarkets, pharmacies and gas stations. Immigrants under supervision have also been arrested when they showed up at ICE’s Miami office for their appointments.

Officers assembled outside a Los Angeles hospital

Erick Gasca, 31, got home Friday night after an evening playing board games with friends. He lives near Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Los Angeles.

An “unprecedented” number of vehicles with tinted windows and no license plates were parked near the hospital’s emergency room entrance, he said.

“I thought they were going to raid the hospital or something,” he recalled.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to explain the officers’ presence there, though Bill Essayli, the top Justice Department prosecutor in Los Angeles, said they were bringing a detainee for medical treatment. Essayli said two people were arrested for assaulting federal agents.

“ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches,” DHS said in a statement.

The agents’ presence attracted some 30 residents and passersby. Footage shot by Gasca’s cousin, Michelle Rivera, shows protesters shouting and officers pinning someone down.

The hospital said it wasn’t involved.

“White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement,” hospital president Daniel Fontoura said in a statement, adding it would not let such activities “compromise our commitment to patient care and safety.”

A couple is arrested at the Phoenix airport

A married couple from Orlando, Florida, was arrested Saturday at the airport in Phoenix while traveling to a funeral.

Gustavo Romanello and Agustin Baccega, both from Argentina, have work permits while they seek asylum after entering the United States about six years ago, according to Jonathan Batchelor, a family friend.

Batchelor was on the phone with them at the time. A mutual friend died Friday and the couple was visiting for the funeral Saturday. As the couple left the airport, two casually dressed officers asked if one was Agustin Baccega. Batchelor heard the officer say, “Asylum seekers are not in the United States legally.”

Batchelor said he could hear Romanello walking alongside his husband during the arrest and asking the officers how to collect his things. Batchelor said they then asked what his name was, “and then the guard said, ‘Oh, do you have another set of handcuffs? This is another one.’”

The voices grew distant, and the call then ended.

Both men remain in detention centers. They worked as acrobats in Florida and had no criminal record, Batchelor said.

“This is just taking good people who have been following the rules out of their lives and out of the lives of those who rely upon them and care about them,” Batchelor said.

DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the arrests.

Twin brothers seized while driving back to college

The brothers were headed back to college after visiting their parents when they were stopped in a small city in central Alabama.

Luis and Carlos Orta-Santoro, 19-year-olds born in Venezuela and living in the U.S. for four years, are soccer players at Wallace State Community College in Hanceville, Alabama.

Relatives say they have pending asylum applications, valid work permits, and no criminal records. Both are now in an immigration detention facility.

“Our family is devastated,” said their aunt, Carolina Orta.

DHS said that while they had entered the country legally, they had “overstayed in defiance of our laws,” and their case would be heard by an immigration judge. It said pending asylum applications do not confer legal status in the U.S.

The school said in a statement, “Both young men are valued members of the Wallace State community, and our thoughts are with them during this difficult time. We sincerely hope for a positive resolution to their situation.”

A Haitian boy is taken into custody, drawing protests in San Diego

An 8-year-old Haitian boy had been living with his uncle in San Diego since his father was deported last year. The uncle, who is not a legal guardian, took him to an ICE office when the boy was summoned Nov. 4 and taken into custody.

That left the boy “without the support of their family, community and their school,” according to a letter to top administration officials from San Diego Unified School District Superintendent Fabi Bagula and school board members.

“Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” they wrote.

ICE has defended its actions.

Johny Oxeda, pastor of the Fairmount Haitian Community Church, which helped get legal representation for the boy, said he’ll ultimately benefit by going through legal channels.

Activists, though, were furious.

“This is not child protection,” said Guerline Jozef of Haitian Bridge Alliance, adding, “this is state-inflicted trauma.”

Associated Press reporters Gisela Salomon in Miami and Elliot Spagat in San Diego contributed.

text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says the Trump administration has no plans to back down from its immigration enforcement policies despite Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress in last week's midterm elections.

Appearing Tuesday on Fox News' The Ingraham Angle, Mullin made it clear that deportations will continue and that providing legal status to illegal immigrants is not part of the administration's agenda.

"Amnesty will never be on the table," Mullin said.

According to Mullin, the Department of Homeland Security is deporting approximately 3,600 people daily, with enforcement efforts increasingly focused on violent criminals, drug traffickers, and cartel members.

The comments come as Democrats prepare to take control of the House and Senate in January, potentially setting up major confrontations with President Donald Trump over immigration policy and federal enforcement priorities.

Mullin expressed skepticism about the possibility of reaching agreements with congressional Democrats, accusing party leaders of seeking to undermine the Department of Homeland Security.

He also criticized the influence of the Democratic Socialists of America, claiming its members want to reduce funding for his department.

Despite the change in congressional control, Mullin pointed out that Trump retains presidential veto authority, which could prevent Democrats from passing immigration legislation opposed by the White House.

Democrats are expected to pursue greater oversight of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and examine the administration's deportation practices. However, significant legislative changes would likely require Republican support or presidential approval.

The administration has maintained that aggressive immigration enforcement is essential to protecting public safety and national security.

Mullin reiterated that position Tuesday, arguing that knowing who is entering and remaining in the United States is fundamental to maintaining a secure country.

His comments signal that immigration enforcement will remain a central administration priority despite the Republican Party's electoral setbacks.

text:
Odd as it might seem, I believe that the best way for the U.S. House to commemorate Veterans Day this year would be to vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Not only has Hegseth bungled the war in Iran and orchestrated a hostile takeover of Venezuela, but he has also besmirched all veterans by demeaning and demoting women, Black people and gay people in the military. Hegseth’s brand of virulent Christian triumphalism is a threat to our national security and the safety of our troops. America needs a savvy, seasoned military commander at the helm who is more concerned about preserving peace than promoting war. It’s time for common sense, not increased testosterone levels.

In other words, they expected voters would be more concerned about (a) failure to prevent financial crimes that (b) were not committed by anyone representing a political party and (c) were not condoned by anyone on the ballot. They expected this to matter more to us than (d) gross inhumanity as a result of a coordinated effort that was (e) instigated by the leader of a political party who was (f) enabled and defended by candidates from that party.

Something has gone badly wrong if it can seem politically reasonable to expect responsibility for preventing theft to matter more than human rights, common decency and killing. Perhaps we should take some encouragement from the fact that, this time, voters defied such cynical expectations. But we should be considerably less encouraged that those expectations seemed reasonable in the first place.

I read the article “How Operation Metro Surge helped fuel Minnesota’s Democratic sweep” with great interest. I noted some elements of reflection from Minnesota Republican Party Chair Alex Plechash and Republican congressional candidate Eric Pratt, perhaps among others who weren’t in the article. Good for them. As a resident of Minneapolis, I assure everyone reading this that the Immigration and Customs Enforcement occupation of our city — cities — was outrageous, disgusting and deadly, and voter turnout was higher than usual in response for a midterm. But then I finished the article and kept reading the newspaper, and saw that the Trump administration had dug in on its “hard-line agenda” and had made Stephen Miller, the “driver of the president’s most muscular actions” on immigration, the administration’s new chief of staff.

So, Plechash, Pratt and other Minnesota Republicans engaging in reflection upon your complete rejection by the voters of Minnesota during these midterms: Look yourselves in the mirror. Because this is who you are now. This is your GOP. And thus, this is the Minnesota GOP. Is this who you want to be? Reflections mean nothing without actions. If you don’t break from your national party — the party of not just President Donald Trump but, more insidiously, that of Miller, whether you like it or not — you’ll continue down the same road that led you to your historic 2026 midterm losses, and you’ll cement your deserved current status as statewide political pariahs.

If there were any doubt in your mind as to what President Donald Trump thinks about the voters in our country, it has been made crystal clear with his appointment of Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff. As Jonathan Capehart said on the PBS News Hour on Nov. 6, Trump has given the American people his middle finger with that appointment. Do not believe, even for an instant, that this president is willing to work with Democrats or accomplish anything for the good of the people in this country. We must continue our resistance until he is out of office and his influence is eradicated.

Monday’s Star Tribune contained two letters highlighting the challenges Rep. Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer face in their attempts to secure for themselves the Democratic Party’s leadership positions in Congress. Both writers are guilty of reading more into Tuesday’s results than is prudent. The safest, most cautious attempt to capture voter sentiment goes something like this: Government is not working for me, President Donald Trump said he was going to fix it, and in fact he made it worse. Voters gave Democrats a limited chance to show that they heard and understood that message and that they can respond appropriately.

As for Schumer, it’s hard not to appear feckless when you don’t have the votes. Reporting in the New York Times reveals some of what he was up to in the months leading up to last Tuesday. In May 2025, he was so smitten with a five-minute speech given by a young Texas legislator that he was convinced the speaker should run for Senate. The speaker was James Talarico.

Point is, people can surprise you. Perhaps it’s time to let the word “representative” in the term “representative democracy” have its day and grant our newly elected representatives the same opportunity to earn our trust that the voters did on Tuesday. Let’s hope they can do so.

Some Democrats, including a recent letter writer (“Common sense beckons”), don’t want Flanagan to vote against Schumer in his bid to become the next Senate majority leader. They don’t want any disruption in the party; they want it to deliver on the issue of affordability posthaste. They expect her to be a cog in the party machinery and to vote without evaluating the merits of the candidate or what moral wrongs that vote will enable to continue. They just want her to go along with the party seniority system. I don’t get why that should be happening. This is a democracy, and we as a party need to seek the moral high ground and get the best leadership we can get.

Schumer is tied to outdated politics and to AIPAC, which lubricates officeholders’ campaign funds so that they support Israel in receiving U.S. aid. I’m not against most forms of U.S. aid, but this aid goes, essentially, to U.S. arms manufacturers, who profit immensely from government largesse, and then to Israel, which uses those arms given to them by the U.S. in its genocide of Palestinians. (More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since October 2023.) I don’t hate Israel, but I hate this. It is wrong for the Democratic Party to fund genocide, and it is wrong for the Democratic Party to keep in power leaders who are enablers of this horror. I’m sure the party can afford the two or three weeks it likely would take to shake off the grip of AIPAC-backed leaders before it focuses on issues of affordability and corruption. The party has to get its house in order first.

text:
The family of a Lodi woman detained by federal immigration agents in September spent days trying to locate her before learning she had been transferred to a detention center in Louisiana, the New York Times reported Tuesday.

Ann Lawani was detained by federal immigration agents at her Lodi home on Sept. 16, taken later that day to a local holding facility, according to the Times.

There, she called her family. But in the days after, Lawani’s whereabouts were unknown, and he could not be found on a public database used to locate detainees in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.

The family would spend three days trying to locate Lawani, of Nigeria, before she phoned from a detention facility in Louisiana.

During her transfers, ICE allegedly attempted to deport Lawani to an undisclosed third country, said Rep. Josh Harder, D-Tracy, in an Oct. 20 letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin where he called for Lawani’s return to California as her immigration case continues.

“Her detention raises serious questions about the Department’s enforcement priorities and its treatment of individuals who pose no threat to public safety,” said Harder in the letter.

Lawani, 39, had lived in Lodi for 13 years, where she cared for her 83-year-old father, Harder said in a news release Tuesday renewing his call for her release. He also said Lawani was a professor at the University of San Francisco and worked as a nurse at John Muir Health in Concord.

In 2007, Lawani entered the U.S. on a visitor visa and later applied for asylum. While an immigration judge denied her asylum request in 2013, they ruled she could not be deported to Nigeria because she “more likely than not” faced persecution there.

Her work permit, issued the next year, would be one she would regularly renew, according to the Times. Her latest permit remained valid until 2029.

The Department of Homeland Security told the Times that Lawani was detained because she had been ordered removed in 2013.

The practice of no longer disclosing where detainees are being held began on Sept. 15, officials with the immigration agency told the Associated Press. In late October, the American Immigration Lawyers Association and other immigrant rights organization filed a lawsuit challenging the practice, saying it interferes with lawyers and families trying to reach detainees.

Harder said there was no “apparent public safety justification” for detaining Lawani miles from her Lodi residence given her lack of criminal history and longstanding ties to the area.

“Our immigration enforcement system should focus on protecting communities from danger, not removing the individuals who dedicate their lives to serving them,” Harder said. “Dr. Lawani’s continued detention undermines that mission while imposing unnecessary harm on her family and the countless people who depend on her.”

Her absence, Harder continued, has disrupted campus life. Eileen K. Fry-Bowers, the San Francisco school’s nursing dean, said Lawani’s continued absence is causing “real and mounting harm” to the students and faculty she mentors.

“I speak with confidence to what I know firsthand: Dr. Ann Lawani is a person of exceptional professional accomplishment and moral character, deeply embedded in our university community, with responsibilities that hundreds of nursing students and, in turn, the patients they will someday care for, depend upon her fulfilling,” she said in a statement shared by Harder’s office.

Lawani’s brother, Samuel Lawani, who was interviewed by the Times, called her arrest “the worst time” of his life. In a statement shared by Harder, he described his sister’s abrupt detainment and transfer across the country as “simply evil and consequential.”

“My family and I want to see my sister returned home safely and as soon as possible,” he said. “Like so many families in our community, we want an end to the chaos caused by these agencies.”

text:
A group of Democratic lawmakers is seeking information from the Trump administration after an 8-year-old Haitian boy was taken into government custody last week.

In a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Tuesday, six Democratic lawmakers asked what steps are being taken to reunite the child with his family.

"Video footage appears to show the use of restraints on a child who seemed to pose no threat to those around him, raising serious questions about the handling of this incident," the lawmakers wrote. "We express concerns about the basis for this action and the harm it may cause a young child who appeared for his required hearing."

The 8-year-old, who lost Temporary Protected Status earlier this year as part of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in last week, according to local advocates and school officials.

The third grader, who attends Fay Elementary School in San Diego, was detained alone after attending an Immigration and Customs Enforcement appointment with his uncle on Thursday.

Advocates and school officials previously said the boy had been living with his uncle and cousins after his father was deported to Mexico last year.

"They did not give the father the opportunity or chance to actually put in place legal guardianship for the kid," said Guerline Jozef, the executive director of the nonprofit Haitian Bridge Alliance.

A spokesperson for ICE told ABC News that agents acted under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act because the uncle could not establish legal guardianship.

"Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child's safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," the spokesperson said.

Jozef called the detention "an excuse for [ICE] to remove the child and potentially put him in deportation proceedings."

"The effects of this action extend far beyond one child and his family," the lawmakers said in their letter.

text:
More than 150 immigrant rights organizations and allied groups are urging Democrats to pursue a pathway to citizenship or permanent legal status for undocumented immigrants, investigate the Trump administration's deportation practices and roll back funding for federal immigration enforcement agencies following the party's midterm election victory.

In a letter first shared with Politico, the coalition called on lawmakers to "prioritize a bold agenda" when the next Congress convenes, arguing that investigations alone would be insufficient to address the consequences of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

The organizations want Congress to examine whether the Department of Homeland Security violated federal law while implementing mass deportations. They also called for changes to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) operations and the recovery of funding allocated to immigration agencies through previous budget reconciliation legislation.

"The harms inflicted on immigrant communities by this administration will echo for generations," the groups wrote. "Congress has the opportunity now to stand with communities under siege and show the world that accountability and justice are possible."

Their demands come as Democrats prepare to control both chambers of Congress following last week's elections. However, divisions remain between progressive lawmakers seeking broader immigration reform and moderates favoring more limited changes to enforcement policies.

Immigration advocates have also begun discussing demonstrations and renewed legalization efforts, according to El País. Francisco Moreno, executive director of the Council of Mexican Federations in North America, warned Democrats against repeating the failure to enact comprehensive immigration reform during Barack Obama's presidency.

"There are grounds for another amnesty," Moreno said, arguing that the election results offer an opportunity to pursue legislation benefiting millions of undocumented immigrants.

One existing proposal is the bipartisan Dignity Act, introduced by Republican María Elvira Salazar and Democrat Veronica Escobar. It would offer eligible undocumented immigrants renewable protection from deportation and work authorization, but generally would not establish a pathway to permanent residency.

Trump, meanwhile, has acknowledged that his deportation policies may have alienated voters. In an interview discussed by PBS News, the president said his approach "might be too tough" and expressed willingness to negotiate with Democrats.

However, Trump's decision to promote Stephen Miller, an architect of his immigration policies, to White House chief of staff raises questions about whether the administration will support the broader reforms sought by advocacy organizations.
