text:
The Trump administration is still detaining pregnant migrant youth in a region of Texas where a lack of specialized obstetric care can be life threatening for them, an investigation by The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom has found. The practice continues despite vocal concern from its own current and former officials, and from members of Congress.

Government records also show that at least four pregnant girls in detention have had to be transferred out of state since last July to receive specialized medical care, including at least one abortion, that is unavailable in Texas.

“The first time that happened should have been a wake-up call for the administration, and they should have stopped placing kids in any remote area where they can’t get care,” said Jen Smyers, who during the Biden administration helped oversee the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), which is responsible for migrant youth who are apprehended without a parent or guardian.

She called the policy to send pregnant children to South Texas “enraging.”

This spring, The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom published a joint investigation revealing the administration’s policy of detaining pregnant unaccompanied minors as young as 13 at a single shelter in the Rio Grande Valley. The investigation detailed serious concerns that health experts inside and outside the government had raised about the policy, given that adolescent pregnancies are inherently high risk and there is a lack of specialized obstetric care in the region.

Since then, the administration has denied the policy exists and said it is ensuring that the girls have access to the care they need.

In an unsigned email in September, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees ORR, wrote that “ORR’s policies for placing children in its custody into care provider facilities are based on child welfare best practices in order to provide a safe environment and place the child in the least restrictive setting appropriate for the child’s needs. This is especially true for expectant minors in ORR care.”

Yet the administration’s own records, as well as interviews with multiple government officials, suggest otherwise.

The documents, which were obtained through a public records request, show that ORR explicitly directed its staff in July 2025 to send all pregnant youth to the shelter in San Benito, just outside Brownsville.

Several months later, internal agency data showed that pregnant girls started being funneled to a different shelter nearby instead, according to three ORR officials who asked not to be named because they feared retaliation.

Forty-eight Democratic members of Congress expressed concerns about the policy in a pointed letter to the Department of Health and Human Services back in April.

They received a response in September from an assistant secretary at HHS, Alex J. Adams, who wrote that ORR “does not make placement decisions for pregnant youth based on a blanket rule or one-size-fits-all approach” and that it “takes seriously its responsibility to protect the health, safety, dignity, and well-being of every unaccompanied alien child in its custody.”

HHS did not respond to requests for comment about the discrepancy between the statements in Adams’ letter and the government’s own records.

“Obviously, they’re not being honest about their policy,” said U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, a Democrat from San Antonio, whose office authored the letter to HHS.

“It’s irresponsible that they would wait several months to respond to basic questions about the care of some of the most vulnerable people within the system,” Castro said, adding that the administration failed to explain “what seems to be an informal but strict policy of sending these girls to deep South Texas, which lacks the medical care that the girls need.”

U.S. Rep. Dan Crenshaw, a Republican from Texas who has been vocal about the welfare of unaccompanied children and serves on a congressional committee that oversees HHS, did not respond to requests for comment.

Unaccompanied migrant children have historically been placed in shelters across the United States, but this summer, the Trump administration began detaining far more of them in Texas.

According to internal reports provided independently by two officials at ORR, both of whom asked not to be named due to fear of reprisal by their supervisors, 95% of the roughly 300 children apprehended by immigration officials in September were placed in detention in Texas, up from 45% in June.

Advocates for unaccompanied migrant children, former government officials, and some members of Congress have criticized the move, arguing that the state is not prepared to handle an influx of vulnerable children who need special care.

The fact that ORR has had to transfer several pregnant unaccompanied minors out of Texas to receive medical care, they say, is proving their point.

“If the government had to fly or transport these pregnant children across the country to get them the medical care they need, why on earth did it deliberately send them to Texas in the first place?” said U.S. Rep. Judy Chu, a Democrat from Southern California, who was unaware of the transfers until a journalist described the newsrooms’ findings.

Chu pointed to the fact that many of the pregnant children who enter federal immigration custody are the victims of sexual assault.

“If there is a 13-year-old girl who has survived rape,” she said, “she should be met with compassion, safety and appropriate medical care. Instead, this administration is placing children like her in a state where they will be deprived of access to basic healthcare. It’s dangerous, and it’s cruel, and there’s no excuse for treating children this way.”

Government records contradict Trump administration’s claims

Unlike Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which detains migrant adults and families in large, prison-like facilities, ORR detains unaccompanied children in group or foster homes overseen by private contractors. Laws, agency regulations and court orders require that the children receive comprehensive healthcare and appropriate education while they’re detained.

In an unsigned email last month, a spokesperson for HHS said that placing children in Texas is “operationally efficient” and that ORR’s facilities in the state “provide all requirements and more.” But records obtained through a public information request cast doubt on that assertion.

The records show between July of 2025, when ORR began placing pregnant girls in South Texas, and May of 2026, four of them had to be transferred to other states to receive medical treatment.

That’s roughly one in five of the more than 20 pregnant girls the agency placed in the region in that time frame, according to one ORR official.

In detailed notes for one of those cases, ORR staff wrote that a pregnant 12-year-old girl was transferred from the Rio Grande Valley to a shelter in New York on the recommendation of ORR’s division of health. The records note that the child needed access to specialists whose availability in South Texas is “extremely limited.”

Four days later, ORR issued a directive to begin placing “any pregnant children” at a shelter in Cameron County called Urban Strategies San Benito.

Tracey Wilkinson, a pediatrician in Indiana who specializes in reproductive healthcare access for minors, said that even if the government is transferring children to get medical care, waiting until they need it puts them in danger.

“When you’re talking about labor or pregnancy complications, every minute counts,” Wilkinson said. “If it was a medical emergency that required this young person to be transported out of the state, the risk to her survival would be lower for no reason other than she was placed in the middle of nowhere, far away from medical care.”

‘They are trying to deliberately mislead Congress members’

Shortly after The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom revealed the Trump administration’s policy of detaining pregnant migrant youth in Texas, Castro launched an inquiry into the practice. He soon arranged a visit to the San Benito shelter.

But by the time of his visit on April 7, internal agency data showed that ORR had stopped placing newly detained children with known pregnancies at the facility, three officials said. Instead, the agency was sending them to a different shelter, in Los Fresnos, just 20 minutes away.

Castro said he was not told of the change at the time of his visit, nor was it mentioned in ORR’s formal response to the congressional inquiry last month.

In a recent interview, he described his visit to the San Benito shelter as “a very secretive process” and said he was not allowed to see or speak with any of the children there.

An HHS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the location change, writing only that “there have been no operational changes regarding the placement of pregnant unaccompanied children.”

Chu, the Congresswoman from California, said she believed the Trump administration made the change in order to “deliberately mislead Congress members as well as the public from really knowing where these pregnant children have been.”

Compass Connections, the San Antonio-based nonprofit that operates the shelter in Los Fresnos where pregnant girls are now being held, is one of the largest ORR contractors; it has been awarded over $1.9 billion in federal grants to house and care for unaccompanied minors over the past four years, according to USAspending.gov. Asked for comment, the company referred the newsrooms to HHS.

In his letter to Castro, Assistant Secretary Adams wrote that “placement and transfer decisions are individualized and consider the child’s safety, medical and behavioral health needs, pregnancy-related needs, available services, legal access, family unity, least restrictive placement requirements, and the best interest of the child.”

‘In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare’

Congress members and advocates in California said the state offers much more support for pregnant girls in federal custody than they can receive in Texas.

As the Trump administration has withdrawn federal support for legal representation of unaccompanied children — and at the same time streamlined the process of deporting them — the state of California, as well as several of its cities and counties, have ramped up funding for their own legal services programs for undocumented kids.

“Pregnant unaccompanied children have rights to medical care, safety, family unity and due process, but those rights mean little without a lawyer to defend them,” said Marion “Mickey” Donovan-Kaloust, director of legal services at Immigrant Defenders in Los Angeles. “California’s support systems can provide pregnant unaccompanied children with the stability, dignity and specialized care they need to be safe and thrive.”

In addition to concerns about their access to healthcare and legal services, advocates worry that the Trump administration is knowingly putting pregnant children at risk to advance an ideological goal: denying them access to abortions by placing them in Texas, where abortion is virtually banned.

Current federal regulations require the government to move detained minors who request abortions to states where it’s legal. In January, the Trump administration announced it plans to rescind that rule, though it hasn’t yet done so.

An HHS spokesperson said in February that claims the department is attempting to restrict unaccompanied children’s access to abortion are “completely inaccurate.”

Congressman Gil Cisneros, a Democrat from Southern California, said, “In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare, and then they could make decisions based on discussions with their healthcare professional and what’s best for them.”

Chu noted that the midterm elections will determine whether Democrats regain control of the U.S. House of Representatives. If they do, she said, they will redouble their efforts to ensure pregnant children in federal immigration custody are given proper care.

“There will be greater oversight,” she said, “and we will hold the decision-makers responsible.”

text:
A Minneapolis woman who was violently pulled out of her car and arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents while she was on her way to a doctor’s appointment in January is suing the federal government.

Aliya Rahman, a Minneapolis resident, filed the lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Minnesota Tuesday claiming that she was the victim of false arrest and imprisonment, negligent supervision, negligence, assault, and battery.

“I am one of many who have been impacted by this government’s vile abuse of power,” Rahman said in a statement. “And while this lawsuit stems from what happened in January, the terror did not start there and has not stopped.”

Rahman, who is autistic and has physical disabilities, was traveling to a medical appointment on January 13 during Operation Metro Surge, the federal government’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota’s twin cities. ICE agents surrounded her car and smashed her window after she said, “They needed to learn how to respect human beings,” her complaint states. They then dragged her out of the car and sent her to a federal detention facility for hours. She said that she was denied medical care while in ICE custody, and had to go to the hospital after losing consciousness.

Her violent arrest was captured on video and went viral online, and she later testified before Congress. She went on to attend President Trump’s State of the Union address in February as a guest of Representative Ilhan Omar, and was arrested by Capitol police for “disruption of Congress,” before the charges against her were dropped in March.

Rahman’s lawsuit comes after multiple attempts to hold ICE agents accountable. She filed a Federal Tort Claims Act claim alleging unlawful force and detention in April, and in June filed a federal complaint with the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. The tort claim was a prerequisite for Tuesday’s lawsuit.

Rahman’s attorney, Jessica Gingold of the MacArthur Justice Center, said at a news conference Tuesday that part of the lawsuit’s goal was identifying the agents responsible for the violent attack.

“We will find the names,” Gingold said. “We have their pictures…. We have a right to depose them. We have a right to get their records to understand who these individuals were who heard Aliya, frustrated and confused, and reacted with such violence.”

Trump officials are destroying documents related to his pet projects in Washington, D.C., according to whistleblowers.

CNN reports that whistleblowers have warned House Democrats that key documents have already been destroyed before Democrats take over Congress in January. Democratic Representative Jared Huffman, the ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, plans to issue letters to the Department of the Interior, as well other federal agencies and private companies involved in the president’s projects, demanding that they “preserve all records and data responsive to oversight.”

Huffman is also sending letters to the National Park Service, the Bureau of Land Management, and the Department of Agriculture, as well as companies such as Lockheed Martin and John Deere, which have donated to Trump’s projects in the past.

The recipients of Huffman’s letters must reply to certify their compliance. This means that they should make efforts to “preserve existing records collections and productions,” as well as “identify and recover any deleted information” and “suspend any destruction and deletion practices.”

“Everything is coming; it’s all coming,” Huffman told CNN. “It’s just going to be an entirely new day.”

Huffman told CNN that his committee could stop some of Trump’s projects, “especially because we have standing to go to court if we have to,” he said. “We’ll have tools to be able to stop a lot of it.”

The Interior Department said that the whistleblowers were “100 percent false,” saying that “the department follows all federal records management obligations as directed by the department’s ethics officials.”

Documents on Trump’s ballroom, his renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, his takeover of the East Potomac Golf Links course, and his triumphal arch could all be at risk.

Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders has added his name to the growing list of liberal-minded lawmakers asking Chuck Schumer to hand over the reins of the Senate.

“I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer,” Sanders said at a joint press conference with Senator Elissa Slotkin Tuesday. “But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.”

The Democratic Socialist encouraged “vigorous debate” as the party searched for an alternative, and highlighted that such a process should take place “out in the open.”

“We need … to show the American people that a new day has come, and that their votes meant a new direction in Washington,” Sanders said.

Sanders told reporters earlier in the day that he would not support Schumer’s bid for Senate majority leader in the new year. When asked by The Washington Times’s Lindsey McPherson if he would support Schumer even if the current leader runs unopposed, Sanders responded: “He’s not going to run unopposed, I don’t think.”

A wave of Democratic voices opposing Schumer’s possible return atop the Senate emerged after the party won an overwhelming majority in Congress last week, rebuking the septuagenarian’s establishment politics. In the days since, Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has emerged as a potential alternative, indicating a rising interest in progressive leadership.

Van Hollen rose as a leading progressive last year, when he travelled out of the country to visit his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García after García was illegally deported by the Trump administration to El Salvador’s notoriously lethal maximum security prison, CECOT.

Whether or not Van Hollen will officially commit himself against Schumer remains to be seen, though the Marylander has already started to draft an opposition platform that could put pressure on Schumer’s politics. On Tuesday, Van Hollen declared that the U.S. cannot spend “a penny more” on the Iran War, daring Donald Trump to either stop funding the war or face the possibility of a government shutdown.

So far, at least 10 major politicos have either peeled away from Schumer outright or indicated an interest in a different Senate majority leader. They include:

Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders

Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin

Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed

Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal

Illinois Senator-elect Juliana Stratton

Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan

Kansas Senator-elect Adam Hamilton

Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson

New Hampshire Senator-elect Chris Pappas

Texas Senator-elect James Talarico

Another 14 senators or senators-elect have not yet committed as to whether or not they will support Schumer, according to an analysis published Monday by Primary Democrats. Altogether, that’s 24 Democrats—or nearly half of the at least 54 Democratic seats that will dominate the upper chamber come January.

New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has also refused to support her home state senator, though the decision is ultimately up to the Senate.

House Republicans elected Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio as their new minority leader on Tuesday.

Jordan, who has served as a representative for Ohio’s 4th district since 2007, won the secret ballot vote 106–73, two people present for the tally told Politico. He was up against Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, who currently serves as the number two Republican in the House.

Jordan was selected following sweeping Democratic victories in the midterm elections that flipped the House and Senate, prompting House Speaker Mike Johnson to announce he would step down from Republican leadership.

There are plenty of reasons that Jordan has previously been kept out of such a powerful position. That is, until now.

Years before Jordan was elected to the House, he served as an assistant coach to Ohio State University’s wrestling team between 1986 and 1994. The Ohio Republican has faced severe blowback for allegedly participating in a coverup of the rampant sex abuse by team doctor Richard Strauss, who committed 1,429 sexual assaults and 47 rapes against at least 177 male student-athletes during his tenure, according to a 2019 university report.

Jordan also has earned a reputation as a vocal election denier who assisted President Donald Trump in his proven efforts to overturn the results of the presidential election in 2020. Along with several of his Republican colleagues, Jordan refused to comply with a subpoena from the House Select Committee that investigated the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. The committee unearthed evidence that Jordan had materially relevant communications with Trump and others related to January 6. In July this year, Jordan referred former special counsel Jack Smith to the Department of Justice for possible prosecution, alleging that he’d made false statements to Congress.

As House Judiciary Committee chairman, Jordan enjoyed playing Trump’s personal attorney. Now he’ll get to lead the much-diminished party as it fends off investigations from Democratic lawmakers.

Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday for “high crimes and misdemeanors.” The eight impeachment articles accuse Hegseth of violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by continuing to attack Iran even after both chambers of Congress ordered the Trump administration to stop. He’s also accused of illegally waging war against Yemen, ignoring laws designed to reduce civilian casualties, overseeing “extrajudicial killings” in attacks on boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific, abducting Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization, and suppressing the free speech rights of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in retaliation for reminding troops not to obey illegal orders. Congressmember Massie outlined the charges during a speech from the House floor.

Rep. Thomas Massie: “Wherefore, Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law, Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States.”

It’s expected the House will vote on Hegseth’s impeachment on Wednesday. Only a few Republican defectors would be needed for a simple majority, setting up a Senate trial on whether to remove Hegseth. On Monday, President Trump said he would stand by Hegseth if he’s impeached.

The Wall Street Journal reports the Pentagon has evacuated aircraft from a second base in the United Kingdom due to another alleged threat from Iran. U.S. refueling tankers were reportedly moved from a base in Mildenhall on Monday. Last month, the Pentagon pulled B-1 bombers out of another British base.

Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says two more ships, including a supertanker, are on fire near the Strait of Hormuz after using what Iranian officials have called an “unauthorized route.” Iran has claimed 11 strikes on ships over a 10-day span. The continued attacks on shipping came as Iran’s Foreign Ministry said it could reopen the strait within 48 hours if the U.S. agrees to Tehran’s list of demands.

Esmail Baghaei: “If the U.S. meets the demands put forward by Iran, the situation in the region could see a positive shift in as little as two days, and security in the Strait of Hormuz could also be restored.”

On Monday, President Trump spoke with Qatar’s prime minister, who’s acted as a mediator in efforts to end the war. After the talks, Trump claimed there was “positive momentum” in negotiations for a deal with Iran.

President Donald Trump: “The military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes. Israel and the entire Middle East are protected from Iranian danger and threats, and we’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon.”

Since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, Trump has claimed more than 40 times that the war was close to an end, that a deal was near, or that the war was already over.

Democrats are continuing to build on their historic wins in last week’s midterm elections as votes continue to be counted. In Mississippi, Scott Colom’s lead over Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith has topped 2,500 votes, with just two batches of ballots left to be counted before a Friday deadline to certify the results.

In Colorado, Republican Congressmember Lauren Boebert is trailing in her bid to hold on to her seat. On Monday, CNN projected Boebert will lose the race to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired U.S. Navy admiral who served on the National Security Council under President Joe Biden.

On Monday, President Trump reversed his previous comment that he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results of the midterm elections. Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, “Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???”

Senate Democrats could be headed for a leadership shakeup, after Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen indicated Monday he’s open to running for Senate majority leader when the new Congress convenes in January. A source close to Van Hollen told Politico the Maryland Democrat is thinking about a run after he “received an outpouring of calls and is now in active listening mode. The door is not shut.”

This comes as a growing number of Senate Democrats have called for new leadership or refused to commit to supporting New York Senator Chuck Schumer for majority leader. Joining the call is a major labor union, the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, which wrote in a letter to Schumer on Monday, “We believe this is the right moment for a new generation to lead Senate Democrats.”

Meanwhile, Connecticut Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal said he’s open to new leadership if a challenger to Schumer emerges.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal: “But we need to have a conversation about leadership going forward, because we need new energy and ideas.”

In more news from Capitol Hill, the Senate voted 73 to 25 Monday to take up a sweeping permitting reform bill. It was advanced by nearly every Republican and 22 Democrats. Environmental groups have called the legislation an “aggressive attack on federal environmental protections in order to facilitate rapid, unregulated development of fracked gas power plants, dirty fossil fuel pipelines, and expensive hyperscale data centers.” Meanwhile, Indigenous leaders, including New Mexico Governor-elect Deb Haaland, argue the bill would undermine tribal sovereignty.

More than 160 health, consumer, religious and environmental groups are calling on Congress to instead pass the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act. It’s sponsored by Michigan democratic socialist Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib, who said, “[The] elections send a clear message that Americans want their representatives to protect their health and environment, not sell them out to Big Tech and Big Oil.”

Here in New York, activists with Climate Defenders, New York Communities for Change and Planet Over Profit protested at Anthropic’s Manhattan offices for over an hour on Monday. Five of them were arrested for blocking the employee security entrance. The protesters blasted Anthropic’s moves toward an initial public offering that could see it valued at $1.4 trillion — far less than previous estimates it could be worth as much as $2 trillion. This comes after major global tech stocks fell sharply last week following the U.S. midterm elections, which sparked concerns among investors that the Democratic takeover of both chambers of Congress will mean tougher regulation of AI. This is activist Jonathan Westin speaking to Democracy Now! as he was being arrested.

Jonathan Westin: “I’m getting arrested because we’re trying to stop Anthropic from crashing the global economy, along with AI. They are not worth the paper they’re printed on. Millions and millions of lives will be affected by it.”

Back in the United States, a deportation flight carrying Iranian nationals to Iran via Pakistan was abruptly canceled Sunday morning, after at least eight Iranians had been loaded onto a plane in Mesa, Arizona, bound first for the Republic of Georgia. The flight would reportedly have been the first deportation of Iranians since the U.S. launched attacks on Iran in February. Back in October, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes ordered the U.S. government to give the court 24-hour notice of any plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country, and five days’ written notice before deportation is carried out.

In San Diego, an 8-year-old Haitian boy is in federal custody after ICE detained him at a scheduled immigration appointment. He had been living with his uncle since his father was deported last year. DHS says the uncle could not establish legal guardianship. Guerline Jozef, executive director of Haitian Bridge Alliance, said, “This is not child protection. This is state-inflicted trauma disguised as immigration enforcement. An eight-year-old child should be sitting in a classroom, learning, playing, and dreaming about his future, not being taken away and retraumatized by armed federal agents. His father has already been taken from him and deported, now this administration has stripped him of the stability, family, and community every child deserves.”

The news outlet New York Focus has uncovered a 2023 lawsuit in which two former Cornell students say the university’s Title IX office ignored their complaints that the same male student sexually assaulted them in 2018 and 2021. A complaint filed by one of the students and their lawyer says, “At least five to ten others are known to have been sexually abused and it is believed that many more were abused but have yet to come forward.” Cornell University and the male student tried to have the case dismissed, but a trial is scheduled for next year. The lawsuit follows another high-profile lawsuit filed by Jane Doe in September over an alleged fraternity gang rape at Cornell in 2024, prompting a massive public outcry and leading to New York Attorney General Letitia James ordering a new investigation.

text:
Military veterans only now have until November 30 to file proof of claim in the Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceeding as court extends prior deadline

AG Ellison’s Office reiterates warning to veterans to beware of claims sharks

November 10, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — In advance of Veterans Day, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison is alerting military veterans that they now have until November 30 to file a proof of claim in the Chapter 11 proceedings of Trajector Holdings, LLC. The bankruptcy court in this case had set an earlier deadline of October 31 for all consumers to file a claim, but has now issued an order extending the filing deadline for military veterans only to November 30.

Trajector Holdings, LLC Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing

Trajector Holdings, LLC and its affiliated entities describe its services as assistance to veterans and individuals with disabilities in pursuing and submitting government VA disability benefits. On July 23, 2026, Trajector Holdings, LLC filed for bankruptcy (case #26-03286), in the federal U.S. Bankruptcy Court, Middle District of Florida, Jacksonville Division. Although a Chapter 11 bankruptcy is a “business restructuring,” the Attorney General’s Office does not know what the outcome of the bankruptcy will be.

Steps to Protect Yourself

Who should file: The new claim deadline applies to veterans only who paid for services and believes Trajector Holdings, LLC, owes them money.

What to do:

Complete a proof of claim form. You can submit an electronic proof of claim on the website of the claim administrator, Verita Global, at https://www.veritaglobal.net/trajector, then clicking the link “Submit Electronic Proof of Claim (ePOC)”. There is also information on the website about how to submit a paper claim form. Remember to include in your claim submission the amount you believe you are owed, along with supporting documents, such as receipts, contracts, payment records, and correspondence.

Preserve your records. Keep copies of all receipts, invoices, and documents related to the services you paid for.

Submit the claim by the November 30, 2026 deadline.

Why it matters: Veterans who have not already filed a claim and miss the deadline may lose the right to share in any distribution from the bankruptcy estate. The previous deadline that applied to all consumers ended on October 31, 2026. Filing a claim does not guarantee payment, and a monetary distribution, if any, depends on the outcome of the case.

In advance of the upcoming Veterans Day holiday on November 11, 2026, the Attorney General also reiterates its warning to veterans to beware of claim sharks. Consumers with questions about the claims process can contact the claims agent at (888) 249-2695.

The Attorney General’s Office cannot provide legal advice to individual consumers about their claims, however.

Attorney General Ellison’s intervention in Trajector Holdings bankruptcy

Attorney General Ellison has joined the attorneys general of Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania, and Virginia in filing a notice of appearance in the Trajector Holdings bankruptcy.

The notice of appearance means that Minnesota and the states are now participants in the bankruptcy proceedings and have standing to object, file a proof of claim, or bring an adversary proceeding in the bankruptcy.

text:
For the second year in a row, the United States has snubbed a UN flagship human rights review – the only country to do so since the Human Rights Council was created 20 years ago. But rights groups and elected officials flocked to Geneva in numbers to make sure the stunt didn’t go unnoticed. The campaigners accuse the Trump administration of evading international scrutiny.

“For the second year, the administration is saying to the world: ‘We don’t care about whether you would review us or not. We are going to continue to violate human rights unabashed’,” Jamil Dakwar, human rights programme director at the US-based American Civil Liberties Union, told journalists in Geneva on Monday ahead of the scheduled review.

The Palestinian human rights lawyer pointed to ICE raids that have landed more than 70,000 people in immigration detention facilities and an ongoing wave of state abortion bans as part of an "unprecedented attack" on human rights.

Asked why the US had decided to not participate in the UPR, a US state department spokesman said by email that it “implies endorsement of the Council’s mandate and activities”, which it exited last year. He further accused the “irredeemably body” of spreading “anti-American rhetoric”.

Precedent weakens rights system

Rights groups argue that the move further cements a precedent that risks weakening the UN human rights system. Under the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), every UN member state must subject itself to an evaluation of its human rights record by other member states. Despite often drawing tough exchanges of criticism, the exercise has so far enjoyed widespread support from member states because many consider that it at least puts all states on an equal footing.

The US absence could prompt others to follow suit, according to the advocates in Geneva. “If the United States is allowed to boycott and not show up for the human rights review, it sends the message to all other countries that are interested in escaping accountability for human rights,” said Dakwar. So far, only Nicaragua has done so, but states have been timid in their reaction to Washington’s actions. The Human Rights Council, which oversees the review, decided on Tuesday to postpone the US evaluation until January, as it did last year, while expressing concern over the US decision and urging it to reconsider.

Taking the floor, the Netherlands said on behalf of the European Union that it “regretted” the US decision, arguing that the UPR is “effective precisely because it is universal”. “Preserving that universality is essential to safeguarding the UPR’s credibility and impact,” the Dutch delegate said.

Cuba’s ambassador to the UN didn’t miss the opportunity to berate his country’s historic rival, accusing it of “hypocrisy”. “This country believes it is better than others, but at the same time claims to be a judge on other countries’ human rights records,” Rodolfo Benítez Verson said during the council meeting.

Reacting to criticism from others, the US state department spokesman said: “As one of the primary founders of the United Nations and the primary champion of individual liberties, the United States will not be lectured about our human rights record by the likes of HRC members China or Cuba.”

Calls for consequences

But rights groups say there should be real consequences if countries want to deter future deserters. In a letter addressed to the council in October, 16 civil society organisations, including ACLU, Human Rights Watch and the International Service of Human Rights, urged the Geneva-based body to mandate the UN high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, to present an update, at the council’s next session, on human rights violations committed by the US government. Acknowledging that countries have failed to show initiative in this regard, Dakwar said Türk should at least hold an informal intersessional briefing, as he has done in other contexts, including Ukraine, or in a similar vein to the previous commissioner’s report on China’s persecution of Uyghurs. The advocates were planning to meet Türk to reiterate their demands on Tuesday.

A ‘welcome’ blue wave

US rights groups hope that the Democratic Party’s sweeping takeover of the US Congress in last week’s mid-term elections may rein in the Trump administration, notably on its deportation plans. They could even force it to halt the war in Iran, which Dakwar described as illegal. The lawyer suggested the newly formed Congress could demand oversight investigations and use budget appropriations to pressure the White House. Tellingly, Trump admitted in an interview this week that the ICE raids had gone too far and that his war with Iran was nearly over. Still, the new Congress won’t begin its work until January.

Kendra Brooks, Philadelphia city council member, told journalists at the briefing that while welcoming the blue wave, international pressure remained key to “holding the government accountable”.

“People are living in fear, whether it’s folks in the ICE detention centres or women being detained by ICE while they are actively going through a miscarriage. We have to come together collectively to fight against this terror,” she said, while noting that she hoped their presence in Geneva would give their fellow citizens back home courage.

text:
What happened with Venezuelan TPS?

In January 2025, the Biden administration announced an extension of TPS for Venezuela. The incoming administration subsequently reversed that decision and moved to terminate TPS protections.

Federal litigation followed, and a district court ruled that the government’s actions were unlawful. However, the government appealed, and the Supreme Court temporarily blocked the district court’s decision from taking effect.

On November 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit granted an additional 14-day administrative stay beginning November 6.

This brings us to November 20, 2026, an important date in the ongoing proceedings.

Does this mean TPS will be restored on November 20?

Not necessarily. The current stay is temporary, and the court may issue additional orders before or after that date. The underlying legal questions have not yet been conclusively resolved.

During the interview, one of the most important questions was whether Venezuelans whose TPS expired should leave the United States or remain while awaiting further developments.

I understand how difficult this uncertainty can be, particularly for individuals and families who have established their lives in this country. However, there is no single answer that applies to everyone.

A person’s immigration history, the TPS designation under which they registered, existing applications, other immigration protections, and individual circumstances may affect their options.

For that reason, I encourage affected individuals to remain informed, preserve their immigration documents, and obtain individualized legal guidance before making significant decisions about travel or their immigration situation.

title: Why a 'doable' bipartisan deal on immigration could happen, but won't
authors: Steve Benen, Ja’han Jones, Jacqueline Alemany, Sydney Carruth

text:
There was an unexpected exchange during Donald Trump’s latest “60 Minutes” interview, in which the president reflected on the unpopularity of his administration’s mass deportation agenda. His comments sparked a conversation of sorts — including criticism from the White House’s allies on the right.

When CBS News’ Ross Douthat asked specifically whether he thought his deportation policy went too far, Trump responded, “I think it might be too tough. … That hurt me.”

As the discussion moved forward, the Republican went further, suggesting that the White House might “work something out” with the incoming Democratic majority, reaching a bipartisan compromise on immigration policy. “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

The reaction from several Republican officials, conservative think tanks and MAGA activists was swift and predictable: They don’t want a bipartisan deal; they want more deportations.

They shouldn’t be too concerned about a breakthrough agreement. In fact, I’m reminded of a story from nearly nine years ago.

In January 2018, as policymakers worked on an immigration deal ahead of a government shutdown deadline, Trump urged Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill to work on a solution, which he vowed to support, explicitly telling them that he didn’t care what was in it.

Soon after, the president spoke to Sen. Dick Durbin, and the Illinois Democrat explained that a bipartisan deal was in place. Trump asked if then-Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham was on board, and Durbin said he was. The president then invited Durbin and Graham to the White House.

Graham and Durbin thought the discussion would be with Trump. It was not: The bipartisan duo were surprised to arrive at the White House and find several anti-immigration hard-liners, whom they didn’t invite to the conversation. It was at that point that the president told Durbin and Graham that the White House wouldn’t support a bipartisan solution after all.

More articles

What happened? The Washington Post reported that Stephen Miller intervened, fearing that Graham and Durbin “would try to trick Trump into signing a bill.”

Nearly nine years later, Miller — the architect of the policy Trump now sees as “too tough” — was promoted to White House chief of staff.

I can understand why the anti-immigration forces on the right were taken aback by the president’s on-air comments, but the idea that Miller will steer Trump toward a deal on immigration policy with congressional Democrats is utterly preposterous.

At a Monday afternoon press conference, a reporter asked House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries whether he believes Miller could be a credible partner for Democrats. “No,” the New York Democrat replied. The likely next House speaker added, “Stephen Miller is a stone-cold racist. His track record speaks for itself, and I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

In the abstract, one can imagine a possible bipartisan deal on immigration policy. In fact, during George W. Bush’s and Barack Obama’s tenures, lawmakers very nearly succeeded on passing a package, only to be derailed by far-right opposition.

But those waiting for another possible agreement shouldn’t expect any meaningful action until 2029 at the earliest.

text:
130 national, state and local nonprofit organizations, law professors, and experts speak to the state of asylum rights in the United States and the U.S.-Canada Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA).

We, the undersigned organizations and individuals, serve and advocate on behalf of asylum seekers in the United States. Since President Trump’s return to office, the United States government has been openly and actively dismantling the asylum and refugee system. We have witnessed the increased incarceration of asylum seekers in dangerous conditions; their forcible deportation to countries where they have no ties and faced harm; the rushed or full disruption of asylum processing and arbitrary dismissal, denial, or termination of meritorious claims; and much more. These changes have not only violated domestic and international law. They have also rendered the United States dangerous for refugees and asylum seekers, particularly for Black, Brown, Indigenous, and LGBTQ+ individuals, children, women fleeing gender-based persecution, and families.

We work every day to avert irreparable harms to asylum seekers in the United States, and we will continue to work with immigrants pursuing claims here. We have witnessed countless survivors of persecution and torture abandon viable claims and leave the United States out of fear that they will face even worse harms at the hands of the U.S. government. Many who are detained fear they will not survive conditions of detention or have been threatened with deportation to dangerous countries that they have never been.

However, the Canadian government is currently turning back asylum seekers who cannot find safety in the United States under the Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA). This can result in an immigrant’s unlawful deportation, prolonged detention and deprivation of medical care and other rights and unlawful deportation to their home country.

The cost of the policy is painfully clear: Human Rights Watch interviewed a Haitian family that was turned away by Canadian authorities this summer and deported by the United States to Haiti on August 27, 2026. The Haitian couple had two sons, ages 5 and 3; the younger child was a US citizen. “My partner, our older son, and I had TPS and had also applied for asylum,” Marc D., the 45-year-old father, told HRW, and had a court hearing scheduled for 2029. When Haiti TPS ended, afraid of being detained by ICE, the family went to Canada to seek asylum but Canadian authorities turned them over to DHS. ICE detained the family in New York, separated the father from his partner and children, and did not allow him to contact a lawyer. He told HRW: “When I told an officer that my youngest son was a US citizen, he told me: ‘Your son can stay, but the state will take custody of him, and you will lose him.’”

The United States is not a safe place for asylum seekers. The United States cannot uphold—in good faith and in compliance with the Refugee Convention—its obligations under the Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA).

text:
“ICE arrests soar as people with no criminal record are increasingly targeted,” read one New York Times headline this year. Late last year, NPR reported that ICE had targeted migrants in the U.S. who “had no criminal record.” And Axios reported that millions of “undocumented” — the media’s favorite euphemism for “illegal” — immigrants “have no criminal backgrounds.”

Such messaging helped create a political atmosphere leading up to midterm elections in which some Democrats campaigned on a platform of eliminating ICE altogether, while others pledged to cut back on immigration enforcement. Whatever the exact position, Democrats won a spectacular victory, with at least 254 seats in the House and at least 54 in the Senate. (Both figures might rise even higher as the last few races are decided.)

The massive defeat certainly got President Donald Trump’s attention. Just days later, in his first postelection interview, with CBS News’s 60 Minutes, Trump was asked to name one issue on which he would like to work with the new Democratic majority. “I’d love to do something on immigration,” Trump said.

Reporter Ross Douthat asked whether Trump thought immigration enforcement had hurt him in the election. “I think it both helped and hurt,” Trump said. With that, he was making the distinction that most observers make — that Trump’s shutdown of illegal crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border has been a huge success, both in terms of policy and voter approval, while his internal enforcement efforts, including the mess in Minneapolis, alienated a lot of voters.

“I think you would agree that I get an A+ for [closing the border],” Trump said. “For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I got hurt because we also took people that had good jobs — that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

“Now, there is a large part of the country that thinks they should be put out,” Trump continued. “And there’s a large part of the country that thinks they should be allowed to stay, if they’re good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes. And there’s a large group of people who think that they should be allowed to stay.”

“So you think your deportation policy went too far?” asked Douthat. “I think it might be too tough, yeah,” Trump said. “And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”

Trump went on to theorize about the possibility of offering some sort of legal status to people who have been in the U.S. illegally for many years. “Get the killers out. Get the rapists out. Get all the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out. But let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them, OK?” Trump said.

Douthat asked whether Trump thought there were any Democrats who might be interested in an agreement along those lines. “I think so, yeah,” Trump said. “People have already called me.”

Trump’s seeming openness to some sort of amnesty deal — although no one said the “A” word — set off alarm bells among a lot of veterans of the immigration policy wars. “Does Trump think the Democrats will do anything except pocket his amnesty and start planning for the next one, when they regain the presidency and open the borders again, Biden-style?” asked the writer Mickey Kaus.

On Fox News, Jesse Watters played a quote from Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL) earlier this year saying, “This idea that unless you’re an axe murderer you should be allowed to stay — that is not consistent with our laws, and it’s also not good policy.”

And Mark Krikorian, of the Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates more restrictive immigration laws, argued that the Trump administration went wrong when it switched to high-profile raids designed to take illegal immigrants into custody. Instead, it should have pursued quieter enforcement in the workplace. “Where are the audits of employer personnel records, which require no guns?” Krikorian asked. “Where are the letters from the Social Security Administration notifying employers that the payroll information they submitted doesn’t match the agency’s records?”

But now the president, after a big defeat at the polls, is talking about some sort of “deal” on immigration. Seeking to quell the uproar, on Monday Trump went to the White House briefing room to insist: “We have a very strong deportation program. There’s no amnesty, no anything, we keep that. But we focus on the worst of the worst.”

text:
TACOMA, Wash. (AP) — Faced with an influx of petitions by people alleging they’re being unlawfully detained by federal immigration authorities, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Washington said Monday that it no longer has the staffing to defend every case and will let judges rule without government opposition.

Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd said in a letter to U.S. District Judge David Estudillo that habeas corpus cases initiate “protracted litigation” with numerous hearings, briefings and motions that consume prosecutors’ resources.

“Thus, going forward, in order to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which the USAO will no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense on behalf of the respondents,” Floyd wrote.

The backlog has “severely impacted the government’s ability to respond” to immigration petitions and prevented prosecutors from dealing with other unrelated civil litigation, he said. As a result, his office will decline to defend “many” habeas cases. He didn’t specify how many cases could be affected.

Judges have often ruled against the administration in cases filed by tens of thousands of detainees arguing that they were being held illegally by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It has been a source of great frustration to administration officials — and to judges and advocates who say ICE has trampled on individual rights amid the Trump administration’s hardline immigration agenda.

Last week, U.S. border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that courts have been weighed down by about 85,000 immigration habeas cases as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.

Floyd is a former judge who, along with three other Washington judges, advocated for prohibiting immigration courts from granting bond to detainees — a question that is now before the U.S. Supreme Court.

The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.

text:
On October 29, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit stayed a preliminary injunction that would have required the U.S. Department of State to open registration for the fiscal year (FY) 2027 Diversity Visa lottery (DV-2027). As of November 2, 2026, DV-2027 registration remains closed while the government’s appeal proceeds.

Quick Hits

DV-2026 visa processing and DV-2027 lottery registration have faced separate disruptions.

DV-2027 registration remains closed, with no confirmed opening date.

Diversity Visa Lottery Background

Each year, the Diversity Visa program offers up to 55,000 immigrant visas to eligible individuals from countries with historically low levels of immigration to the United States. The process begins when individuals enter the lottery, and the State Department randomly selects entrants. Those selected may then apply for an immigrant visa or, if eligible, seek adjustment of status to lawful permanent residence in the United States.

As discussed in our June 2025 article on the DV lottery, selection does not guarantee a visa. Principal applicants must still meet education or qualifying work experience requirements and complete the remaining immigration process.

The program’s name identifies a federal fiscal year, not the calendar year in which people enter the lottery. For example, the State Department selected DV-2026 entrants on May 3, 2025. For DV-2027, the State Department has identified October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027, as the visa application period, even though registration has not opened.

Key Events Leading to the DV-2027 Stay

September–November 2025. The State Department adopted a $1 lottery entry fee, then delayed DV-2027 registration without announcing an opening date.

December 2025–early 2026. The State Department paused DV visa issuance, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) held decisions on DV green card applications. These measures affected people already selected, not the separate delay in opening DV-2027 registration.

March–April 2026. The State Department adopted a DV-2027 rule requiring most entrants to submit passport details. The rule took effect April 10, but registration remained closed.

August 19, 2026. Red Eagle Law, L.C., sued in its own name to require the State Department to open DV-2027 registration.

August 28, 2026. In a separate case, Medani v. Trump, a court ordered DV visa processing to resume. The State Department said its December 2025 issuance pause was no longer in effect. DV-2027 registration remained closed.

September 30–October 1, 2026. The DV-2026 visa year ended, and the DV-2027 visa year began without an open registration period.

October 14, 2026. In Red Eagle Law, L.C. v. Rubio, the court ordered the State Department to launch DV-2027. Under the revised timetable, the State Department had to:

announce entry dates and requirements by October 29;

open registration for thirty days by November 1; and

notify selected entrants by December 3, 2026.

The October 14, 2026, order also required timely processing of DV-2027 visa applications. The government appealed.

Recent Updates

October 29, 2026: The Ninth Circuit temporarily stayed the district court’s order requiring the State Department to open DV-2027 registration. The appeals court granted the government’s request for an emergency stay. A stay temporarily suspends the lower court’s requirements while the appeal proceeds. As a result, the State Department was no longer required to meet the injunction’s October 29 announcement, November 1 registration, and December 3 selection-notification deadlines while the stay remains in effect.

November 1–2, 2026: DV-2027 registration remains closed. The previously ordered November 1 opening did not take place, and no confirmed replacement opening date is available. The stay does not finally resolve whether the State Department’s failure to launch the program is lawful.

text:
Updated November 10, 2026 at 10:53 AM PST

GENEVA, Switzerland — The United States has left an empty chair at a key United Nations human rights review for the second year running, becoming the only U.N. member state ever to do so.

The review, known as the universal periodic review, is meant to be just that: universal. Each state is reviewed every four to five years by fellow member states. The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.

As well as diplomats from countries under review, civil society groups are allowed to submit evidence too. Several made the trip to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."

In fact, leaving the council, which has 47 elected members, does not mean the U.S. can easily get out of the review process, which is obligatory for all 193 U.N. member states. Human rights groups see Washington's stance as part of a pattern of disengagement and even active opposition to multilateral organizations, pointing to U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the decision to leave the World Health Organization.

So what happens now? The U.N. has few sanctions against a country that does not cooperate with the review process. Israel skipped one review back in 2013 in protest at what it said was anti-Israel bias, but returned nine months later after the U.N. rescheduled. Until today's no-show by the U.S., no country has ever failed to turn up twice.

Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S. Member states had already drawn up a list of questions for Washington's diplomats, including questions about the use of the death penalty and restrictions on abortion.

But U.N. insiders fear that holding the review when there is no one to answer those questions could set a risky precedent. Even authoritarian regimes such as North Korea take part in the review process. If the U.N. allows a review to go ahead without U.S. participation, it could encourage other member states to stay away, too, leaving rights groups to present their evidence, as one put it, "in a vacuum."

For now, the U.N. has decided to postpone tricky deliberations about how to react until early next year. In the meantime, a process regarded as a last resort for the victims of human rights violations is not available to U.S. citizens. It is, one rights activist said in Geneva, "a crisis of accountability."

A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit from a Portland-based immigration law firm seeking to ensure federal agents allow detained immigrants access to legal counsel.

The decision comes nearly one year after the CLEAR Clinic first filed the lawsuit alongside Pineros y Campesinos del Noroeste, Oregon’s largest Latino labor union also known as PCUN, and Leon X, an anonymous 32-year-old Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program recipient from Mexico.

In her Thursday ruling, U.S. District Judge Ann Aiken approved the group’s request to dismiss the case without prejudice, meaning they could file a similar lawsuit.

The ruling follows Aiken’s September decision denying a preliminary injunction, or an order that would have prevented federal agents from denying legal counsel to detained immigrants while the case proceeded. Aiken found that the plaintiffs didn’t provide enough evidence to back their claims that agents were purposefully denying people in detention access to counsel before transferring them out of state.

It’s a blow for immigrant rights advocates, who filed the lawsuit in the wake of Operation Black Rose, an operation the federal government launched in October 2025 to arrest immigrants living across the Willamette Valley. The effort resulted in more than 1,200 immigration arrests in the last three months of 2025, reflecting the impact of President Donald Trump’s directive requiring U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to raise its daily arrest quotas from 1,000 to 3,000.

To achieve its goal, the Trump administration denied people in detention access to counsel or cut them short after only a few minutes of contacting legal help, the plaintiffs alleged, adding that ICE agents pressured people to waive their rights and sign voluntary departure orders.

Aiken in her September ruling also determined that PCUN and Leon X lacked standing in the lawsuit.

PCUN, which was suing on behalf of its members, didn’t name a single member in the suit who had been denied access to counsel after their immigration detention. Aiken called this “fatal” to having standing. Meanwhile, she said Leon X’s fear of being detained is reasonable, but it’s not different from how any other immigrant across the country may feel right now.

Although the lawsuit didn’t result in the relief immigration advocates sought, it resulted in extensive evidence proving federal immigration’s interference with Oregonians’ access to counsel, said Jordan Cunnings, the legal director at Innovation Law Lab, which represented the plaintiffs.

“Documenting ICE’s disregard for the fundamental right to an attorney is a win that we can build on,” she said in a blog post.

The federal government did not immediately respond to the Capital Chronicle’s request for comment.

text:
HOUSTON – In a major victory for Houston’s immigrant rights community, the State of Texas dismissed its lawsuit against FIEL Houston Inc. on November 9, 2026, bringing an end to a legal battle that had threatened to dissolve the nonprofit’s charter.

Previous story: Appeals court allows Paxton to move forward with case against FIEL Houston

What Was the Lawsuit About?

Attorney General Ken Paxton filed suit against FIEL Houston — accusing the nonprofit of violating federal 501(c)(3) rules. Specifically, the state alleged FIEL crossed legal lines by urging people not to vote for former President Donald Trump and by opposing border-security legislation.

Under Texas law, the state can seek to dissolve a nonprofit’s charter if it believes the organization violated federal or state requirements — even though revoking federal tax-exempt status is handled separately by the IRS.

The case gained momentum in October 2025, when a Texas appeals court reversed a lower-court ruling that had blocked Paxton from moving forward. That decision sent the case back to state district court, where FIEL — represented by the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund (MALDEF) — prepared to fight back.

The Dismissal: “We Are on the Right Side of History”

More than a year after the appeals court ruling, the state dropped the case entirely.

FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa responded with a statement:

“History will remember who was on the right side and on the wrong side of it. Today proves once again that we continue to be on the right side of History. This lawsuit has been very burdensome for us as an institution. Now that this is over, we can return to committing 100% of our time and energy to protecting, educating, and empowering our community. We want to thank MALDEF for their unwavering support and all of our supporters who have never left our side.”

Why This Case Mattered Beyond FIEL

Constitutional law professor Josh Blackman of South Texas College of Law Houston had previously noted the case could set a significant precedent for nonprofits and advocacy organizations across the state.

“There are two things nonprofits usually can’t do: endorse political candidates and lobby for or against legislation,” Blackman explained during the case. “Groups engaging in public advocacy have to be very clear about not crossing those lines.”

Faith communities were also watching closely. Reverend Heather Tolleson of First Christian Church in Katy said the uncertainty extended to churches engaged in advocacy work. “It feels like some groups are held to one standard and others to another,” she said.

With the dismissal, those concerns — at least in this case — are now resolved.

What’s Next for FIEL Houston

FIEL says it’s ready to refocus entirely on its mission. The organization advocates for just immigration laws, access to higher education regardless of immigration status, and the rights of people in vulnerable situations.

“There’s better things to do out there than to go into legal battles,” Espinosa had said during the height of the case — and now, the organization can do exactly that.

text:
FOREST HEIGHTS, Md. — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday that he and President Donald Trump haven’t yet discussed any concrete immigration policy changes in the aftermath of the midterm elections as the president shifts his tone on deportations and says he’s open to working with Democrats on the issue.

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a conference near Washington, D.C., Mullin also said he is strongly opposed to any amnesty for people living in the U.S. illegally — long a red line for Republicans that has contributed to the intractableness of the immigration issue.

The midterms highlighted voters’ disaffection toward the administration’s hard-line immigration enforcement activities and Trump has since said not only that he could work with Democrats on immigration but also, during an interview with “60 Minutes” Sunday, said that his deportation policy was too aggressive for voters.

Mullin on Monday reiterated Trump’s willingness to work with Democrats on the issue.

Mullin, who was a senator and house representative before becoming Trump’s Homeland Security secretary earlier this year, said after the election he’s been fielding calls from Democrats that he worked with in Congress on bipartisan issues.

“I’ve let the president know that those calls are coming in. And the president has said, you know, let’s start working with them and then let’s meet at some point. So that’s the extent of the conversation,” Mullin said in a briefing with reporters. “We haven’t had any conversation just on policy.”

Trump since the election has elevated Stephen Miller, the key architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff, raising questions about how cooperation with Democrats might look so long as enforcement remains strict. Mullin called him in a post on social media last week an “excellent choice.”

Mullin, who said he worked with Democrats while he was in Congress including on immigration reform, said he thought a bipartisan approach was the only way to get anything done. But the secretary also pushed back decisively against any type of agreement that would include amnesty for people living illegally in the U.S.

“I was working on immigration reform when I was in the House and when I was in the Senate. I think the only way you can actually get it is by a bipartisan approach. But amnesty’s never going to be a solution. We’re never gonna allow amnesty to happen. So that’s a full stop,” said Mullin.

The Homeland Security secretary raised the issue of DACA — a form of protection from deportation for children brought to the country illegally by their parents. He said figuring out a way to legalize their status would be up to Congress.

“Now, if we wanna have an immigration reform to where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that’ll be up to Congress to do that,” Mullin said.

Mullin spoke on the sidelines of a conference about drones and counter-drone technologies in the Washington, D.C., suburbs.

text:
The Mamdani administration is “evaluating next steps” after a federal judge ruled City Hall must comply with a federal subpoena seeking information about certain residents of a South Bronx shelter for migrant men, according to spokesperson for the mayor.

Ivonne Rodriguez, spokesperson for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, had no further comment after U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan in Manhattan ruled the city must provide to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement the names and birthdates of any shelter residents who had “serious criminal histories.” That includes residents charged with any of eight crimes: murder, manslaughter, rape, robbery, assault, grand larceny, burglary or assault of a law enforcement officer.

An ICE official previously stated in a sworn affidavit that the agency is aware of 20 immigrant residents of the shelter who have entered the country illegally and 12 who had been charged with a “serious” criminal offense.

City attorneys have fought the subpoena, arguing the request would require the city to conduct an unduly broad and burdensome investigation to produce the information.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to comment on the matter, citing ongoing litigation.

The legal action focuses on the last emergency shelter for migrants in the city. During the peak of the “migrant crisis,” as former Mayor Eric Adams termed it, the city maintained more than 260 shelters, including in sprawling tent cities and hotels across the five boroughs and in upstate communities, to house an influx of more than 240,000 migrants and asylum seekers.

Over 1,400 single adult migrant men resided at the Bronx shelter as of the end of June, according to City Hall data provided to City Council. The Bronx shelter's population has slowly shrunk over the course of this year, down from 1,670 residents in February, according to the data. The shelter was originally designed to hold up to 2,200 residents.

As of the end of June, shelters across the city were housing 27,120 migrants and asylum seekers, the vast majority of whom are families with children, according to the City Council data. That’s down from a peak of nearly 68,000 in January 2024, according to city comptroller data.

The ruling comes amid a drop-off of in visits by federal immigration officers to city shelters, seeking access to and information about immigrant residents. Federal immigration officers visited city shelters six times in the second half of last year and four times in the first half of this year, according to quarterly city reports.

That follows a surge in such visits in the first six months of President Donald Trump’s second term, a trend first reported by Gothamist. The Gothamist analysis of those visits found that federal immigration officers were able to enter private areas of city shelters or obtain resident information without presenting judicial warrants at least five times earlier this year, raising questions about whether both federal officers and local shelter employees were following the law.

The Bronx shelter opened in February 2025. Soon after taking office Jan. 1, 2026, Mamdani announced plans to close the shelter by the end of the year.

While thousands of other migrants and asylum-seekers continue to reside in the city’s shelter system, the Bronx shelter is unique in that it’s the only shelter specifically designated for migrants and operating outside of the normal Department of Homeless Services system. That allows the city to operate outside the framework of laws governing city shelters, including restrictions on size. City law currently prohibits most shelters larger than 200 people.

The shelter is currently run by the mayor’s office of Housing Recovery Operations. It is the last official Humanitarian Emergency Response and Relief Center, generally large-scale migrant shelters first announced by former Mayor Eric Adams’ administration in September 2022.

The Bronx shelter has been plagued by concerns of bed bugs and poor food, as reported by local news outlets the City Reporter and Documented. Before opening, the shelter also garnered the ire of local residents and officials, who saw the placement of the shelter in their borough as further representation that the Bronx was unfairly shouldering the city’s undesirables.

Aliya Rahman, the disabled Minneapolis resident dragged out of her car and detained by federal immigration agents last January, has tried over and over to get some accountability from the government that harmed her.

text:
Aliya Rahman, the disabled Minneapolis resident dragged out of her car and detained by federal immigration agents last January, has tried over and over to get some accountability from the government that harmed her. Today, she filed an assault and false imprisonment lawsuit against the federal government—one she hopes could be “copy and pasteable” onto other people’s cases.

“What happened to me is not just about ICE, and lawsuits are only one tool for fixing what is really going on,” Rahman said at a press conference Tuesday. “These things happened because it was already culturally normal for law enforcement officers to operate without accountability.” The day Rahman was arrested, the Department of Homeland Security’s X account posted a message “to all ICE officers,” telling them “you have federal immunity in the context of your duties.” In the following months, Rahman tested every possible strategy to prove that statement false.

In February, Rahman testified before Congress that ICE agents smashed her windows, pulled her out of her car, ignored her assertions that she is a US citizen, taunted her for her disability, and withheld medical care until she blacked out on the floor of a cell.

She filed a tort claim against ICE and DHS this April, seeking personal injury damages through one of the few avenues an individual can legally use to sue an otherwise-unaccountable federal agency. Then, in June, Rahman filed a complaint with DHS’ internal Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. But that office was gutted after Trump’s return to office, so Rahman didn’t expect much of a response. “It’s hard to imagine that sending a letter to DHS to ask them to respect our civil rights will do anything,” she told me at the time.

Rahman’s tort filing from April also went unanswered. As the six-month timeline for a government response ran out, she filed a new lawsuit today, alleging assault and false imprisonment—and joining a growing number of people who are demanding legal restitution for violence done by ICE and DHS. Carlos Jimenez, a US citizen from Southern California who was shot in the back and shoulder by an ICE agent, sued the government for $25 million yesterday; in August, 54 people represented by the ACLU filed tort claims over harm done by ICE agents nationwide.

“We followed their process; they didn’t respond,” Jessica Gingold of the MacArthur Justice Center, Rahman’s lawyer, said Tuesday, referring to Rahman’s previous attempts at accountability. “Nearly seven months later, we have heard nothing. The federal government has chosen to hide.” The names of the officers who hurt Rahman are currently unknown. Through the lawsuit process, Gingold said, they will be unmasked.

“We have their pictures; we have a right to know their names. We have a right to depose them. We have a right to get their records.” Images of the six masked officers who were there that day are attached to the lawsuit as an exhibit.

Almost a year since the beginning of Operation Metro Surge, Rahman is far from the only Twin Cities resident still dealing with the repercussions of ICE’s months-long occupation. As the global NGO Human Rights Watch wrote in June, the ICE operation—which left two civilian protesters dead and entire communities traumatized—was a “humanitarian crisis.” The city of Minneapolis estimates that the surge caused $700 million in damages; the Department of Homeland Security says 4,000 people were detained.

But months after the ouster of former Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino and ICE’s partial retreat from Minnesota, Rahman says the fight isn’t over. Less than two weeks ago, an investigation by KARE 11 revealed that the Trump administration used taxpayer funds to purchase a detention center in Western Minnesota from CoreCivic—for $420 million more than the building was worth.

“When I see ICE Out signs, I wonder what they mean now,” Rahman said Tuesday. Getting rid of ICE in Minnesota, she said, means addressing the cash bail industry, extractive prison labor, and qualified immunity for police. “I desperately hope that beyond pushing Greg Bovino out of town, we will fight the things that gave rise to Metro Surge. Those are the body parts ICE is made of.”
