text:
In Brief

Supreme Court lifts injunction on Big Bend border project.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissents from majority ruling.

Trump administration cites Illegal Immigration Reform Act.

Big Bend Sector includes 150 miles of 30-foot border wall.

The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for construction to resume on one of the longest and most controversial sections of President Donald Trump’s security project along the Mexican border.

The more than 500-mile stretch of road, cameras, vehicle barriers and sensors planned to cut through Texas‘s iconic Big Bend National Park has generated significant backlash. It includes segments where a 30-foot border wall will be built, although the administration has backed off plans for a wall inside the park.

The justices’ ruling allows work to continue while a legal challenge filed by an environmental group, preservationists, and a river guide and landowner plays out in court. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson noted her dissent.

“Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area,” the majority wrote. But the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 “reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert.”

A federal judge in Texas halted work on the project in October, siding with the challengers, who argued that the Trump administration violated the Constitution by waiving dozens of laws to speed construction. The high court lifted that block after the Trump administration appealed.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone had ruled that the administration would have to comply with the laws before construction could resume.

“As Plaintiffs have demonstrated, without an injunction, they and the public at large stand to permanently lose protected wilderness that benefits tourism, recreation, farming, ranching, spirituality, aesthetic sensibilities and education,” Cardone wrote in her opinion.

In its appeal of that ruling to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration said the project was urgently needed to stop the flow of migrants and illegal drugs across the border.

“Plaintiffs’ environmental, recreational, and aesthetic interests do not outweigh the harm to the public,” the government wrote in court filings.

More than 89,000 people were apprehended trying to enter the United States between 2021 and 2025 in the area known as the Big Bend Sector, according to government court filings. About 15 percent of drugs seized along the border in recent years were recovered in the sector.

Citing the flow of migrants and drugs, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi L. Noem found earlier this year that the administration did not have to comply with dozens of mostly environmental laws because there was “an acute and immediate need” for the barrier.

The plaintiffs questioned whether the accelerated timeline was necessary.

They pointed out that the Big Bend Sector had by far the least number of migrant apprehensions of any of the border’s six sectors, accounting for about 2 percent of the total number. The drug seizures amount to less than 1 percent of all non-marijuana drugs.

Anna Claire Beasley of No Big Bend Wall, one of the groups opposed to the project, said she was dismayed by the high court’s decision.

“The consequences of this decision are not theoretical. Every road cut into the desert, every stretch of land cleared, and every barrier built changes this landscape in ways that may never be undone,” Beasley said. “Big Bend is not an empty stretch of border waiting for development. It is a living landscape, home to communities, wildlife, cultural history, and a globally significant natural environment.”

Asked for comment on the decision, the White House referred to a message Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival posted on X celebrating the victory.

‘When we filed in the Supreme Court, I called the district court’s order halting wall construction ‘as unprecedented as it is flawed.’ We just won,” Percival wrote.

The Trump administration is building hundreds of miles of new border wall across California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas, after Congress included $46.5 billion in funding in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill. The Big Bend sections total $1.7 billion.

Conservationists fear that the administration’s move to bypass environmental laws during construction will damage otherwise remote wilderness and irreversibly alter iconic landscapes enjoyed by outdoor enthusiasts.

The wall expansion originally included plans to build a barrier through Big Bend National Park, the most-visited national park in Texas with more than half a million people entering in 2025.

The park, which consists of 800,000 acres in southwest Texas, is renowned for its views of the mountains and steep cliffs that descend to the Rio Grande, drawing hikers and kayakers.

But in the face of outcry from local landowners, tourism businesses and politicians, the administration reversed course, opting instead to build patrol roads through the park and install vehicle barriers and additional surveillance technology.

Conservation advocates argue that even building a road would require blasting through the mountains with dynamite, although Customs and Border Protection denies that.

In the wider Big Bend region, the administration still plans to build more than 150 miles of the 30-foot wall, according to the CBP website.

The construction has moved forward rapidly in many areas thanks to the 2005 Real ID Act, which granted the Department of Homeland Security the ability to waive some environmental laws for building a border wall. That has allowed it to forgo reviews of potential damage to the environment and archaeological sites, which can often delay projects months or years.

Inside the national park, contractors in August began bulldozing scrubland along the Rio Grande to clear a path for the new patrol road. That land would typically be protected by the Endangered Species Act as the Fish and Wildlife Service has designated it as critical habitat for the yellow-billed cuckoo.

Following local outcry, CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott paused that work to consult with local stakeholders.

Efforts to oppose the wall elsewhere have been less successful. In Arizona, activists blocked wall construction for more than two months by occupying a giant tree along the border, before a dramatic raid by more than 50 CPB agents ousted them and downed the tree. Construction preparations are also moving ahead on Arizona’s nearby Tohono O’odham Nation, after a judge denied the Native American reservation’s request for a preliminary injunction.

text:
A disabled Minneapolis resident whom Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers violently arrested in January is suing the federal government over her arrest and subsequent detention.

Aliya Rahman, whose treatment fueled outrage over the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota, filed a lawsuit Tuesday accusing the officers of unlawfully arresting her, using excessive force to do it and failing to provide adequate medical care during her detention, despite her repeated pleas.

Rahman’s attorneys submitted an administrative complaint against the Department of Homeland Security in April under the Federal Tort Claims Act, the first step toward suing the government. Civilians cannot sue a federal employee for civil rights violations the way they can a police officer, but the FTCA allows people to sue the United States for a federal employee’s actions.

Rahman’s legal team also separately filed a complaint to the department’s Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties in June.

Jessica Gingold, Rahman’s attorney and senior counsel at the MacArthur Justice Center, told MS NOW that those complaints had gone unanswered. She said that to her knowledge, DHS had taken no action against the officers — whose identities are still unknown.

“Perhaps they can ignore our administrative complaint, but once we go to court, they have to answer,” Gingold said. “And we have all the tools at our disposal to get discovery, to depose the agents that were involved in this incident and to demand that there is some accountability for what happened.”

Rahman was arrested Jan. 13 during the Trump administration’s “Operation Metro Surge” in the Minneapolis area while she was driving to a doctor appointment. Video captured by a bystander shows ICE officers surrounding her car before dragging her out, restraining her with her arms behind her back and then carrying her by the arms in that position.

According to the complaint, Rahman encountered the officers while driving, and they banged on her car windows and yelled at her as she tried to move out of the intersection as ordered. Rahman grew frustrated and told the officers that “they needed to learn how to respect human beings,” the complaint states, at which point an officer broke her car window.

“Though an officer had just smashed her window without any legal basis, covering her with broken glass, other officers immediately yelled at Ms. Rahman to ‘go,’ ‘get out,’ and ‘get out of here,’ gesturing eastward on East 34th Street,” the complaint states. “Terrified and in shock, Ms. Rahman attempted to comply and drove forward, eastbound on East 34th Street. But at this point, officers stopped her, reaching through her windows at Ms. Rahman and pulling open her car doors.”

Rahman was then detained at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building in Fort Snelling, where she was denied medical care even though her condition was deteriorating, according to the complaint.

More articles

DHS disputed Rahman’s account at the time, calling her an agitator who “ignored multiple commands by an officer to move her vehicle away from the scene.”

The department did not immediately respond to MS NOW’s request Tuesday for comment about the lawsuit.

Rahman, who has said she has autism and a traumatic brain injury, said she continues to experience severe stress and anxiety as a result of the encounter.

“She had been going to the traumatic brain injury center on the day that this happened, and this kind of rerouted her whole healing journey,” Gingold said. “And she had to spend the last several months mostly focused on physical therapy for her shoulders after being carried like an animal through the street for 215 feet.”

Rahman’s arrest took place just days after an ICE officer shot and killed a Minneapolis resident, Renee Good, and it further stoked outrage among local residents over the administration’s immigration crackdown.

Less than two weeks after Rahman’s ordeal, ICE officers shot and killed another Minneapolis local, intensive care unit nurse Alex Pretti.

text:
New York Times highlights Dr. Ann Lawani’s life in the Valley threatened by aggressive ICE policies(link is external)

Image

Harder wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin demanding Dr. Lawani be returned to California for legal proceedings after being abruptly transferred across the country

WASHINGTON – Today, Rep. Josh Harder (CA-09) sounded the alarm on outrageous new deportation tactics by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that caused a local constituent to be detained, arrested, and abruptly transported across the country. Dr. Ann Lawani – a nurse, caregiver, and 13-year resident of Lodi in the U.S. legally under judicial protection – was sent thousands of miles away to Louisiana in violation of a federal court order. In response, Harder wrote to U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin to demand Dr. Lawani’s immediate return to California for any further legal proceedings.

Dr. Lawani lives in Lodi, where she is a caregiver for her 83-year-old father. She also oversees the education of 230 nursing students at the University of San Francisco, and she practices as a nurse at John Muir Health. Her abrupt absence has already caused significant disruptions on campus and pulled yet another healthcare worker away from a community facing severe shortages. Dr. Lawani’s story(link is external) was featured this morning in the New York Times.

“Given her longstanding compliance, lack of criminal history, and substantial community ties, there is no apparent public safety justification for keeping Dr. Lawani detained thousands of miles from home while her case proceeds,” wrote Rep. Harder. “Our immigration enforcement system should focus on protecting communities from danger, not removing the individuals who dedicate their lives to serving them. Dr. Lawani's continued detention undermines that mission while imposing unnecessary harm on her family and the countless people who depend on her.”

In his letter, Harder demanded that ICE release Dr. Lawani under an order of supervision and facilitate her immediate return to California, and that DHS provide her and her attorney with the proposed country of removal, supporting travel documentation, and an explanation of the basis for her continued detention.

“My sister is an amazing caregiver, healthcare leader, and educator in our community, and I was devastated not just at her unacceptable arrest, but the decision to send her across the country and detain her unnecessarily. Not only is Dr. Ann a scholar in her profession, but an extremely skilled nurse with unmatched dedication to her patients and students alike. She gives everything she has, daily, to save lives and train the nurses of the future to be as trained, ready and dedicated as she is. As a recognized expert in palliative care as well, I can assure anyone, countless lives have been lost due to her absence, since her wrongful detainment. For someone that vital to the community to be tracked, abruptly vacuumed into an abyss and moved across the country, is simply EVIL and consequential. My family and I want to see my sister returned home safely and as soon as possible, and like so many families in our community, we want an end to the chaos caused by these agencies. I want to thank Congressman Harder for his work to bring Ann home as well as the USF family for their relentless support,” said Samuel Lawani, brother of Dr. Lawani.

“I speak with confidence to what I know firsthand: Dr. Ann Lawani is a person of exceptional professional accomplishment and moral character, deeply embedded in our university community, with responsibilities that hundreds of nursing students and, in turn, the patients they will someday care for, depend upon her fulfilling. Her continued absence causes real and mounting harm to the students and faculty who rely on her mentorship, to our accreditation-mandated curriculum work, and to the safety-net partnerships she has built,” said Eileen K. Fry-Bowers, Dean of the School of Nursing and Health Professions.

Read Harder’s full letter to DHS Secretary Mullin here.

Harder has been pushing for reforms at ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for months, including successfully calling for former Secretary Kristi Noem’s firing. Following her departure, Harder demanded the new Secretary Markwayne Mullin prioritize clear standards for enforcement, bans on face coverings, mandatory identification, new use-of-force policies, and bans on racial profiling. Harder has also continued to oppose any new federal funding for ICE until these reforms are enacted, and he has repeatedly conducted oversight investigations at the Stockton ICE facility.

title: Top US Court Wary of DOL In-House Immigration Penalty Power - Bloomberg Law
description:
The US Supreme Court’s conservative majority appeared skeptical that the Labor Department’s in-house judges could order a New Jersey farm to pay penalties for violating a seasonal worker visa program.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump appointee, took the most aggressive stance during argument, calling into question the power of the government to seek any such penalties outside of court.
The case could have serious ramifications for agency power by further limiting what they can enforce in administrative proceedings.
Justice Elena Kagan, an Obama appointee, asked the government’s lawyer what’s at stake in the case for immigration enforcement.

text:
The US Supreme Court’s conservative majority appeared skeptical that the Labor Department’s in-house judges could order a New Jersey farm to pay penalties for violating a seasonal worker visa program.

During oral argument Tuesday, several Republican-appointed justices seemed to doubt that the H-2A program’s requirements on employers fell within the “public rights” exception to adjudication in federal court.

Justices critical of agency tribunals drew a distinction between denying entry or ordering deportation — a clear instance of public rights in the immigration space — and enforcing a visa program’s mandates through monetary penalties. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump appointee, took the most aggressive stance during argument, calling into question the power of the government to seek any such penalties outside of court.

The case could have serious ramifications for agency power by further limiting what they can enforce in administrative proceedings. Enforcement actions before agency tribunals generally move faster and more efficiently compared to federal court.

Justice Elena Kagan, an Obama appointee, asked the government’s lawyer what’s at stake in the case for immigration enforcement.

“If the proposition were that the only types of things that could be in executive adjudication are things that happened at the border, I think it would be catastrophic,” Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris told the justices. “Just the volume of immigration-related cases for the aliens themselves, things that make you inadmissible after you enter the country — huge.”

The high court holding that civil penalties across the board can only be imposed in court would be the “nuclear option,” Harris said.

The Supreme Court is reviewing a decision by the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit overturning an administrative order against Sun Valley Orchards LLC to pay more than $500,000 in penalties and back wages for violations of the visa program.

Regulating Farmworker Visa Rules

The court’s three liberal justices seemed to embrace the government’s argument that the H-2A program imposes obligations on employers to protect domestic workers being undercut by foreign labor, and adjudicating alleged violations of those promises is a classic public right.

Harris buttressed that argument by repeatedly citing the Supreme Court’s 1909 decision in Oceanic Steam Navigation Co. v. Stranahan, which permitted $100 administrative fines on shipping companies for every immigrant they brought to the US who suffered from a contagious disease.

But Oceanic Steam seems “significantly different,” said Chief Justice John Roberts, a George W. Bush appointee. There’s no justification to extend the broad authority the executive branch gets for the admission of immigrants to H-2A workers who’ve been in the country for months, he said.

Justice Clarence Thomas, a George H.W. Bush appointee, said “kicking someone out” of the program for violating its requirements would be a “clear way” of regulating it.

The Supreme Court made a “fairly definitive statement” in its 1987 decision in Tull v. US that civil penalties can only be enforced in courts of law, Kavanaugh said.

There’s already judicial review of enforcement actions, so the main differences for courts if agencies can’t penalize in administrative proceedings would be the standard of review they use and their volume of cases, he said.

text:
“Our next 9/11 is coming,” one witness warned the Committee …

Officials allege that cartels could use them as staging area…



In a major judicial development, the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) issued a decision Monday allowing President Donald Trump’s administration to continue border construction in Texas’ Big Bend region.

The decision follows a lower court’s order to halt construction last month .

A lawsuit filed by Friends of the Ruidosa Church in April — the current crux of the Big Bend border dispute — alleges that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's waiving of federal rules in order to precipitously build border infrastructure in the region violated a swath of federal rules. The federal rules waived deal mostly with environmental and conservation-related protections.

Last month, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted a preliminary injunction in the matter, stating that the plaintiffs were “likely to succeed on the merits” of at least one of their allegations in the lawsuit.

On Monday, SCOTUS reached a different conclusion, staying the preliminary injunction as requested by the federal government and allowing continued construction in the Big Bend region.

U.S. Senator-elect and state Rep. James Talarico (D-Austin) commented on SCOTUS’ decision, “They’re allowing out-of-state contractors to get rich by destroying the crown jewel of Texas. We can work with President Trump to fix this broken immigration system without desecrating our sacred land.”

Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that she would deny the stay.

In the administration's decision to build border infrastructure in the area, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) relied on Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA). These sections of the IIRIRA allow for particular legal requirements to be waived in pursuit of border security.

Plaintiffs invoked the “major-questions doctrine,” arguing that the lack of congressional approval invalidates DHS’ use of these waivers, according to the SCOTUS decision. The lower court found that the plaintiffs would “suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest weigh in their favor,” U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone previously said.

The judge’s order suspended the DHS’ waivers and halted construction. The lower court also found that the major questions doctrine claim would likely succeed because of the absence of congressional approval.

SCOTUS, however, found the lower court “lacking jurisdiction," and agreed with the federal government’s request to stay the preliminary injunction.

SCOTUS argued that the plaintiffs' claim was not constitutional but statutory, saying, “Although styled as constitutional, that claim simply alleged that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority in issuing the waivers.”

“There is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim,” the court stated.

The court also concluded that the injunction “impedes” the federal government from advancing its interests in “border security and integrity.”

The court’s decision also cites a Customs and Border Protection employee's claim that the government is “incurring nearly half a million dollars” in irrecoverable costs per day if the injunction “prevails at the end of this litigation.”

The court concluded, “The Government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents.”

Hillary Pierce, director of communications for No Big Bend Wall and a board member of Conserve Big Bend, two organizations both advocating against Big Bend sector border construction, stated about the legal developments in an emailed press release, “This isn't the end of our fight. The justices didn't decide whether Big Bend actually qualifies as an area of high illegal entry.”

Conserve Big Bend filed a lawsuit in September claiming the U.S., in calling the region a "high entry” zone, did not accurately designate the area.

“The government's own numbers show Big Bend has the fewest Border Patrol apprehensions along the southern border. That's exactly what we're challenging in our lawsuit in Washington,” Pierce added in the emailed press release.

U.S. Senator John Cornyn released an op-ed on Monday in the San Antonio Express-News, stating, “Big Bend deserves border security that reflects the realities of its geography, the input and experience of local law enforcement, and the rights of the people who live there.”

He argued that the area was not a region of “high illegal entry,” but that the sector “recorded the lowest number of apprehensions among the nine Border Patrol sectors along the southern border.”

Cornyn contended for better use of technology, rather than physical border construction, in the area.

While yesterday marked a major development in the judicial branch on the issue, the Texas Legislature also began moving to weigh in.

State Rep. Eddie Morales (D- Eagle Pass) filed a bill on Monday, the first day of pre-filing, related to “a prohibition on the installation or construction of border security infrastructure on state park property.” He was joined by state Rep. John Bucy III (D-Austin), who, in addition to filing various Medicaid bills on Monday, filed a bill related to “a prohibition on agreements to use state park property for border security infrastructure or related improvements.”

Texas Democrats are hitting the ground running after their historic flip of the Texas House and every statewide office on Election Day. Texas’ 90th Legislative Session will begin on January 12, 2027.

text:
A federal judge on Monday pressed the acting head of Denver's U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement field office over an order to quickly re-arrest immigrants a court had ordered released from detention. She is now deciding whether contempt proceedings are appropriate.

U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney called the re-arrests concerning, both for due process and for the fear they instill among immigrant detainees.

Court testimony revealed at least 18 detainees were released and then quickly re-arrested over about a week at the GEO facility in Aurora. The arrests prompted a series of protests outside the detention center and led to Monday morning's hearing.

Nathan Rasper, acting director of ICE's Denver field office, testified that beginning October 27, he told his team that detainees subject to release following habeas corpus proceedings could be re-arrested "based on our statutory authority." Rasper, who became acting director on October 14, said he was under the understanding that some detainees had been arrested without the proper paperwork, so serving them with those warrants after their release would solve the issue.

Rasper said he believed such arrests would not violate court orders but told the judge the practice has stopped, saying he ordered an end to the practice on November 4.

The American Civil Liberties Union said ICE's actions have a specific aim "where cruelty seems to be the point."

"What we're seeing is instructions from Washington that amount to abuses, and it's happening day in and day out," said Tim Macdonald, Legal Director for ACLU of Colorado. "With the elevation of [Stephen] Miller, we should all be concerned that this administration didn't get the message from the midterms and they're going to continue their abusive practices."

Last week, an unnamed Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told CBS Colorado that ICE complies with lawful court orders and that prohibiting the re-arrests is "nothing short of sabotage."

At Monday's hearing, the assistant U.S. attorney quickly distanced himself and his office from that statement, saying they did not know it was being submitted to the press.

Sweeney is now weighing whether contempt proceedings are appropriate.

text:
When is there judicial review of an executive determination for which a statute provides that “[t]here is no judicial review”? More often than you’d think — but less frequently after Mullin v. Doe, in which the Supreme Court construed a statutory reviewability bar to preclude most challenges to Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designations and terminations. The Court rightly rejected a distinction between procedural and substantive challenges that, when prevailing in the lower courts, had allowed judicial scrutiny of the reasons behind executive decisionmaking. But to give full effect to the provision, it should have extended that logic to preclude constitutional equal protection claims as well.

TPS originated as a discretionary exercise of executive grace. Since 1960, under a program known as Extended Voluntary Departure (EVD), the executive branch had granted temporary relief from removal for nationals of countries suffering from severe political or humanitarian disaster — an exercise of enforcement discretion that the D.C. Circuit considered unreviewable.

In 1990, Congress created TPS as a statutory replacement for EVD, establishing a process by which the Secretary of Homeland Security “may designate” a foreign state suffering from armed conflict, natural disaster, or other “extraordinary and temporary conditions,” permitting eligible nationals relief from removal and work authorization. The statute requires periodic review of TPS designations, in four steps: The Secretary must “consult[] with appropriate agencies,” “review the conditions in the foreign state,” “determine whether the conditions for [TPS] continue to be met,” and publish “notice of each such determination” in the Federal Register. It further provides: “There is no judicial review of any determination of the [Secretary] with respect to the designation, or termination or extension of a designation, of a foreign state . . . .”

TPS designations have often been criticized for outlasting the “temporary” conditions that prompted them. So on January 20, 2025, President Trump directed that designations be “appropriately limited in scope.” Within days, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem vacated her predecessor’s extension of Venezuela’s designation and, over the following year, terminated every designation that came up for review — thirteen in all. Each termination was swiftly followed by litigation, in a reprise of the first Trump Administration, during which attempts to revoke six TPS designations produced extensive litigation but ultimately no effective terminations before President Biden took office.

These challenges only got off the ground because, prior to Mullin, district courts had reached a consensus that § 1254a(b)(5)(A) barred substantive, but not procedural, challenges to TPS revocations. Most relied on McNary v. Haitian Refugee Center, Inc., which had held that a provision barring review of “a determination respecting an application” for agricultural-worker status covered challenges to rulings on particular applications but not to the “practice[s] or procedure[s] employed in making” those decisions. Correspondingly here, courts could not entertain a “challenge [to] the content of the decision” to revoke TPS, but could instead scrutinize “how the Secretary went about making her determination.” And if the “distinction between decision and process [was] the ballgame,” the district courts afforded challengers a very generous strike zone: Even “garden-variety arbitrary-and-capricious claim[s],” one court explained, “fall on the procedural side” of the line. Against this backdrop of widespread review, two cases reached the merits docket of the Supreme Court.

Doe v. Noem concerned Syria, designated in 2012 for “extraordinary and temporary conditions” arising from its civil war. In September 2025, after the fall of the Assad regime, Secretary Noem announced the termination of the designation, citing Syria’s trajectory toward “stable institutional governance.” Seven Syrian TPS recipients sued in the Southern District of New York, arguing that the Secretary had not fulfilled § 1254a(b)(3)(A)’s procedural requirements and had acted arbitrarily and capriciously in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Judge Failla granted interim relief, postponing the termination. She construed the review bar to permit challenges to “agency patterns and practices” affecting TPS determinations, and found plaintiffs’ APA claims likely to succeed because the Secretary had failed to conduct the statutorily required review of country conditions and interagency consultation. The Second Circuit denied a stay, finding no irreparable harm from the temporary presence of Syrian TPS holders during the pendency of the litigation.

Miot v. Trump concerned Haiti, designated in 2010 after a catastrophic earthquake. Haiti’s designation had proved a flashpoint in the 2024 presidential election, in which then-candidate Trump and vice-presidential candidate JD Vance repeated various pejorative statements about Haitian TPS recipients, including, notably, accusations of “eating the dogs . . . [and] the cats” of Springfield, Ohio. Perhaps unsurprisingly, Secretary Noem sought to terminate Haiti’s designation in 2025; five Haitian TPS holders sued in the District of Columbia, raising APA claims alongside a Fifth Amendment equal protection claim that anti-Black and anti-Haitian animus motivated the termination.

Judge Reyes granted the plaintiffs’ motion to postpone the termination. She adopted the consensus interpretation of the reviewability bar, and found several APA claims likely to succeed: that the Secretary had failed to consult adequately, that her review of country conditions was either contrary to the evidence or absent entirely, and that her decision was preordained. Judge Reyes also found the equal protection claim likely to succeed in light of the President’s and the Secretary’s disparaging statements. The D.C. Circuit denied a stay, without opining on the merits, because the government’s claimed injury — “improper intrusion” — was too generalized to constitute irreparable harm. Judge Walker dissented, reasoning that the determination was likely unreviewable, and that the Supreme Court’s grants of stays in earlier TPS cases should “inform ‘how [lower courts] should exercise [their] equitable discretion in like cases.’”

The government applied to the Supreme Court for stays of both orders. The Court treated the applications as petitions for certiorari before judgment, granted them, and consolidated the cases, deferring consideration of the requested stays.

In both cases, the Supreme Court reversed. Writing for a six-Justice majority, Justice Alito concluded that the statutory reviewability bar precluded respondents’ nonconstitutional claims. He laid out a straightforward textual case. Section 1254a(b)(5)(A) bars “judicial review of any determination of the [Secretary] with respect to the designation, or termination or extension of a designation.” If “determination” is read to encompass “the chain of events leading up to a decision,” judicial review of the procedures used to arrive at the decision constitutes judicial review of the determination itself. Or, if “determination” refers to a discrete act, then each of the Secretary’s decisions made pursuant to statutory requirements — including what conditions to consider and with whom to consult — is a “determination” made “with respect to” the ultimate termination.

By contrast, reading “determination” to refer to only the ultimate decision on whether the conditions for TPS are satisfied artificially narrows the term from its ordinary meaning and other uses in the same statute. It also runs afoul of traditional administrative law principles : Just as an agency’s preliminary or subsidiary actions “merge” into its final action for purposes of review, so too should the Secretary’s preliminary decisions merge into her final termination decision for the purposes of a reviewability bar. Finally, Justice Alito distinguished McNary; there, the statutory provision referred to “a determination respecting an application” — an individual disposition separable from the processes governing all applications — whereas § 1254a’s reference to “any determination” sweeps more broadly.

With respect to the constitutional claims, the majority fractured. Joined by three other Justices, Justice Alito declined to pass on the reviewability of constitutional challenges to TPS determinations. Ordinarily, a court must resolve such jurisdictional questions prior to reaching the merits. But Justice Alito asserted that a ruling on interim relief assesses only likelihood of success on the merits — an analysis which can incorporate doubts as to either jurisdiction or merits. Consequently, although the full Court reached the (likelihood of success on the) merits of the equal protection challenge, Mullin does not conclusively establish that such claims evade the reviewability bar.

On the merits of those equal protection claims, Justice Alito, again writing for the Court, held they were unlikely to succeed. He assumed without deciding that Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp. supplied the relevant standard. And at its first stage, he reasoned that plaintiffs had not shown that race was a “motivating factor” in the decision, because the statements from President Trump and Secretary Noem — although “derogatory” and “heated” — were not “overtly racial,” instead reflecting an assessment, albeit harsh, of conditions in Haiti. Moreover, he reasoned, the Administration’s uniform revocation of every TPS designation reviewed — a centerpiece of plaintiffs’ preordainment claims — cut against a finding of racial animus against particular countries.

Justice Thomas concurred, pressing two additional points. First, he asserted, the reviewability provision also bars constitutional challenges to TPS determinations. Its text does not distinguish between statutory and constitutional claims. And constitutional avoidance does not justify reading it differently, because the Constitution does not require a federal judicial forum for all constitutional claims. Second, Justice Thomas reiterated his view that the Fifth Amendment contains no “equal protection component” applicable to the federal government. Its Due Process Clause protects private rights and liberties against deprivation — but admission and permanent residence are public privileges. And while the Citizenship Clause may provide citizens some further guarantee of equal treatment, TPS recipients, as noncitizens, cannot invoke its protection.

Justice Kagan dissented. She interpreted the statutory reviewability bar narrowly, reading “determination” to cover the Secretary’s decision as to “whether the conditions for such designation . . . continue to be met,” but not subsidiary or preliminary decisions leading up to it. She relied upon cases defining determination as the “settling and ending of a controversy” and “a single act,” as well as the presumption of reviewability, which, she argued, favors narrowly construing even an express nonreviewability provision. Consequently, plaintiffs could challenge the Secretary’s compliance with statutory prerequisites to the determination. On the merits, Justice Kagan concluded that Secretary Noem engaged in no interagency consultations regarding country conditions, as statutorily required, even if she did elicit the State Department’s views on “foreign policy concerns.” With respect to the equal protection claim, Justice Kagan concluded that plaintiffs had carried their burden under Arlington Heights, given the “racial undertones and overtones” of the President’s comments.

The district courts’ prevailing approach to the reviewability bar played only a bit part in the Court’s debate in Mullin: Justice Alito dispatched McNary textually, while Justice Kagan distinguished between preliminary decisions and the ultimate determination instead. But Mullin could have rejected the district courts’ approach more squarely. Their substance-procedure distinction permitted challengers to recast their substantive objections to the reasons for action as challenges to the procedure by which that action was taken, defeating the reviewability bar’s function of forestalling scrutiny of the adequacy of the Executive’s reasons. Moreover, given that function, the provision should arguably extend to equal protection claims of the type raised in Miot — challenges that, despite their constitutional stature, entail the same comparison of reasons for action, and raise the same concerns of judicial second-guessing.

At the heart of administrative law is the demand that agencies act for adequate reasons. This guarantee is secured by a mixture of substantive and procedural requirements, often enmeshed in the same provision of law. The APA’s notice-and-comment procedures, for example, require not merely pro forma responses to comments but meaningful engagement with the arguments raised therein. And arbitrary and capricious review is conventionally described as incorporating both procedural and substantive aspects, requiring that an agency’s action be not only reasonable in the ends and means selected but “reasonably considered” and “reasonably explained” as well. Such entwinement is neither surprising nor objectionable: Because ideally, good reasons provide both a temporally antecedent catalyst and a substantive justification for action, a decision made arbitrarily, or for insufficient reasons, will naturally be deficient both procedurally and substantively. As a result, many challenges to the adequacy of an agency’s reasons can easily be cast as procedural or substantive.

Correspondingly, district courts entertained many ostensibly procedural objections to TPS terminations that entailed scrutiny of the Administration’s reasons. One recurring argument was that the Secretary had violated the change-in-position doctrine: that an agency deviating from a settled course must “display awareness” of its departure and give sufficient reasons for alternative factual findings. District courts found this requirement violated when the government invoked new considerations, such as “the national interest,” in revoking TPS without “effectively articulat[ing] why” it was served, or even when it revoked TPS on the basis of country conditions a previous administration thought to support a designation or extension — an approach that embeds a sufficiency-of-reasons analysis in a procedural requirement. Elsewhere, district courts attempted to police Secretary Noem’s reliance on “verifiably inapposite or false assertion[s],” or what the court viewed as her incorrect weighing of Haitian TPS recipients’ economic contributions against the competition they pose to U.S. workers, as an “entire[] fail[ure] to consider an important aspect of the problem” — implying that sufficiently substantively inadequate reasons themselves amount to a procedural failure. Although the district courts maintained that the Secretary could reach the same conclusion later after a better-considered judgment, their assessments required a competing substantive judgment about which factors, in what balance, a well-reasoned termination would weigh.

Most significantly, arguments that the Administration’s decision to revoke TPS was preordained or that its stated reasons were pretextual require especially searching scrutiny of the reasons given. Under Department of Commerce v. New York, although an agency need not state all its reasons for action on the administrative record, the reasons there stated must be “genuine” rather than “contrived” or “pretextual.” But absent extra-record discovery from an agency head, which is usually unavailable, the basis for concluding that a given reason is pretextual or contrived is its relative strength: A flimsier explanation on the record supplies evidence that the agency’s real motivation lies elsewhere. Frequently, district courts reached this conclusion by second-guessing the very judgments that they could not directly review. Miot reasoned that the Secretary’s “gross generalizations” and disregard of “key aspects of the analysis” suggested that she had preordained the result. Other district courts held up their own assessments as evidence of pretext — that the weight of the record evidence contradicted the Secretary’s judgment, or even that other TPS determinations were also wrongly decided.

These claims illustrate why, as the D.C. Circuit has elsewhere recognized, a statutory reviewability bar should be construed to extend to procedural claims that require scrutiny of an agency’s reasons for action. Although legislative history sheds little light on § 1254a(b)(5)(A)’s intended function, most of the justifications offered for reviewability bars are reasons to avoid judicial scrutiny of an agency’s reasons simpliciter. If the bar is justified by comparative institutional competence, as Judge Silberman supposed, judicial superintendence of these determinations would require an “extraordinarily precise statutory standard” because courts have difficulty assessing foreign country conditions and weighing foreign policy concerns. Congress’s decision to further specify the criteria for designation in absolute terms does nothing to alter this comparative disadvantage. Alternatively, a reviewability bar intended to insulate decisionmaking processes from external scrutiny cannot permit review of some reasons but not others, since any alleged impermissible reason would be weighed against the plausibility of alternative, valid reasons. Finally, § 1254a(b)(5)(A) may aim at efficiency, considering that the statutory timeline for periodic review envisions a far speedier process than the courts have managed to date. But it would fail to limit the challenges available if perceived inadequacies in the substantive reasons could be repurposed as evidence of procedural defects. Justice Alito’s dismissal of McNary and the substance-procedure distinction therefore rests on solid practical as well as textual grounds.

If the statutory reviewability bar extends to every claim that puts the Secretary’s reasons on trial, why should a claim under the Fifth Amendment fare any differently? The logic of Mullin’s reviewability holding supplies a reason to extend the provision to the equal protection claims the Court instead resolved on the merits.

Equal protection challenges to TPS revocations require the same scrutiny of agency reasons as the statutory claims the Court held barred. As the Court explained in Mullin, the first step of the equal protection analysis requires a showing that “a ‘discriminatory purpose [was] a motivating factor in the decision.’” But because direct admissions of racist motives are rare, demonstrating a discriminatory motive is often an exercise in excluding other possible motivations. The Court in Mullin acknowledged the comparative nature of this analysis, observing that “a strong, race-neutral explanation” for official action supplies evidence against race as a motivating factor. Lower courts followed the same approach. Miot credited the discriminatory-purpose claim after concluding that the Administration’s asserted reasons for action did not hold water. Other district courts held that evidence of political influence, preordained decisionmaking, or an “unreasoned” change in position — all statutory challenges in their own right — also supply evidence of an impermissible discriminatory motivation. One district court put the point squarely: “The lack of bona fides of [the] purported justifications” itself “gives rise to an inference” of discriminatory motive.

Consequently, reading § 1254a(b)(5)(A) to preclude equal protection claims is consistent with the provision’s function. This interpretation construes the statute to remedy the core mischief it aimed to address: a court reweighing an administration’s reasons for making, extending, or terminating a designation.

Mullin did acknowledge that, to preclude review of constitutional claims, Congress’s intent “must be clear.” That heightened requirement is justified “in part” on the basis of constitutional avoidance, but also partly on an ordinary inference of congressional intent in light of the stature of such claims. Such a default rule can be defeated by statutory context, including that an alternative reading would render the provision ineffectual.

Avoidance, meanwhile, operates only where ordinary interpretation leaves the text ambiguous. But § 1254a already speaks expressly to judicial review without “turn[ing] on the source of law for the underlying claim.” Some special imputation of congressional intent would be necessary to read in a constitutional-statutory distinction; the structural parallel between equal protection claims and core precluded statutory claims counsels against such an inference.

Nor would every constitutional claim be precluded under this approach. Some constitutional provisions constrain government action regardless of motivation, and can therefore be resolved without examining the adequacy of its reasons. The Constitution’s equal protection guarantees, under current doctrine, are sui generis, affording a distinct process entitlement against state action otherwise squarely within the scope of its authority. Such a provision can be exceptionally powerful but may merit exceptional treatment with respect to a reviewability bar as well.

Other arguments for preserving review of equal protection claims are certainly possible. Perhaps the Court was right to hypothesize that the Constitution requires a judicial forum for constitutional claims, or at least for process entitlements that cannot be vindicated through alternative channels. Or there may be independent political-process justifications for the Court to police the authenticity of stated reasons for executive actions. These external arguments are beyond the scope of this comment. But ordinary statutory interpretation, accounting for congressional intent reflected in the statute’s text and function, may justify precluding review of certain claims that Mullin was unwilling to declare unavailable.

Limiting Mullin to statutory claims leaves the door open for substantive claims, once recast as procedural, to be reforged into constitutional claims taking the same form — leveraging judicial dissatisfaction with the justifications for TPS revocations to interfere with executive determinations explicitly shielded from judicial review. Such reformulations are already underway. Only the modest extension of Mullin’s logic and holding to equal protection claims will give full force and effect to § 1254a(b)(5)(A)’s as-yet-unfulfilled promise: that with respect to TPS determinations, “[t]here is no judicial review.”

title: Supreme Court clears the way for border wall construction in Texas's Big Bend to resume
description:
Landowners and business owners in the Big Bend region, environmentalists and others who’ve opposed the construction project were bitterly disappointed with the court’s decision.
She ordered an immediate stop to all construction-related activity in the area, which includes Big Bend National Park as well as land up and down river in state and private hands.
The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in Big Bend.
David Keller lives in the Big Bend region, is a member of the board of Conserve Big Bend and is a plaintiff in a separate lawsuit of landowners opposing the border wall projects.
The government in August paused construction activity in Big Bend National Park that sparked outrage when bulldozers were spotted breaking ground in the park.
text:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, a blow to bipartisan opponents who had argued the project is a waste of money that threatens the unique landscape.

The border wall is a signature project of President Donald Trump, who has long vowed to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.

Landowners and business owners in the Big Bend region, environmentalists and others who’ve opposed the construction project were bitterly disappointed with the court’s decision.

“This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the groups that sued to stop the construction. “They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”

Republicans in Congress last summer funded the project with $46 billion, and Customs and Border Protection has been rapidly erecting 12 miles of barriers a week across the entire border with a goal of eventually covering the entire 2,000-mile border with a mixture of 30-foot-tall steel walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology designed to stop illegal immigration and smuggling.

The government has pushed forward by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass regulations. Those rules are aimed at protecting the environment, but have historically slowed down major construction projects.

Big Bend residents of both parties oppose the project

In Texas’s Big Bend region, bipartisan opposition has rallied to fight back against the project, which would include 30-foot-tall steel walls in some areas as well as vehicle barriers and new roads.

They’ve argued that the barriers are a waste of money that threaten the local economy and lifestyle in an area of historically low illegal immigration. They say the job could be better done using only surveillance technology like drones.

A judge in Texas sided with opponents, finding that Congress likely had not clearly authorized such broad waivers for an area with the southern border’s lowest rate of migrant apprehensions. She ordered an immediate stop to all construction-related activity in the area, which includes Big Bend National Park as well as land up and down river in state and private hands.

The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in Big Bend. More traffic could also be funneled there if there’s a gap in the wall, federal attorneys argued.

Customs and Border Protection head Rodney Scott said in an interview with The Associated Press that if the Big Bend area were left without a wall or other border infrastructure while other areas along the border get those fortifications, he’s convinced it would be swiftly overrun by cartels.

The Supreme Court agreed that the law sharply limits judges’ powers to intervene when the federal government decides speedy border barrier construction is necessary. The majority paused the lower court decision as the case plays out. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.

CBP did not immediately respond to questions about how swiftly construction could restart. The agency started building an initial section of border wall in one area of the roughly 500-mile stretch that makes up the Big Bend region, but that was stopped with the judge’s order.

Construction activity in national park sparked outrage

The agency has encountered intense opposition from landowners up and down the region when it comes to getting permissions to enter their land to survey and build.

The Center for Biological Diversity sued over the construction, along with Friends of the Ruidosa Church and a river guide in the Big Bend area. Jordahl said it was the first time the government had waived a broad set of environmental laws inside a national park.

David Keller lives in the Big Bend region, is a member of the board of Conserve Big Bend and is a plaintiff in a separate lawsuit of landowners opposing the border wall projects.

He called the court’s decision devastating: “Everything is on the line again.”

Keller called the border infrastructure projects the “industrialization of one of the last best open undeveloped wild places in the lower 48 states.”

“We can’t afford to lose any more. Not an ounce. Not an acre,” he said. “We need wild country to be who we are, to be fully human, to be American I would say.”

The projects have drawn criticism from both Democrats and Republicans, including outgoing Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, who wrote an op-ed arguing against the project published Monday in the San Antonio Express-News hours before the court’s decision.

“A combination of modern technology, adequate staffing, and meaningful cooperation with local officials and landowners offers a more sensible and effective path forward than indiscriminate construction of unnecessary barriers,” Cornyn wrote.

The government in August paused construction activity in Big Bend National Park that sparked outrage when bulldozers were spotted breaking ground in the park.

The government has repeatedly said no steel walls are planned for the national park. Initial plans included a new road as well as some vehicle barriers in the park. CBP has said in court filings that it will come forward with a finalized plan for what it intends to build in the national park but so far hasn’t done so while the case was at the Supreme Court.

title: Attorney General Bonta Briefs Court on Inhumane Conditions of Confinement at California ...
description:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Friday filed an amicus brief in support of the plaintiffs in Ruiz v. ICE, who are challenging the unconstitutional conditions of confinement at California City Detention Facility.
Last year, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) opened California City Detention Facility, the largest detention facility in the state, without ensuring it was adequately prepared to receive civil immigration detainees.
“California City Detention Facility opened before it was ready — and detainees have suffered the consequences,” said Attorney General Bonta.
In May, Attorney General Bonta released the California Department of Justice’s fifth report on cruel, inhumane, and unacceptable conditions at immigration detention facilities operating in California.
Attorney General Bonta recently sponsored two bills, signed into law, meant to protect and codify the rights of immigrants living in California.
text:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Friday filed an amicus brief in support of the plaintiffs in Ruiz v. ICE, who are challenging the unconstitutional conditions of confinement at California City Detention Facility. Last year, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) opened California City Detention Facility, the largest detention facility in the state, without ensuring it was adequately prepared to receive civil immigration detainees. While inspecting the facility pursuant to its authority under Assembly Bill (AB) 103, the California Department of Justice (DOJ) discovered serious problems with conditions at the facility and a lack of adequate medical care. In the brief, Attorney General Bonta shares with the court DOJ’s findings of inadequate healthcare infrastructure and systems, limitations on attorney access, insufficient clothing for excessively cold temperatures, and unsanitary living spaces, among other concerns.

“California City Detention Facility opened before it was ready — and detainees have suffered the consequences,” said Attorney General Bonta. “My team inspected this facility last year and discovered shockingly inadequate conditions, from understaffing to a lack of medical care to inhumane living conditions. We are committed to shining a light on conditions at detention facilities across California — and to supporting efforts to hold these facilities accountable to ICE’s own detention standards. I urge the Ninth Circuit to uphold the lower court’s injunction. These are human beings, and it’s the bare minimum that ICE takes steps to ensure they are treated as such.”

In November 2025, seven California City detainees filed a class action lawsuit against ICE, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and officials of those agencies in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California. The detainees allege violations of their constitutional rights, allegations supported by DOJ’s inspections of the facility around the same time. During its inspection, DOJ staff found numerous violations of ICE’s own detention standards — including the premature opening of the facility without adequate staffing, crisis-level understaffing for healthcare, denial of access to outside medical specialists, exposure of detainees to extremely cold temperatures, rainwater and plumbing leaks into detainees’ living quarters, inadequate food, excessively long lockdowns, and a failure to provide detainees with recreational time, among other problems, raising serious concerns about the facility’s ability to safely detain a growing population.

In the brief, Attorney General Bonta argues that these violations, documented and reported by DOJ, support the district court’s order that ICE and DHS provide facility access to a third-party monitor, ensure detainees’ access to counsel, and improve clothing and recreational access for detainees. The Attorney General urges the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit to uphold the preliminary injunction as urgent and necessary corrective action to protect the health and safety of detainees while litigation continues.

Attorney General Bonta is committed to standing up for California’s immigrant communities and shining a light on the unacceptable conditions at immigration detention facilities across the state. In May, Attorney General Bonta released the California Department of Justice’s fifth report on cruel, inhumane, and unacceptable conditions at immigration detention facilities operating in California. He also filed an amicus brief opposing the conditions of confinement at Adelanto ICE Processing Center in March.

Attorney General Bonta recently sponsored two bills, signed into law, meant to protect and codify the rights of immigrants living in California. The bills, SB 942 (Caballero) and SB 1399 (Durazo) respectively serve to hold detention facilities accountable when they violate detainees’ rights and permanently establish mandatory reviews for detention facilities.

Earlier this year, Attorney General Bonta and the County of Santa Clara secured a preliminary injunction blocking the illegal construction of an ICE facility in an unincorporated area of Santa Clara County near Gilroy, California. Attorney General Bonta also sent a letter raising serious concerns with an ICE directive to stop investigating and reporting on the deaths of individuals who die within 30 days after being released from ICE custody.

title: Houston Mayor Whitmire opposes effort to enshrine HPD-ICE executive order as an ordinance
authors: Dominic Walsh, Dominic Anthony Walsh, www.houstonpublicmedia.org, dominic-walsh
description:
Council member Alejandra Salinas is among the group pushing to make the executive order permanent.
"Executive order cannot override city ordinance," Salinas said.
Abbott and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton have not commented on Whitmire's executive order.
On Wednesday, City Attorney Arturo Michel indicated his department raised legal concerns about Whitmire's executive order.
"The executive order accomplishes our goal," his spokesperson said.
text:
Days after Mayor John Whitmire ordered Houston police officers to reduce contact with federal immigration agents, his office said he opposes an effort by city council members to codify the executive order as an ordinance.

On Friday, Whitmire signed an executive order instructing the Houston Police Department (HPD) to only contact U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) about immigration warrants when they arrest someone on a jailable offense. The measure prohibits contact under all other circumstances, including traffic stops.

Council member Alejandra Salinas is among the group pushing to make the executive order permanent.

"Executive order cannot override city ordinance," Salinas said. "We need to change the law to make it, in fact, the law of Houston that we will follow these new directives, and ensure that something so important is not just left at the whim of this mayor or any mayor, but is in fact the law of Houston."

Salinas spearheaded an ordinance in April, which Whitmire initially supported, that prohibited officers from detaining people due to civil immigration warrants. Whitmire and other city council members reversed the measure after Gov. Greg Abbott threatened to revoke public safety funding.

On Friday, Whitmire said the blue wave sweeping Republicans out of statewide office in January prompted him to change HPD’s policy.

In a written statement, a spokesperson for Whitmire said he "stands by his executive order as the City's approach to addressing these challenges."

"He believes that amending the ordinance to include additional provisions would put the City of Houston at even greater risk of violating state law," Whitmire's spokesperson said.

Abbott and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton have not commented on Whitmire's executive order.

In April, Paxton launched legal action against the city's attempt to curtail HPD-ICE coordination before city officials walked it back. He argued it ran afoul of Senate Bill 4, which prohibited cities and counties from limiting local law enforcement agencies' involvement in immigration enforcement.

On Wednesday, City Attorney Arturo Michel indicated his department raised legal concerns about Whitmire's executive order.

"We did review the executive order, and we understand there are risks, and I mean, the mayor has been on record that he’s willing to take a stand on that even if there are adverse consequences," Michel told Houston Public Media. "As any lawyer will tell you, you never have a client who always agrees with what may be the legal standard and so on. He’s got the right to do that."

By contrast, Michel said, the council members' effort must first pass legal review before it can be taken up for a vote by the city council.

"I think the issue here is if you’re putting in something that on its face violates Senate Bill 4, it’s hard to say that it’s lawful," Michel said. "I mean, people may see that as a bit of a dichotomy between the executive order and the ordinance, but I think it’s a function of the different processes that they are."

Whitmire's spokesperson said the executive order and ordinance are "totally separate issues."

"The executive order accomplishes our goal," his spokesperson said. "One violates state law; one doesn't."

Whitmire's office said the incoming Democratic leadership in Austin should revisit Senate Bill 4, and the U.S. Congress should "pursue meaningful immigration reform."

title: Count of Kentucky police, sheriffs in ICE program surges - Louisville Public Media
description:
Kentucky law enforcement officers also are arresting more immigrants for ICE, a recent data analysis by KyCIR found.
Federal data for 2026 show more local law enforcement agencies, especially in the South, joining the 287(g) program and making more ICE arrests.
Police and sheriffs for the state’s biggest cities – Louisville, Lexington and Bowling Green – are not in the 287(g) program.
KyCIR also contacted several other Kentucky sheriffs and police chiefs whose agencies joined the 287(g) program this year, but did not hear back.
Staverman, with the Northern Kentucky Against ICE collective, said the 287(g) program is just one way local agencies may collaborate with ICE.
text:
Nearly 60 law enforcement agencies across Kentucky have signed up for a controversial program that gives some powers of federal immigration enforcement to state and local officers.

The count marks an uptick from the 17 agencies taking part in the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s 287(g) program at the end of last year.

The Kentucky Center for Investigative Reporting reviewed federal data, published by ICE, that shows 34 sheriff’s offices, 22 police departments and three county jails across the commonwealth are participating in the program as of Nov. 4. Unlike neighboring Indiana, Missouri and West Virginia, Kentucky’s state police department hasn’t signed up.

Kentucky law enforcement officers also are arresting more immigrants for ICE, a recent data analysis by KyCIR found. In June, 287(g) arrests accounted for 18% of ICE arrests in Kentucky, hitting a record high for the state under President Donald Trump’s administration.

What’s happening in Kentucky mirrors national trends. Federal data for 2026 show more local law enforcement agencies, especially in the South, joining the 287(g) program and making more ICE arrests.

“I think many people, regardless of where they may stand on immigration, should be highly concerned that so many police forces across the nation are federalizing in this way. And it's severely affecting our immigrant neighbors, first and foremost,” said Michael Staverman, a member of the community collective Northern Kentucky Against ICE. “People that have to go work outside of a metro area or simply travel on a highway have to worry about what counties are safe and what counties are not.”

There are three 287(g) models that police agencies can participate in, with each option giving them certain immigration enforcement powers. Almost all the Kentucky agencies signed up for the controversial task force model, which lets state and local officers detain immigrants for ICE out in the community.

Former President Barack Obama canceled the task force model in 2012 amid mounting evidence that it fueled racial profiling by police. Trump resurrected the model last year as part of his aggressive effort to deport millions of immigrants.

An October report by FWD.us, a Washington D.C.-based immigrant advocacy group, found that 80% of law enforcement agencies in the task force model operate in communities with under 50,000 residents.

Likewise, in Kentucky, many of the participating agencies are based in rural areas and small towns. Police and sheriffs for the state’s biggest cities – Louisville, Lexington and Bowling Green – are not in the 287(g) program.

ICE’s website says the federal agency “recognizes the importance of its relationships with law enforcement partners — including state and local agencies — to carry out its critical mission.”

It says the 287(g) program enhances such collaboration “to protect the homeland through the arrest and removal of aliens who undermine the safety of our nation’s communities and the integrity of U.S. immigration laws.”

Kelly Young is a member of the Oldham County-based community group Kentucky Citizens for Democracy, which she said is opposed to 287(g) agreements. Their county sheriff’s department joined the 287(g) task force model in May, and their county jail joined last year.

A big worry, she said, is that local law enforcement’s decision to help ICE arrest immigrants, by joining the 287(g) program, will make people afraid to report a crime or ask officers for help.

“I think it just changes the relationship between the people who live here and local law enforcement,” she continued. “Does an ordinary encounter with a deputy now – does that feel threatening?”

Young, who writes about local immigration enforcement in an online newsletter, said Oldham County Sheriff Tim Wakefield has been “pretty open” about his office’s 287(g) involvement, readily answering her requests for information and documents on it. KyCIR requested an interview with Wakefield but did not receive a response.

KyCIR also contacted several other Kentucky sheriffs and police chiefs whose agencies joined the 287(g) program this year, but did not hear back.

The growth in ICE’s 287(g) program, both nationally and in Kentucky, follows the federal government’s rollout of financial incentives that encourage state and local agencies to join.

The incentives can help agencies get equipment and vehicles, cover some of their participating officers’ salaries and give performance-based bonus payments based on how much assistance they provide to ICE.

In Kentucky, 287(g) sign-ups by local law enforcement have steadily grown this year, data show. At least two agencies joined the program every month from January through October 2026, whereas there were five months in 2025 when none did.

Staverman, with the Northern Kentucky Against ICE collective, said the 287(g) program is just one way local agencies may collaborate with ICE.

In northern Kentucky’s Campbell, Kenton and Boone counties, for example, no agency has signed up for the controversial task force model, but all three county jails earn fees from the federal government to hold people already detained by ICE. (The Kenton County jail also participates in the 287(g) program’s jail enforcement model, which lets officers interrogate people in the local jail about their immigration status and serve warrants for immigration violations on people in the jail.)

Staverman said he’d like all collaboration between ICE and local agencies to end.

“287(g) agreements are important to focus on,” he said. ”But it's certainly not the whole picture.”

description:

Juan Vargas, a California Democratic congressman, told NBC on Monday that the third-grader’s whereabouts are unknown – and that he was working to try to reunite him with loved ones.

The US president acknowledged in an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes that aggressive immigration enforcement actions had “both helped and hurt” – and hinted at a softer approach for his remaining two years in office.
text:
Relatives of an eight-year-old Haitian boy who was taken into custody by federal immigration authorities in California are unable to locate the child, according to a Democratic lawmaker who described the case as “despicable”.

Video obtained by NBC News shows the boy being led away by three armed officials after he was summoned to what his family said was a routine immigration appointment in San Diego on 4 November.

Juan Vargas, a California Democratic congressman, told NBC on Monday that the third-grader’s whereabouts are unknown – and that he was working to try to reunite him with loved ones.

“Targeting a child, taking them away from their community and classmates, and forcing them into detention is despicable. It is inhumane,” Vargas told the network’s San Diego news affiliate KNSD.

The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, said the boy, who attends the city’s Fay elementary school, was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.

Guerline Jozef, the group’s executive director, told NBC she learned he was taken into custody after the uncle took him to the appointment, then later transferred to the office of refugee resettlement (ORR), a government agency under the direction of the health and human services department.

A spokesperson for the homeland security department said Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.

The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.

“Allegations that ICE took a third grader into custody to be placed in detention are false, and any suggestion otherwise is a depraved attempt to smear our ICE law enforcement officers and undermine the work of President Trump and [DHS] Secretary [Markwayne] Mullin to protect children,” the statement said.

It added that the boy lacked legal immigration status and was brought to the US by his father, who was then deported to Mexico by Customs and Border Protection (CBP), another federal immigration enforcement agency.

Jozef told NBC that the father’s abrupt deportation meant there was no opportunity to transfer formal legal guardianship to relatives of the boy in the US.

“His father has already been taken from him and deported, now this administration has stripped him of the stability, family, and community every child deserves,” she said. “I’m sure he is fearful, he is traumatized.”

Community leaders, including the board and superintendent of the San Diego unified school district (SDUSD), wrote to ICE expressing concern about the Trump administration’s decision to revoke temporary protected status (TPS) safeguards for Haitians in the US and its impact on families.

“ICE understands that this is absolutely not where this child should be,” Cody Petterson, a trustee of SDUSD, told NBC.

“For us, it’s a very clear case in which there’s no question that the best place for this child is with their caregiver, their uncle, and one of the worst places they could possibly be is in a cage somewhere with nobody they know, not understanding the process, and not understanding what’s about to happen to them.”

Jozef said the Haitian community was living “under a cloud of terror”, and that the loss of TPS protections was “incredibly painful” for families who had built lives in the US.

“The moment they kidnap or take a person within the community, we don’t know if we will ever hear from them again,” she said.

In an interview on Sunday, Donald Trump conceded that the mass deportation policy he pursued during his second presidency has been “too tough” for many people – and had contributed to the Republican party’s stinging losses in the 3 November midterm elections.

The US president acknowledged in an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes that aggressive immigration enforcement actions had “both helped and hurt” – and hinted at a softer approach for his remaining two years in office.
