title: Afghan Migrant Death Toll At Iran-Türkiye Border May Rise To Nine
description:
Munir Khan Safi told Afghanistan International that his brother, Hamed Safi, died on Thursday night in the border area between Iran and Türkiye.
Junaid, 20, accused Turkish border police and human smugglers of mistreating and abusing migrants in an interview with Afghanistan International.
In recent days, several Afghan asylum seekers have sent videos to Afghanistan International complaining of violence in Turkish border areas.
In her letter, she referred to similar incidents involving migrant deaths in Turkish border areas.
The country also hosts many Afghan migrants, some of whom live and work there without valid residence documents.
text:
Munir Khan Safi told Afghanistan International that his brother, Hamed Safi, died on Thursday night in the border area between Iran and Türkiye. According to him, Hamed's death was separate from those of the eight migrants whose bodies had previously been discovered and are currently being held in Van, Türkiye.

Afghanistan International has examined documents showing that Hamed, the son of Abdul Qayum, was approximately 22 years old and originally from Imam Sahib district in Kunduz province.

Hamed's family said his body is currently being held in a government mortuary in the Chaldoran border area on the Iranian side. Afghanistan International has also seen a photograph of Hamed's body.

The outlet has also examined other photographs which, according to the young man's family, show him in the Chaldoran area before he set off towards the Turkish border.

Junaid, 20, accused Turkish border police and human smugglers of mistreating and abusing migrants in an interview with Afghanistan International.

He said he and Hamed crossed the Turkish border wall in the Chaldoran area on Thursday night but were caught by border forces after entering Turkish territory.

According to Junaid, border guards mistreated and beat them. He alleged that officers forced the migrants to stand barefoot in the snow in freezing conditions and poured cold water over their naked bodies.

Turkish border police were also accused of stripping the migrants of all their clothing before forcing them back over the border wall towards Iran.

Junaid said he and Hamed lost consciousness after walking for hours in the cold. When he regained consciousness, he realised he had been moved to a room and that Hamed had died.

Afghanistan International has been unable to independently verify the exact cause of Hamed's death.

According to meteorological data, temperatures in the Chaldoran area dropped to around zero degrees Celsius on Thursday night and Friday last week. Daytime temperatures ranged between approximately 5°C and 10°C.

Hamed's family believes that exploitation and extortion by smugglers, what they describe as torture and violence by Turkish border forces, the forced return of migrants and extreme cold contributed to his death.

The cause of Hamed's death has not yet been independently confirmed.

The accounts provided by Junaid and Hamed's family represent one of the cases Afghanistan International has investigated concerning conditions faced by migrants along the Iran-Türkiye border. Other migrants may have had different experiences, and the causes of their deaths may also differ.

In recent days, several Afghan asylum seekers have sent videos to Afghanistan International complaining of violence in Turkish border areas.

They have reported extortion and mistreatment by human smugglers and border forces, as well as extreme cold along migration routes.

Bodies of Eight Afghan Migrants Discovered

In one incident, a video showing the bodies of eight young Afghan men in the border area between Türkiye and Iran was circulated, prompting widespread reactions.

Sharif Nazari, the brother of one of the victims, told Afghanistan International on Tuesday, 10 November, that he had identified his brother, Reza Nazari, among the eight men.

According to him, Reza is the last person visible in the video showing the bodies and was probably the youngest victim of the incident.

Afghanistan International has examined documents showing that Reza Nazari, the son of Ali Chaman Nazari and a native of Bamyan province, was born on 24 September 2009.

Under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, anyone under the age of 18 is considered a child.

Sharif Nazari called on Turkish, Iranian and Taliban authorities to cooperate in transferring Reza's body to Kabul so his family could bury him.

According to Sharif Nazari, the victims' bodies are being held in the Turkish city of Van, and their families have not yet been given access to them.

On Sunday, 8 November, informed sources sent Afghanistan International a video showing the bodies of eight Afghan migrants.

The footage shows the bodies of eight young men whose chins appear to have been tied with strips of material.

The person recording the video can be heard speaking with an Afghan Persian accent, identifying the deceased as travellers.

The Afghan Refugees Association in Türkiye also confirmed the deaths of the eight migrants in an interview with Afghanistan International.

The association said Afghans living in Van had not yet been permitted to visit the hospital to identify or view the bodies.

Turkish media reported that the bodies of eight young men were discovered near the Yukarı Tulgalı area of Özalp district in Van province, approximately three kilometres from the Iranian border.

The reports did not identify the victims and attributed their deaths to extreme cold.

However, the cause of death of the eight migrants has not been independently verified.

Calls for Investigation Into Migrant Deaths

Özkan Öztaş, a Turkish journalist, told Afghanistan International on Monday that the local administration in Van had ordered information relating to the case to remain confidential.

The incident has prompted reactions from several Turkish opposition politicians.

Gülcan Kaçmaz Sayyiğit, a member of the Turkish parliament representing the Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), wrote to the country's Interior Minister on Monday, calling for a judicial investigation, the identification of the victims and the arrest of any potential suspects.

In her letter, she referred to similar incidents involving migrant deaths in Turkish border areas.

According to Sayyiğit, the bodies of 19 Afghan migrants were discovered in May 2002 after snow melted in the Chaldoran area of Van province.

She also referred to the deaths of several migrants in the Başkale area and along migration routes in 2019.

Highlighting the impact of regional conflicts and economic crises on migration, the lawmaker called for stronger measures to protect migrants' rights in border regions.

She also requested information from Turkiye's Interior Ministry about the number of migrants held in removal centres in Van province, deportation figures over the past five years and the number of people who had entered the province from Iran since 2020.

Sayyiğit further questioned the ministry about government action against human-smuggling networks, the number of people arrested in connection with such networks over the past five years and measures to prevent violations of migrants' rights in removal centres.

Seracettin Bedirhanoğlu, head of the Republican People's Party (CHP) branch in Van, also attributed the incident to failures in migration management, shortcomings in border monitoring and disregard for human life.

He called for a comprehensive investigation into the incident and the identification of anyone potentially responsible.

Türkiye is one of the main migration routes used by Afghans travelling towards Greece and other European countries.

The country also hosts many Afghan migrants, some of whom live and work there without valid residence documents.

text:
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Washington said it does not have the resources to defend every case against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and will let judges rule on "many" petitions without government opposition.

In a letter to U.S. District Judge David Estudillo last month, Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd said his office is dealing with a huge volume of immigration-related habeas corpus cases. These allow people to legally challenge their detention by the government, with dozens being filed each week.

As a result, he said his office will not defend "many" such cases going forward. His letter did not provide any details about how many cases could be affected.

Read More on News

It comes as judges have repeatedly ruled against President Donald Trump’s administration in cases filed by detainees who say their detention by ICE is illegal.

Case numbers have surged to record highs amid the administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown, with more than 93,000 immigration-related habeas cases filed across the country since Trump returned to office in January 2025, according to a ProPublica tracker.

The rulings have frustrated administration officials, while judges who have ordered the release of detainees have called out ICE for disregarding due process rights and, in some cases, violating court orders.

Newsweek has contacted Floyd’s office and the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, for comment via email.

What Did Floyd’s Letter Say?

In his letter, Floyd said the surge in cases being filed has "severely impacted the government’s ability to respond" and also impacted the ability to deal with other unrelated civil litigation in the district.

Responding to each case initiates "protracted litigation" that consumes prosecutors’ time, including preparing and filing status reports, briefings and responses to motions and orders, he wrote.

"The USAO unfortunately does not have the available resources, at this juncture, to continue entering AUSA appearances" in every case, he wrote.

"Thus, going forward, in order to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which the USAO will no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense on behalf of the respondents."

Trump Says Mass Deportation Policy ‘Too Tough'

In an interview that aired Sunday, Trump conceded that his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that it hurt Republicans in last week’s midterm elections.

Trump told CBS’ 60 Minutes that his immigration crackdown "both helped and hurt" Republicans in Tuesday's midterms, which saw Democrats recapture control of both the House and Senate.

"I think I got an A+ for closing up the border," he said.

"I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.

"There is a large part of the country that think they should be put out and there's a large part of the country that they should be allowed to stay—if they are good people, working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

Asked if he thought his deportation policy went too far, Trump said: "I think it was too tough. I think it might be too tough, yeah."

Trump’s remarks came after he promoted Stephen Miller, a key architect of the administration’s hardline immigration policies, to the role of White House chief of staff. Last year, Miller said the White House was exploring ways to expand its legal power to deport undocumented migrants, including by suspending habeas corpus.

Supreme Court to Review Mandatory Detention Policy

The U.S. Supreme Court in October said it would review a Trump administration policy denying bond hearings for certain immigrants. Floyd, a former immigration judge, has advocated for prohibiting immigration courts from granting bond to detainees.

The justices will consider whether immigrants accused of entering the country illegally must remain in government custody throughout their cases or if they are entitled to bond hearings before an immigration judge.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told Newsweek at the time that the agency is "glad that the Supreme Court will hear arguments regarding mandatory detention and opinions from the Board of Immigration Appeals and multiple federal courts of appeals that reflect the soundness of the Department's legal position."

The plaintiffs are immigrants represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU).

Michael K.T. Tan, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants' Rights Project, said courts "have repeatedly and resoundingly rejected the Trump administration's radical misinterpretation of the law."

"Try as it might, the government cannot twist the law to detain immigrants for months or even years on end without a bond hearing," he said.

Most federal appeals courts have concluded that prolonged detention without bond hearings violates federal law, while the Fifth and Eighth Circuits have sided with the administration and ruled that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the U.S. must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.

Oral arguments in the case are expected in late February or early March 2027, according to the ACLU. A decision would be expected before the court’s term concludes in the summer of next year.

text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. – Viral videos show ICE agents taking at least one person from a southwest Albuquerque construction site as another video showed agents at a bakery.

KOB 4 visited the southwest Albuquerque site near Coors and Sage after videos showed ICE agents going through homes still under construction.

Witnesses said nearly 10 ICE vehicles pulled into the neighborhood last week. They said some construction workers ran but agents caught them, while others went into homes being built and agents arrested them.

Anna Bencomo lives in the neighborhood and described what she saw.

“I was actually concerned for like the community safety, on both parts, on ICE’s part and on the illegal immigrants that are running from ice, I was concerned on both sides because what if there are kids in the neighborhood?” said Bencomo. “I just felt like it was, it was unsafe, luckily I stay home from work but even people in the surrounding area could have been affected by the recklessness, like there was reckless driving on both parts” said Anna Bencomo.

KOB 4 also asked the Department of Homeland Security for more details about that raid and another at El Dorado Bakery in Albuquerque. The department has not responded yet.

On 60 Minutes, President Trump said he wanted to work with Democrats on immigration and said he believed his policies may have been too tough. It remains undetermined what that may mean for raids in New Mexico.

In Santa Fe, immigrants’ rights attorneys told the state Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee last week that local law enforcement agencies hand certain suspects over to ICE.

They said state law bars formal agreements between law enforcement agencies and ICE but does not block informal work between agencies.

“It does not bar informal arrangements, it does not bar local, city or county police in any city or county in New Mexico from informally calling ICE, there is no law that prohibits that” said Teague González of the New Mexico Immigrant Law Center.

The attorneys are pushing for statewide policies for how local agencies should work with the federal government.

Rep. John Block, R-N.M., raised questions about what any new policy would mean for local police.

“Let’s just say somebody who has multiple DWI convictions for example and they’re arrested for like something such as aggravated battery or something, would this prohibit local law enforcement whether it be state, county sheriff, city police, from releasing information to ICE and what… what would that look like?” said Rep. John Block.

The attorneys said there were 20 ICE arrests statewide in July 2024. They said there were more than 700 this past July.

SCARBOROUGH, Maine (WGME) -- An increased presence of ICE agents was reported at a facility in Scarborough on Monday as armed protesters gathered outside the building.

The video also shows an "Abolish ICE" sign and a person wearing fatigues with the words "NOT A COP" written on the back.

According to Congresswoman Chellie Pingree, ICE says the armed protesters are the reason additional agents have been deployed to the facility.

However, Pingree criticized the increased ICE presence, arguing it will make Maine less safe.

"Their presence has left people scared to leave their homes, scared to send their kids to school, scared to go to work, and scared to go about their daily lives. The impacts — on families, on our communities, on businesses, on our economy — have been devastating," Pingree said.
